  • Computer Programming

    • Learn to design, trace, debug and justify small programs.
      • C++17 is the default for valid C++ examples; Java-specific behavior is labeled.
      • The official blueprint allocates six items.
    • Trace a small state table before looking at output choices.
      • Check types, precedence, side effects, control flow and bounds in that order.
    • Write one function, one array traversal and one loop correctness argument from memory; test boundaries and invalid inputs.
    • Use comparisons for revision, but derive answers from rules; malformed questions are explicitly qualified in the reference index.
    • Sections in this course
      Turn a problem into a programAlgorithm properties and paradigmsLanguage levels, generations and portabilityCompilation, linking, loading and Java translationIdentifiers, keywords and commentsDeclarations, initialization, constants and typesLiterals, conversions and sizeofArithmetic and compound updatesPrefix, postfix and evaluation safetyBoolean, relational, bitwise and short-circuit logicConditional and comma expressionsTrace decisions and recognize flowchartsSwitch selection and fall-throughWhile, do-while and for mechanicsBreak, continue, return and gotoCount iterations and diagnose nonterminationFunctions, parameters and reusable modulesValue, reference and pointer parametersOverloads, default arguments and inlineScope, lifetime and persistent static localsRecursion, base cases and call tracingArrays and boundsArray algorithms and two-dimensional indexingC strings and C++ string objectsPointers, dereferencing and assignmentScaled pointer arithmetic and dynamic allocationStructures and member accessConsole input, output and headersFile streams, modes and safe readingMathematical functions and iterative powersCorrectness by logic, invariants and inductionDebugging, errors, exceptions and maintenanceStatic typing and Java-specific detailsRepairing malformed questions without inventing answersQuestion wording and option defects

    • CP01 Turn a problem into a program

      • Identify inputs, outputs, legal ranges and edge cases before coding.
        • Solve one small case manually, choose an algorithm, express it as pseudocode or a flowchart, implement, test and maintain.
        • For the largest of three numbers, initialize best to the first input, compare the second and third, then report best.
        • Initializing best to zero fails when all inputs are negative.
      • Programming includes writing, testing, debugging and maintaining instructions.
        • A program can execute without solving its intended problem; compare its actual result with the required result.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP02 Algorithm properties and paradigms

      • An algorithm gives precise, executable steps and terminates for every legal input.
        • Definiteness means each step has an unambiguous meaning; effectiveness means a step can actually be performed.
        • Inputs may be absent, but a useful algorithm specifies a result.
        • Correctness means the result meets the specification.
        • Efficiency is desirable and measurable, but an inefficient terminating algorithm is still an algorithm.
        • The module sometimes lists efficiency among its desirable properties.
      • Procedural programming organizes operations in procedures; structured programming combines sequence, selection and iteration; object oriented programming organizes state and behavior in objects; functional programming emphasizes function evaluation.
        • A conditional statement is a construct, not a separate programming paradigm.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP03 Language levels, generations and portability

      • Machine instructions are conventionally first generation; symbolic assembly is second; general high-level languages such as C++ and Java are third.
        • Database query and application generators such as SQL are conventionally fourth generation.
        • Fifth generation is a loose historical category associated with declarative logic, constraints and AI/expert systems.
        • Generations do not determine whether an implementation uses an interpreter.
      • Machine and assembly code depend on an instruction set.
        • High-level source is easier to read and often portable after recompilation, provided it avoids platform assumptions.
        • People can write both assembly and high-level programs.
        • Python, Perl and PHP are commonly called scripting languages; C++ is conventionally compiled.
        • These labels describe common use, not an absolute technical prohibition.
      • References: CP-M, CP-U

    • CP04 Compilation, linking, loading and Java translation

      • In the conventional C++ toolchain: source → preprocessing → compilation proper → assembly → object files → linking → executable → loading → execution.
        • Preprocessing handles directives such as #include; compilation may emit assembly; the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file.
        • The linker resolves external symbols and combines object files and libraries.
        • The loader places an executable and required components in memory and starts it.
      • GCC documents the first four stages explicitly.
        • A compiler need not emit a complete executable or even native machine code.
        • Java javac produces bytecode, which a JVM interprets or compiles at runtime.
        • Interpreters execute a program representation; “one source line at a time” is a beginner approximation.
        • Compilation uses multiple passes, so “whole program in one step” is not literally universal.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N, CP-C

    • CP05 Identifiers, keywords and comments

      • In the basic ASCII identifier rules, start with a letter or underscore; continue with letters, digits or underscores.
        • Do not use a keyword.
        • C++ is case sensitive: exitExam and ExitExam differ; delete and float are keywords, but FLOAT is a legal identifier. variable_1234 is valid; 4thInput, T-3 and names containing spaces are not single identifiers.
        • Avoid reserved underscore patterns in application code.
      • Comments use // to the line end or /* ... */ for a block.
        • They explain intent and assumptions for maintenance; ordinary comments do not execute or automatically improve speed, reliability or portability. main is the conventional entry function name, not a C++ keyword.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP06 Declarations, initialization, constants and types

      • Write type name; or type name = value; for ordinary variables: int age = 20;.
        • Declaration introduces a name and type; initialization gives its initial value; later assignment replaces a value. a=b copies a scalar value, so later changes to b do not change a. A pointer or Java object reference instead copies an address/reference.
      • Use int for whole numbers, float/double for fractional approximations, char for a character and bool for logical values in C++.
        • Type sizes depend on the implementation; do not import Java widths into C++. short n, short int n and int short n denote the same signed short type. const int n=5 and int const n=5 are equivalent; an ordinary const int needs initialization. typedef creates an alias, not a distinct new type.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP07 Literals, conversions and sizeof

      • Single quotes denote a character literal, such as 'A'; double quotes denote a string literal, such as "A".
        • A string includes more storage than just its visible characters when a terminator is required. sizeof reports size in bytes, with sizeof(char)==1; the byte width and other sizes are implementation dependent. sizeof(array) gives total array storage before conversion to a pointer.
      • With int x=5,y=2, x/y is 2.
        • Assigning that quotient to double gives 2.0, not 2.5. static_cast<double>(x)/y performs floating division and yields 2.5.
        • Converting an in-range fractional floating value to int truncates toward zero.
        • Cast before the operation if a fractional result is needed.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP08 Arithmetic and compound updates

      • Multiplication, division and remainder have higher precedence than addition and subtraction; equal-precedence arithmetic groups left to right.
        • Integer division truncates toward zero.
        • For integers, a == (a/b)*b + a%b when the division is valid. % requires integral operands in C++; (8.0*3)%5 is invalid.
        • Division by zero and signed integer overflow cannot be given ordinary numeric outputs.
      • x+=y, x-=y, x*=y, x/=y and x%=y update x using the operation and conversion to its type.
        • For simple variables, trace them as x=x op y. Starting p=q=n=8, p+=n gives 16 and p/=q gives 2.
        • Starting x=10, x+=5 then x/=2 gives 7. x=x+x doubles; it does not generally add one.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP09 Prefix, postfix and evaluation safety

      • Prefix ++x changes x and yields the new value; postfix x++ yields the previous value and also increments x. Separate the value used in the expression from the stored value after it.
        • Starting a=8,b=5, a++ + --b uses 8+4, gives 12, and leaves a=9,b=4.
        • Starting x=1,y=10,z=-3, (x++*y--)+ ++z gives 8 and leaves x=2,y=9,z=-2.
      • Precedence determines grouping, not a universal evaluation order.
        • Avoid expressions that modify a variable multiple times without sequencing.
        • In C++17 and later, chained operator-form stream insertions are sequenced left to right: with x=5, cout<<x++<<" "<<++x prints 5 7.
        • Before C++17 this expression has undefined behavior.
        • None of the bank options 5 6, 5 5, 6 5, 6 6 is a correct C++17 answer.
      • References: CP-M, CP-E

    • CP10 Boolean, relational, bitwise and short-circuit logic

      • Relational and equality operators test values; && and || combine truth values; ! negates.
        • In C++, zero converts to false and a nonzero number to true.
        • Streams display bool as 0 or 1 unless boolalpha is set.
        • With a=3,b=5, cout<<(a==b) prints 0.
      • && evaluates its right operand only if the left is true; || only if the left is false.
        • Thus false && dangerousCall() skips the call.
        • Bitwise & operates on bits and does not short circuit.
        • With x=1,y=0,z=4, (x&y)||++z evaluates ++z, leaving z=5 and the Boolean result 1.
        • The precedence ladder is grouping/postfix, unary, multiplicative, additive, shifts, relations, equality, bitwise &, ^, |, &&, ||, conditional, assignment, comma.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP11 Conditional and comma expressions

      • condition ? yes : no evaluates the condition and exactly one alternative.
        • The comma operator evaluates its left expression, then its right, and yields the right value.
        • Do not confuse it with commas separating function arguments.
      • For a=6,b=8,x=2,y=4, c=(x>y ? (a--,x) : (b--,y)) takes the false branch. b becomes 7, c receives 4 and a remains 6.
        • Both alternatives are not executed.
        • A semicolon in place of the internal comma is invalid syntax; restoring it must be stated as an interpretation.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP12 Trace decisions and recognize flowcharts

      • A standalone if may execute independently of the following if.
        • An else binds to its nearest unmatched if; an else-if ladder executes the first true branch only.
        • In nested if(c1){if(c2) S1; else S2;}, S2 requires c1 true and c2 false.
        • Braces determine grouping.
      • With ph=15.3, an invalid-range if can print its warning, and a separate classification ladder can also print Alkaline.
        • They are not mutually exclusive unless linked by else or an early return.
        • A flowchart decision is a diamond, processing a rectangle, input/output a parallelogram and start/end a terminator.
        • A pre-test loop checks before its body; a post-test loop checks after.
        • Without the actual arrows and condition placement, a missing flowchart cannot identify a particular loop.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N, CP-D

    • CP13 Switch selection and fall-through

      • A traditional C++ switch selects using an integral or enumeration value. case labels are constant expressions.
        • Execution starts at the matching label, then continues through subsequent statements until a break, return or the end. default handles an unmatched value but need not be the last physical label.
      • If case 2 prints Bus. and case 3 prints Truck. before the first break, input 2 prints Bus.Truck.
        • A break exits the nearest switch or loop; it does not by itself terminate the entire program.
        • A case label is an entry point, not an automatically isolated if branch.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP14 While, do-while and for mechanics

      • while(condition) checks before each body execution and may run zero times. do {body;} while(condition); runs the body once before checking; it repeats while the condition remains true.
        • Use it when a menu or input attempt must occur at least once.
      • for(initialization; condition; update) executes initialization once, then condition → body → update → condition.
        • A missing condition in for(;;) acts as true.
        • A for loop is convenient for a known count but can also be condition controlled.
        • To print indices 0 through n-1, use i=0; i<n; ++i. Starting i=0 with i<5 and i+=2 prints 0 2 4.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP15 Break, continue, return and goto

      • break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch. continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration: a for loop then runs its update; a while loop goes directly to its condition. return leaves the current function and may supply a result.
        • In main it ends the program normally.
      • A goto transfers to a label within its function; follow the label reached rather than reading lines in source order.
        • In the bank sequence a: print Graduating; goto b; c: print Year; goto a; b: print fourth;, entry at a prints Graduating fourth and reaches the end.
        • Year is not printed.
        • Structured alternatives usually make such logic easier to reason about.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP16 Count iterations and diagnose nontermination

      • Make a table with condition inputs, body output and updated values.
        • For i=0,j=8; i<j; i++,j--, body entries are (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(3,5).
        • If odd i triggers continue, printing occurs twice.
        • With outer i=1; i<5; i+=5, the outer loop runs once; an inner j=10; j>i; --j prints nine times.
      • For n=1; n<=18; n+=2, print n unless n%7==0 then break: output is 1 3 5.
        • A while(a>b) with fixed a=6,b=5 never changes its true condition.
        • In data[10]={5,10,...,50}, i=0, advancing i only if data[i]%10==0 causes no progress because data[0]=5.
        • It prints nothing and loops indefinitely; changing <=10 to <10 alone does not repair progress.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP17 Functions, parameters and reusable modules

      • A function groups a named task.
        • C++ definition: int add(int a,int b){return a+b;}.
        • Call it with add(x,y);, without parameter type declarations at the call site.
        • Parameters are names in the definition; arguments are supplied expressions or values.
        • A void function produces no return value but can have side effects and return; to exit early.
      • A method is a function associated with a class or object; methods can return values.
        • Modules group related responsibilities behind interfaces.
        • Reuse reduces duplication; independent functions are easier to understand and test.
        • A library provides reusable components; a framework also supplies an organizing structure and often calls application callbacks.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP18 Value, reference and pointer parameters

      • A C++ value parameter is a separate object initialized from the argument.
        • In func(int a,int b){a*=5;b+=5;return a+b;}, calling func(9,3) returns 53 and leaves the caller values 9 and 3 unchanged.
      • An int& parameter aliases the caller variable, so swap(int& a,int& b) changes both originals.
        • An int* parameter copies an address; *p=value changes the pointed-to object, but p=anotherAddress only changes the local pointer.
        • An array parameter int a[] is adjusted to int*: elements can change, and the length must be passed separately.
        • Java always passes by value, including a copy of an object reference; it does not pass caller variables by reference.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP19 Overloads, default arguments and inline

      • Overloads share a name but differ in parameter count or types/order.
        • Return type alone cannot distinguish them.
        • Choose a candidate using argument types, then required conversions; report ambiguity if there is no unique best match. int sum(int x,int y,int z=0) allows two or three arguments; defaults occupy trailing positions in ordinary declarations.
      • inline does not compel the compiler to copy a function body at a call.
        • Small frequently used functions may be good optimization candidates, but actual expansion is the optimizer’s decision.
        • Inline also has language linkage/definition rules, so it is not simply a speed command.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP20 Scope, lifetime and persistent static locals

      • Scope is where a name can be used; lifetime is when its object exists.
        • A local name is restricted to its block; an outer name may be shadowed.
        • A namespace/global variable is available where its declaration is visible, not magically in every file.
        • C++ ::name selects a global name hidden by a local one.
      • An automatic local is created anew on entry.
        • A static local is initialized once and retains its value across calls even though its name remains local.
        • If static x=0 changes by +1 when even and +2 otherwise, five calls return 1,3,5,7,9, whose sum is 25.
        • Namespace/static storage integers are zero initialized; an ordinary uninitialized local int has no usable assumed zero value.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP21 Recursion, base cases and call tracing

      • A recursive function calls itself directly or indirectly.
        • It needs a base case and progress toward it for all supported inputs. factorial(0)=1 and factorial(n)=n*factorial(n-1) for positive n. factorial(3) expands to 3*2*1*1=6.
        • Negative inputs require rejection or a separate definition; they do not reach zero under n-1.
      • Evaluate conditions before expanding a recursive call.
        • For if(n<m) return 0;, f(1,4) returns immediately; unreachable recursive branches add nothing.
        • Record each call’s local parameters and pending operation, then unwind returned values.
        • Recursion commonly uses smaller instances, but merely having a base-case branch does not prove it will be reached.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP22 Arrays and bounds

      • A built-in C++ array has a fixed number of same-type elements in contiguous storage: int a[4]={10,20,30,40};.
        • Valid indices are 0 through 3. a[4] is outside the array; accessing it has undefined behavior.
        • Java checks bounds and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
        • Do not predict a C++ out-of-range value from nearby memory.
      • A standard built-in array bound must be a compile-time constant; variable-length local arrays are compiler extensions. int a[5]={1,2,3}; fills the remaining elements with zeros.
        • An uninitialized automatic array of int is different. a[i] equals *(a+i), so elements can be accessed using pointer notation without explicitly writing brackets.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP23 Array algorithms and two-dimensional indexing

      • For a sum, start total=0 and add each element once.
        • For a maximum/minimum, initialize from a[0] only after confirming the array is nonempty.
        • For 50 inputs where nonpositive values are skipped, use a count-controlled loop and either if(x>0) total+=x; or continue for x<=0.
        • These constructs solve different parts of the task.
      • int a[R][C] has R rows, each with C elements. a[r][c] uses zero-based row then column.
        • Its element offset is r*C+c in row-major storage.
        • For the bank 4x4 matrix, a[1][1]=6, a[2][3]=6 and a[3][3]=2.
        • In Java, length belongs to each array; a traversal ending at arr.length-2 visits fewer elements than a full traversal.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP24 C strings and C++ string objects

      • A C string is a character array ending in '\0'. "Hello" needs six char positions; strlen counts five visible characters and excludes the terminator. sizeof a fixed char array reports its allocated bytes, which can exceed strlen+1. cout<<a prints a terminated char sequence, not its numeric address.
      • <cstring> supplies strcpy(destination,source), strcat(destination,source), strlen and strcmp.
        • Supply enough destination capacity; strcmp returns zero for equal content, otherwise a sign, not necessarily exactly -1 or 1.
        • C++ std::string in <string> owns resizable text; + concatenates, == compares content, size()/length() counts stored characters and substr(start,count) extracts a segment.
        • Standard std::string has no Java-style toUpperCase() or trim() member.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP25 Pointers, dereferencing and assignment

      • int x=10; int* p=&x; stores x’s address in p. *p reads or writes x; &p is the address of the pointer variable itself.
        • With p=&a,q=&b, p=q redirects p to b and leaves a and b unchanged.
        • By contrast *p=*q copies the pointed-to value.
        • Never dereference an uninitialized, null or dangling pointer.
      • An array expression commonly converts to a pointer to its first element, but the array is not itself an assignable pointer variable.
        • A pointer-to-pointer int** pp=&p allows **pp to reach x. A void* can hold an object address but requires conversion to a suitable object pointer before dereferencing in C++.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP26 Scaled pointer arithmetic and dynamic allocation

      • If p points inside an array, p+k advances k elements, or k*sizeof(*p) bytes.
        • Under the explicit assumption sizeof(float)==4 and first address 7000, p+3 has numeric address 7012. cout<<p++ displays the old address then advances p; cout<<*p++ displays the old element then advances p. ++*p changes the element.
        • Pointer addition p+q is invalid; subtracting pointers within the same array gives an element distance.
      • Arithmetic must stay within an array or its one-past position; one-past may not be dereferenced.
        • C++ new T creates a dynamic object, delete releases it; new T[n] pairs with delete[].
        • Prefer resource-owning standard containers in real programs.
        • Allocation does not automatically initialize every primitive value unless initialization is requested.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP27 Structures and member access

      • A struct groups named members, possibly of different types. struct House{double price; int rooms;}; defines a type; House h{150000,3}; creates an object. h.rooms uses a dot.
        • House* p=&h; p->rooms is equivalent to (*p).rooms.
        • The pointer must refer to a live object before member access.
        • A type definition alone does not create an ordinary instance.
      • Aggregate initialization assigns members in declaration order.
        • Modern C++ permits default member initializers such as int rooms=3;.
        • C++11 list initialization rejects narrowing; a constant floating value exactly representable in the target floating type can be permitted, so 25.00 to float is not necessarily narrowing.
        • Use 25.0f for clarity and check the language version.
        • Structures can be copied, passed and returned; a structure cannot contain a full instance of itself, but may contain a pointer to its own type.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP28 Console input, output and headers

      • Include <iostream> and qualify std::cin/std::cout or introduce the names explicitly. cout is the standard output stream; << inserts values. cin is standard input; >> extracts formatted values. std::endl inserts a newline and flushes.
        • C++ names must retain their case: Cout, Int and std: :cout are not equivalent valid spellings as printed.
      • Read a full line with getline(cin,text).
        • After formatted numeric extraction, consume the pending newline before a line read when required.
        • Input failure must be tested before trusting a value.
        • Console output formatting matters: by default a double storing an exact 4 may print 4 rather than 4.0.
        • Text, spaces and newlines are part of an output trace.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP29 File streams, modes and safe reading

      • Include <fstream>. ofstream writes, ifstream reads, and fstream can do both.
        • The constructor’s default ofstream mode argument is ios::out; its ordinary effect is to create/truncate the file.
        • Distinguish that signature from a choice describing effective out|trunc behavior. ios::app places each write at the end; ios::ate initially seeks to the end; ios::binary requests binary mode.
      • Check if(!file) after opening.
        • Read using while(file>>record) or while(getline(file,line)), because end-of-file is discovered by an attempted read. while(!file.eof()) can process an invalid extra record.
        • Close or rely on stream destruction to release the resource. “ofstream” is a class, whereas <fstream> is the header.
      • References: CP-M, CP-F

    • CP30 Mathematical functions and iterative powers

      • Use <cmath> for sqrt, pow, floor and ceil; integer abs is also provided by <cstdlib>. sqrt(16)=4; pow(3,4)=81; abs(-7)=7. ceil(x) is the least integer-valued result >=x; floor(x) the greatest <=x. Thus ceil(-2.7)=-2 and floor(-2.7)=-3; truncation toward zero differs from floor for negatives.
      • C++ has no built-in exponentiation operator: ^ is bitwise XOR and ** is not a power operator.
        • To compute b^e for a nonnegative integer e, start r=1 and repeat r*=b exactly e times; b=4,e=3 gives 64.
        • Large powers and factorials can overflow fixed-width types; specify a valid input range.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP31 Correctness by logic, invariants and induction

      • To prove an implication P⇒Q, a direct proof derives Q assuming P; a contrapositive proves not Q⇒not P; a contradiction assumes the claim false and derives an impossibility.
        • A single counterexample disproves a universal claim.
        • Induction proves a base case and proves P(k+1) assuming P(k).
      • For sum=0,i=1; while(i<=n){sum+=i;++i;}, use invariant sum=(i-1)*i/2.
        • It holds initially.
        • Adding i gives i*(i+1)/2, then incrementing i restores the invariant.
        • Exit gives i=n+1 and sum=n*(n+1)/2.
        • Termination needs a separate decreasing nonnegative measure n-i+1 while the guard holds.
        • Assume n>=0 and no arithmetic overflow.
        • This connects mathematical proof to actual code.
      • References: CP-P, CP-M

    • CP32 Debugging, errors, exceptions and maintenance

      • A syntax error violates grammar; a type error can be syntactically well formed but rejected during semantic checking.
        • A runtime error occurs during execution; a logic error gives the wrong behavior.
        • A bug is a defect; debugging locates and corrects it.
        • Read the first useful compiler diagnostic, inspect nearby tokens and declarations, repair and rebuild; a debugger is useful after a runnable program exists.
      • Test ordinary, boundary and invalid inputs and trace the first point where actual state differs from expected state.
        • Exceptions transfer control to a matching handler for exceptional conditions; they do not make arbitrary undefined behavior recoverable.
        • Refactoring improves internal structure while preserving observable behavior.
        • Version control records changes, supports comparison and rollback; documentation explains use, design and maintenance assumptions.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP33 Static typing and Java-specific details

      • Static typing checks types before execution; type inference can still infer a static type, as with C++ auto.
        • Dynamic typing checks operations using runtime values; it does not mean variables must have explicit static declarations.
        • The bank option claiming static typing always requires explicit type annotations is only an inaccurate approximation.
      • Java uses boolean, fixed-width numeric primitive types and references to objects.
        • Java String is immutable, substring(begin,end) uses an exclusive end, equals compares content and == compares references.
        • Java arrays have a length field.
        • Scanner nextInt() can leave a newline for nextLine().
        • C++ std::string is mutable and uses substr(start,count); the two APIs must not be merged.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP34 Repairing malformed questions without inventing answers

      • A program trace requires the complete code, and a diagram question requires its edges, conditions and labels.
        • The retained Q00102 diagram was visually checked: entry reaches the body rectangle before the decision diamond; a decision branch returns to the body.
        • It is a post-test do-while loop (B).
        • Distinguish a literal invalid program from a clearly labeled intended trace when an OCR correction is documented.
      • Q00074 has no fully correct pointer-member option as printed: Cout/Cin, C1 and car_mode do not match cout/cin, c1 and car_model.
        • Q00071’s offered full outputs incorrectly add Year.
        • Q00100’s option layout is corrupted; the intended trace yields z=5 then a=1.
        • Q00998 prints Z although only z is declared.
        • Q00103 needs <@ clarified to <0; Q00104 needs standard int main().
        • NS0301 needs Int/Cout case, quotes and comma-expression punctuation repaired.
        • No unique literal output should be invented.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

    • CP35 Question wording and option defects

      • Some banks ask for one answer when multiple or no options are defensible.
        • Q00051 mixes linking with loading.
        • Q00336 overlaps binary/machine/executable terminology.
        • Q00668 has both a correct member claim and a correct possible-initialization claim.
        • Q00989 repeats equivalent short declarations.
        • Q01577 depends on the C++ version and narrowing rules.
        • SM0030 ignores equivalent pointer access.
      • AM0260 omits a fully accurate static-typing definition.
        • AM0266 gives no ordinary int x; style declaration.
        • AM0270’s void definition is complete, while int myFunction(){} can compile but reaching its end is undefined behavior.
        • AM0272/AM0277 omit the correct meaning of break.
        • AM0280 offers two const spellings without required initialization.
        • SS167 mixes counting with skipping; SM0276 confuses loop termination with iteration termination.
        • CS0092 says final step while its useful option describes inspection; rebuilding and retesting complete the repair.
      • References: CP-M, CP-N

  • Fundamental of Database Systems

    • Design a correct schema from explicit business rules, then use constraints, dependency tests and queries to justify it.
      • This chapter addresses all three official design outcomes and the additional concepts encountered in the question banks.
    • Work in order: requirements → ER/EER → relational mapping → keys/FDs → normalization → SQL and physical choices.
    • Practice drawing and constructing the registration/dormitory schema without looking; explain why every key and reference exists.
    • For each MCQ, check literal syntax, assumptions and overlapping choices; do not memorize a weak supplied key.
    • Recalculate closure, product counts, join preservation and group filters; compare similar terms through concrete examples.
    • Sections in this course
      Database approach, benefits and costsData models and product namesRelations, schemas, instances and metadataThree-schema architecture and data independenceRequirements through implementationEntities, attributes and ER notationSuperkeys, candidate keys and primary keysWeak entities and identifying relationshipsCardinality, participation and directionMap entities, composite and multivalued attributesMap 1:1 and 1:N relationshipsMap M:N, recursive and n-ary relationshipsEER inheritance and category constraintsFan traps and chasm trapsIntegrity and constraint taxonomyWrite and enforce SQL constraintsFunctional dependencies and attribute closureFind all keys before deciding normal formInsertion, deletion and update anomaliesFirst and second normal formsThird normal form, BCNF and higher formsDecomposition: lossless and dependency preservingChoose data types and storage levelsRecords, pages and primary file organizationOrdered, dense, sparse and multilevel indexesSQL command categories and exact scopeSELECT and its result columnsPredicates, strings and NULLINSERT, UPDATE and DELETECREATE and ALTER tablesJoin behavior and preservationAggregation, GROUP BY and HAVINGSubqueries and viewsSet operations and type conversion in SQLRelational algebra: calculate resultsRelational calculus: state the desired factsTransactions and the ACID propertiesChoose a design technique from the requirementIntegrated design: student registration and dormitory allocationResolve malformed and overlapping questions

    • FDB01 Database approach, benefits and costs

      • A database is a coherent collection of related facts with meaning for an application.
        • A DBMS is software that defines, stores, retrieves, updates, protects and shares that data.
        • The database is the content; the DBMS manages it.
        • A database system also includes applications, people and infrastructure.
      • Traditional file applications define their own formats and access procedures.
        • Separate files can repeat facts, disagree after updates, isolate useful data and make shared integrity or concurrent updates difficult.
        • A DBMS centralizes metadata and supports multiple views, authorization, transactions, backup and recovery.
        • It controls redundancy rather than guaranteeing zero duplication.
        • Complexity, administration, storage and licensing can outweigh benefits for a tiny fixed application; lightweight embedded DBMSs also exist.
        • Concurrent access itself is useful; uncontrolled concurrent access causes anomalies.
      • The DBA manages access authorization, backup/recovery, availability, monitoring, tuning and routine maintenance, coordinating database use; designers define the schema and application developers build user-facing programs.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB02 Data models and product names

      • A data model supplies concepts for structure, relationships, constraints and operations.
        • Conceptual ER models describe entities and relationships.
        • Relational models use tables; hierarchical models organize records in a parent–child tree; classic network models connect records through pointer-based owner/member links, allowing multiple parents.
        • Object models represent objects with identity, state and behavior.
        • A physical model specifies record layouts and access paths.
        • These are different representation choices, not stages of one query.
      • PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and IBM Db2 are relational DBMS products.
        • MongoDB is a document DBMS.
        • Java is a programming language.
        • IBM alone names a vendor, not a database product.
        • A question offering IBM as a system needs a product name.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-NOTE

    • FDB03 Relations, schemas, instances and metadata

      • A relation is a set of tuples, represented as a table.
        • A tuple/row/record contains related attribute values; an attribute/column/field describes a property.
        • Degree counts columns; cardinality counts rows.
        • Classical relations have distinct tuples, atomic cells and domains for attributes; row order has no meaning.
        • Column order has no logical meaning when attributes are identified by name.
        • SQL tables can contain duplicate rows unless constrained.
      • A schema describes names, structures and constraints; an instance, state or snapshot is the data at a particular time.
        • Inserting a student changes the state, while adding a column changes the schema.
        • Metadata is data describing data.
        • The catalog or data dictionary records table definitions, types, constraints and often access privileges and optimizer statistics.
        • A schema diagram draws tables and key references; labels such as database diagram can overlap.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB04 Three-schema architecture and data independence

      • The external level gives each user group a selected view.
        • The conceptual level describes the whole logical database: entity types, relationships, data types and constraints.
        • The internal/physical level describes files, record placement and access paths.
        • These are abstraction levels, distinct from client/server deployment tiers.
      • Physical data independence permits changing internal storage without changing the conceptual schema, for example adding an index.
        • Logical data independence permits conceptual changes while preserving affected external views and application interfaces, for example splitting a table while maintaining a compatible view.
        • It is harder because applications depend on logical meaning.
        • Data abstraction hides irrelevant details; program–data insulation separates data definitions from application code.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB05 Requirements through implementation

      • First collect business facts, required transactions, reports, volumes, privacy rules and quality targets.
        • Conceptual design turns them into an ER/EER model.
        • Logical design maps the conceptual model to relations, keys and constraints and checks normalization.
        • Physical design chooses file organization, indexes and storage.
        • Implementation creates and loads the actual objects; testing checks requirements.
      • Logical relational design is tied to a data model but can remain independent of a particular DBMS.
        • Vendor-specific implementation details may be introduced during later refinement.
        • Therefore a question calling logical design either universally DBMS-dependent or universally independent needs its methodology stated.
        • Conceptual design usually proceeds from a whole enterprise view downward; normalization can refine structures from dependencies upward.
        • These are useful approaches rather than mandatory directions for every modeling activity.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB06 Entities, attributes and ER notation

      • An entity is a distinguishable real or conceptual thing, such as one student or one course.
        • An entity type describes common properties; its current collection of entities is an entity set.
        • A relationship associates entities.
        • In Chen notation rectangles represent entity types, diamonds relationships and ellipses attributes; double ellipses denote multivalued attributes and dashed ellipses derived attributes.
        • Always inspect the diagram legend.
      • Simple versus composite asks whether a value has meaningful components: Address may split into City and Street.
        • Single-valued versus multivalued asks how many values one entity may have: a student may have several phone numbers.
        • These dimensions differ: one address may be composite and single-valued.
        • Age derived from birth date is derived, even if also single-valued.
        • Attribute names alone do not establish multiplicity.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB07 Superkeys, candidate keys and primary keys

      • A superkey uniquely identifies a tuple.
        • A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any component loses uniqueness.
        • Minimal means no unnecessary attribute, not necessarily the fewest columns among all keys.
        • A primary key is one selected candidate key; remaining candidates are alternate keys.
        • A composite key contains multiple attributes and need not be the chosen primary key.
      • If ID is unique, both {ID} and {ID,City} are superkeys, but only {ID} is minimal.
        • A table can have several candidates and foreign keys but at most one declared primary-key constraint, possibly containing several columns.
        • String columns can be keys.
        • Prefer stable, compact identifiers when practical, but Email, SSN or EmployeeID is a candidate only if business rules guarantee uniqueness.
        • Four single-column choices do not supply a composite-key example.
      • Worked example
        • Given candidate keys CustID, Email and ContactNo, all are eligible primary keys. CustID is preferable only with an explicit stability/size policy; uniqueness alone does not choose it.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB08 Weak entities and identifying relationships

      • A weak entity lacks a complete independent key.
        • Its owner is normally a strong entity, so owner entity set and strong entity set may both describe the associated set.
        • Its partial key, also called discriminator, distinguishes weak entities of the same owner.
        • Identification combines the owner key and partial key.
      • For Dependent(EmployeeID,DependentName,BirthDate), suppose names are unique only within one employee's dependents.
        • Then (EmployeeID,DependentName) is the key, and EmployeeID is a foreign key.
        • The weak entity participates totally in its identifying relationship.
        • Chen notation uses a double rectangle, double identifying diamond and dashed underline for a partial key.
        • A weak entity is not merely any table with a foreign key.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB09 Cardinality, participation and direction

      • Cardinality specifies maximum associated occurrences: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. Minimum cardinality specifies optional/partial participation (zero permitted) or mandatory/total participation (at least one).
        • A maximum of one does not mean participation is compulsory.
        • Relationship degree counts participating entity roles: unary recursive, binary or ternary.
      • Read business rules in both directions.
        • If each employee belongs to one department and each department has many employees, Employee→Department is N:1; Department→Employee is 1:N. Building→Location could also be N:1, so names alone cannot select a unique example.
        • Under the common arrow convention, arrows from advisor to both Instructor and Student impose maximum-one at both ends, giving 1:1.
        • Without a notation convention, arrows are unsafe evidence.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB10 Map entities, composite and multivalued attributes

      • Create one relation per strong entity type, preserve its simple attributes and select a candidate key.
        • Expand composite attributes into their useful simple components; do not copy a composite ER structure unchanged into a flat atomic design.
        • Derived values can usually be calculated, avoiding stale stored copies.
      • Map each multivalued attribute to a separate relation containing the owner key and one value.
        • StudentPhone(StudentID,Phone) has primary key (StudentID,Phone) and a foreign key to Student.
        • Store separate rows for two phone numbers, not a comma-separated list or repeated Phone1/Phone2 columns.
        • This explicitly supplies the mapping step omitted from the brief module.
        • Table names may follow entity names; naming does not invalidate a mapping.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-ER

    • FDB11 Map 1:1 and 1:N relationships

      • For 1:N, place the one-side key as a foreign key in the many-side table; store relationship attributes there.
        • Department(DeptID) and Employee(EmpID,DeptID,HireDate) implement many employees per department.
        • If participation is total, make the reference NOT NULL.
        • If partial, a nullable reference can represent no assignment.
      • For 1:1, one side may hold the other key with a UNIQUE constraint.
        • Prefer the totally participating side to reduce NULLs; NOT NULL enforces that side's mandatory reference.
        • Merging entities is reasonable only when their lifecycle and participation rules permit it.
        • For A→B many-to-one, A can absorb the relationship reference under either total or partial participation; requiring total participation as the only possible case overstates the rule.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB12 Map M:N, recursive and n-ary relationships

      • A binary M:N relationship needs an association table in addition to the two entity tables.
        • Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade) references Student and Course; (StudentID,CourseID) is a key if one enrollment per pair is allowed.
        • Repeated attempts require Term or AttemptNo in the key.
        • This ordinarily produces three tables.
      • A recursive M:N friendship uses UserLink(UserID,OtherUserID), two foreign keys to User; decide whether links are directed and whether self-links are allowed.
        • A recursive 1:N supervision uses a nullable SupervisorID reference in Employee.
        • For a ternary Supply(SupplierID,PartID,ProjectID,Quantity), preserve all participating references; binary replacements can lose which triple occurred.
        • Choose the association key from actual cardinalities rather than automatically assuming every reference is necessary.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-ER

    • FDB13 EER inheritance and category constraints

      • EER extends ER with superclass/subclass structure.
        • A subclass inherits the superclass attributes and relationships.
        • Specialization divides Student into Undergraduate and Graduate; generalization combines common properties into Student.
        • Disjoint subclasses cannot overlap; overlapping subclasses can.
        • Total specialization requires every superclass member in some subclass; partial specialization does not.
      • Map Person(PersonID,Name) and Student(PersonID,Program) with Student.PersonID both primary key and foreign key to Person.
        • This preserves inherited identity.
        • A category/union subclass draws members from a union of different superclasses, such as Owner drawn from Person or Company; it differs from an intersection subclass requiring membership in both.
        • Object models also support inheritance, so a question offering ER and object modeling must specify whether ER includes EER.
        • Structural EER inheritance alone does not define executable object methods.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB14 Fan traps and chasm traps

      • A fan trap occurs when two 1:N relationships fan from a common entity and a path suggests an association it cannot determine.
        • Department→Employee and Department→Project do not reveal which employee works on which project; joining through Department pairs every employee with every project in that department.
        • Record WorksOn explicitly when that is the fact needed.
      • A chasm trap occurs when an apparently useful path fails for some occurrences because an optional relationship breaks it.
        • For example, a branch's property may be lost from a path that requires an assigned staff member when some properties have none.
        • Add the required direct relationship or revise the model.
        • Multiple 1:N relationships are legitimate; eliminating all fans is not a universal repair.
        • A missing path describes a chasm, not the defining ambiguity of a fan.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-FAN

    • FDB15 Integrity and constraint taxonomy

      • Domain integrity restricts type and allowed values.
        • Key integrity enforces uniqueness.
        • Entity integrity requires every primary-key component to be non-NULL.
        • Referential integrity requires a non-NULL foreign-key value to match an eligible referenced unique/candidate key; self-references are allowed.
        • A parent need not have a child.
      • Inherent constraints come from the data model; schema-based constraints are declared through the DDL; semantic/application rules may need triggers or application logic when DDL cannot express them.
        • Integrity improves data validity; authorization controls who may access it.
        • Uniqueness and domain validation are both integrity mechanisms.
        • If a Department primary key is NULL and Manager=107 lacks a referenced employee, entity integrity certainly fails and referential integrity also fails if that foreign key is declared.
        • One INSERT can violate multiple constraints.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB16 Write and enforce SQL constraints

      • Example: CREATE TABLE Enrollment (StudentID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(StudentID), CourseID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Course(CourseID), Grade INTEGER CHECK (Grade BETWEEN 0 AND 100), PRIMARY KEY (StudentID,CourseID)); Each column declaration gives its name then type, with commas between declarations.
        • CHECK is a constraint clause, not a standalone GRANT-like statement.
        • POSITIVE is not a general SQL constraint keyword; CHECK (Amount > 0) expresses positivity.
      • PRIMARY KEY implies uniqueness and non-NULL.
        • UNIQUE does not generally imply NOT NULL; NULL treatment differs by DBMS.
        • A CHECK can pass when its result is unknown, so add NOT NULL if missing values must be forbidden.
        • Parent updates/deletes may use NO ACTION/RESTRICT, CASCADE or SET NULL.
        • A referenced key is not inherently unchangeable: legality depends on matching children and the declared action.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-CONSTRAINT

    • FDB17 Functional dependencies and attribute closure

      • X→Y means every legal pair of tuples agreeing on X also agrees on Y. It is a business constraint, not a correlation observed in one sample.
        • Full dependency requires all determinant attributes; partial dependency holds through a proper subset.
        • A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key; a nonprime attribute belongs to none.
      • To compute X+, start with X and repeatedly add the right-hand side of any dependency whose left side is already present.
        • Stop when nothing changes.
        • X is a superkey exactly when X+ contains the whole relation.
        • Remove attributes and recompute to test minimality.
        • Reflexivity gives X→Y when Y⊆X; augmentation permits XZ→YZ from X→Y; transitivity derives X→Z from X→Y and Y→Z.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB18 Find all keys before deciding normal form

      • For R(A,B,C,D), let C→D, C→B and B→C. A never appears on a right-hand side, so every key needs A. (AB)+ gives ABCD through B→C→D; (AC)+ also gives ABCD.
        • AB and AC are minimal keys.
        • BC cannot derive A and is not a key.
        • A, B and C are prime; D is nonprime.
      • D depends on C alone and also on B through transitivity, proper subsets of those keys.
        • Thus 2NF fails; assuming atomic values, the highest form is 1NF.
        • This resolves the prior image-verified interpretation of the damaged dependency stem.
        • If only the corrupted string C3D,C>PB,BOC is available without that verified transcription, ask for the actual dependency set rather than calculating from guessed symbols.
      • Worked example
        • For F={A→B,B→C} on R(A,B,C), A+=ABC makes A the key. The chain through nonkey B causes a 3NF violation. If instead B were a candidate key, a dependency chain would not by itself prove such a violation.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB19 Insertion, deletion and update anomalies

      • Suppose Enrollment repeats StudentName for every course.
        • An update anomaly requires changing every copy of the student's name; missed copies disagree.
        • An insertion anomaly prevents recording a new student until some enrollment exists.
        • A deletion anomaly loses the only record of a student's details when their last enrollment is deleted.
        • Revoke anomaly is not a normalization anomaly.
      • Normalization separates facts according to their determinants, reducing avoidable repetition and associated anomalies.
        • It does not require seeing bad current data: declared dependencies suffice.
        • Adding a generated row ID may make insertion technically possible, but does not remove repeated facts or fix the dependency design.
        • Reduced redundancy can improve integrity and storage use, but extra keys and joins mean neither storage savings nor faster retrieval is guaranteed.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB20 First and second normal forms

      • 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen relational domains and no repeating groups in cells.
        • It does not mean merely declaring a primary key.
        • A mapped ER design that correctly splits composite and multivalued structures gives ordinary 1NF tables; ER drawing alone guarantees no higher form.
      • 2NF requires 1NF and no nonprime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.
        • For Enrollment(SID,CID,SName,CTitle,Grade), assume key (SID,CID), SID→SName and CID→CTitle.
        • Split into Student(SID,SName), Course(CID,CTitle) and Enrollment(SID,CID,Grade).
        • Grade still depends on the whole pair.
        • A relation whose every candidate key is single-attribute has no nonprime partial-key dependency.
        • Higher forms inherit 2NF, so no partial dependencies establishes the minimum guaranteed stage only when 1NF is also assumed.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB21 Third normal form, BCNF and higher forms

      • For every nontrivial FD X→A, 3NF permits it when X is a superkey or A is prime.
        • BCNF requires X to be a superkey.
        • The mnemonic whole key and nothing but the key describes the common single-key case; it cannot replace the full tests when keys overlap.
        • Remove dependencies of nonprime facts on nonkey determinants.
      • In Sale(Date,Customer,Product,Vendor,VendorCity,SalesRep), assume key (Date,Customer,Product), Product→Vendor and Vendor→VendorCity.
        • Product is a proper subset of the key, so Vendor and VendorCity violate 2NF.
        • With atomic values the highest form is 1NF, even though a transitive dependency also exists. 4NF addresses nontrivial multivalued dependencies with nonsuperkey determinants; 5NF addresses join dependencies.
        • Do not confuse a multivalued dependency with a list stored inside a cell.
      • Worked example
        • Employee(EID,DeptID,DeptName), EID→DeptID and DeptID→DeptName, splits into Employee(EID,DeptID) and Department(DeptID,DeptName). Each department name is stored once.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB22 Decomposition: lossless and dependency preserving

      • A lossless decomposition reconstructs exactly the original legal tuples by joining its parts; a lossy one creates spurious combinations.
        • For a binary decomposition into R1 and R2 under FDs, it is lossless when their common attributes determine all of R1 or all of R2.
        • Sharing a column without this condition is insufficient.
      • Dependency preservation means the original constraints can be enforced on the individual relations without joining them.
        • Losslessness and dependency preservation are separate properties.
        • A practical 3NF synthesis uses a minimal FD cover, creates a relation for each determinant and its dependent attributes, removes contained relations, and adds a relation containing a candidate key if none already does.
        • BCNF decomposition removes an offending X→Y by separating XY and the remaining attributes with X; it can sacrifice dependency preservation.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-NORMAL

    • FDB23 Choose data types and storage levels

      • CHAR(n) is fixed length; VARCHAR(n) has variable length up to a limit.
        • DATE represents a date and BLOB binary content such as images.
        • INTEGER represents whole numbers; DECIMAL(p,s) represents exact decimal values, making it suitable for money when scale is specified.
        • FLOAT/REAL/DOUBLE are approximate; names, widths and precision depend on the DBMS.
        • The module's universal numeric-width claims should not be memorized.
      • Primary storage includes RAM and processor cache and is usually volatile.
        • Secondary storage includes persistent SSDs/HDDs used online; database pages are copied into buffers before CPU processing.
        • Tertiary storage includes tape or removable archive media.
        • Choose types from meaning, range and accuracy requirements, not a blanket rule that integers are always faster than strings.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB24 Records, pages and primary file organization

      • A page/block is a unit of database I/O and holds several records.
        • For fixed unspanned records of size r in usable page space B, the blocking factor is floor(B/r), and n records occupy ceil(n/blocking factor) pages.
        • Page headers and slots reduce usable space.
      • A heap has no search-key order and supports simple inserts, but searches may scan all pages.
        • A sorted file supports efficient range scans and binary search on the ordering field, with more costly insertions or overflow handling.
        • A hashed file chooses a bucket by hash(key), supports equality lookup well and requires collision/overflow handling; hash order does not support ordinary ranges.
        • Choose organization from actual reads, writes and predicates.
        • Partitioning splits a large dataset; replication copies it; migration moves it; archiving removes older data from active service.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB25 Ordered, dense, sparse and multilevel indexes

      • An index stores search keys with pointers or row identifiers.
        • It often speeds selective retrieval but consumes space and must be maintained on writes.
        • A full scan can win for a tiny table or a query returning most rows.
        • Indexes do not themselves establish referential integrity.
      • In the module's terminology a primary ordered index is on the file's ordering key and can have one entry per page, hence sparse.
        • A clustering index is on a nonunique ordering field, often with an entry per distinct value.
        • Secondary indexes provide other access paths and must represent all searchable values with record pointers or pointer lists.
        • A dense index represents each search value; sparse indexes rely on ordered data between entries.
        • Multilevel indexes index lower index levels.
        • B/B+ trees support ordered and range search; hashing targets equality; bitmap indexes suit some analytic workloads.
        • No one type is universally best.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB26 SQL command categories and exact scope

      • DDL changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, commonly RENAME and TRUNCATE in textbook classifications.
        • DML retrieves or changes data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
        • Some texts separate SELECT as DQL.
        • DCL manages privileges through GRANT and REVOKE.
        • TCL includes COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.
        • Classify a statement by its effect, not its length.
      • DELETE removes rows and keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table object; ALTER changes its definition.
        • TRUNCATE empties a table using implementation-specific mechanisms.
        • PostgreSQL allows transactional rollback of TRUNCATE, so no rollback information is retained is not a universal SQL property.
        • SQL Server permits DROP DATABASE Sales, suppliers; that comma-list syntax is vendor-specific.
        • SQLite's .databases lists attached names/files in its command-line shell; .database is not the documented command.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-TRUNCATE, FDB-MSSQL, FDB-SQLITE

    • FDB27 SELECT and its result columns

      • SELECT Name,Address FROM Customer; produces only those mailing-label fields.
        • SELECT * selects all columns; DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; AS supplies an alias; ALL permits duplicates and does not mean all columns.
        • SQL normally preserves duplicates without DISTINCT.
        • A query reading table columns needs an appropriate FROM source.
        • A literal-only query such as SELECT 1 may legally omit FROM.
      • Typical written clause order is SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY ….
        • Conceptually form FROM/JOIN rows, filter WHERE, group, filter HAVING, select expressions and then order the result.
        • SELECT alone normally reads without changing the database state.
        • WHERE alone is a clause rather than a complete read-only statement, so it cannot be compared as an equivalent executable command.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB28 Predicates, strings and NULL

      • Use single quotes for SQL string literals: WHERE ID = 'B001'.
        • Standard double quotes delimit identifiers, although some vendor modes accept them for strings.
        • Qualify ambiguous columns with aliases such as E.Department.
        • Conditions use =, <>, <, >, AND, OR and NOT; use parentheses to make precedence clear.
        • LIKE 'Ab%' matches a prefix, and BETWEEN includes its endpoints.
      • NULL represents a missing/unknown value.
        • Comparisons such as Salary = NULL are unknown, not true; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
        • WHERE retains only true conditions.
        • An index-friendly year predicate for timestamps is BirthDate >= DATE '2000-01-01' AND BirthDate < DATE '2001-01-01', avoiding omitted times on December 31.
        • Expression indexes can support functions, so functions do not universally prevent indexing.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB29 INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE

      • INSERT INTO Hotel(HotelID,HotelName,SubCity) VALUES (1,'Hilton','Yeka'); pairs each named column with a compatible value.
        • Counts and types must match; keys and other constraints still apply.
        • Without a column list, values must follow the table's declared column order.
      • UPDATE Book SET Price = 600 WHERE ID = 'B001'; changes matching rows.
        • UPDATE without WHERE targets every row.
        • DELETE FROM Publisher WHERE Name = 'XWZ'; deletes matching publisher rows, subject to reference policies.
        • DELETE FROM r; removes every row but leaves r defined.
        • Both clear relation entries and delete rows describe that effect.
        • Several UPDATE statements can all be valid while performing different tasks; most appropriate requires a requested change and a specified quoting dialect.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB30 CREATE and ALTER tables

      • CREATE TABLE Employee (EmpID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80)); declares two columns.
        • The name and its type stay together; the comma separates whole column declarations.
        • To add a primary key later: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD PRIMARY KEY (EmpID); existing data must be unique and non-NULL.
        • A table cannot gain a second primary key without replacing the existing constraint.
      • ALTER TABLE Employee ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(120); adds a column in PostgreSQL-style syntax.
        • ALTER TABLE Employee DROP COLUMN Email; removes it.
        • ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (Email); adds a named constraint.
        • If an option literally begins DALTER, or separates column_name and column_type with a comma, it is malformed; explain the intended repair without claiming the printed statement executes.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB31 Join behavior and preservation

      • An inner join returns matching pairs satisfying ON.
        • An equijoin uses equality; a theta join permits another comparison.
        • A natural join is ordinarily an inner equality join on every same-named column and merges those duplicate columns.
        • JOIN … USING (DeptID) specifies shared join columns explicitly.
        • CROSS JOIN forms every pair without a matching condition.
      • LEFT OUTER JOIN also preserves unmatched left rows, padding right columns with NULL; RIGHT preserves right rows and FULL preserves both.
        • Therefore inner and natural inner joins both discard unmatched rows.
        • A self-join uses aliases for two occurrences of one base table.
        • Each ordinary join operator combines two inputs, but its inputs can be earlier joins, so one query can join many tables.
        • Distinguish base-table count, table occurrences and binary operator arity.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-JOIN

    • FDB32 Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING

      • COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(x) counts non-NULL x values; SUM and AVG summarize non-NULL numeric values.
        • SQL's usual average function is AVG, not AVERAGE.
        • GROUP BY creates one group per distinct grouping value; HAVING tests aggregate groups after WHERE has filtered individual rows.
      • SELECT Department, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Department <> 'Sales' GROUP BY Department HAVING AVG(Salary) > 35000; lists qualifying department averages.
        • An ordinary AVG(Salary) predicate cannot be placed directly in WHERE.
        • Selecting EmpID, FirstName and LastName while grouping only by Department is also invalid unless the DBMS can establish the required functional dependence.
        • The grouping column need not itself appear in SELECT; that is not the defect in the damaged employee query.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-GROUP

    • FDB33 Subqueries and views

      • A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement.
        • It may appear in WHERE, HAVING or FROM, not only the first two.
        • IN tests membership; EXISTS tests whether at least one qualifying row exists.
        • Correlated subqueries refer to the outer row.
        • A scalar subquery must produce an appropriate single value.
        • Beware NOT IN when its subquery can return NULL; NOT EXISTS often expresses the intended absence more safely.
      • CREATE VIEW CSStudent AS SELECT StudentID,Name FROM Student WHERE Major = 'CS'; stores a query definition and presents a virtual table.
        • Views can simplify repeated queries, expose derived values and restrict access when configured correctly.
        • An ordinary view does not necessarily store its result; a materialized view does.
        • Rewriting a subquery as a join can change duplicates, and does not guarantee faster execution.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB34 Set operations and type conversion in SQL

      • SELECT ID FROM A UNION SELECT ID FROM B; combines compatible result columns and removes duplicate rows by default.
        • UNION ALL retains duplicates.
        • Explicit UNION DISTINCT is accepted in some dialects, including PostgreSQL; it is not a separate algebra rule.
        • INTERSECT returns common rows; EXCEPT returns first-result rows absent from the second.
        • Inputs need the same column count and compatible corresponding types.
      • CAST('42' AS INTEGER) converts an expression to a requested type if the value permits it.
        • CONVERT is vendor-specific and can also perform type conversion, so a general conversion question offering both needs a dialect.
        • In SELECT xyz FROM table1 UNION xyz FROM table2, the second SELECT is missing.
        • After repair xyz is a selected column/expression, not a table name.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-UNION, FDB-CAST

    • FDB35 Relational algebra: calculate results

      • Selection σ filters tuples; projection π retains attributes and removes duplicate tuples under set semantics.
        • Rename ρ changes relation or attribute names.
        • Union, difference and intersection require union-compatible schemas.
        • Difference R−S is not commutative; union and intersection are.
        • Inner joins are commutative up to attribute order when predicates are adjusted; left outer joins are not generally commutative.
        • A vague join question must identify the variant.
      • A Cartesian product has |R|×|S| tuples and degree degree(R)+degree(S), renaming conflicting attributes if necessary.
        • Thus 200×100=20,000 and 5×7=35.
        • Join equals selection over a product; intersection can be derived from difference.
        • A common minimal basis contains selection, projection, union, difference, product and rename.
        • Assignment is a useful notation, not an indispensable primitive; lists of basic operations vary across textbooks.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB36 Relational calculus: state the desired facts

      • Relational algebra specifies a sequence of operations and is procedural at the logical level.
        • Relational calculus specifies a predicate describing desired results and is declarative/nonprocedural.
        • A tuple variable ranges over tuples; a domain variable ranges over individual attribute values.
        • Safe/range-restricted expressions produce results bounded by the database's active domain.
      • Tuple form {s | Student(s) AND s.Major='CS'} selects student tuples with that major.
        • A domain form can request names n satisfying ∃i,m (Student(i,n,m) AND m='CS').
        • Existential quantification means some matching tuple exists; universal quantification means every required case meets a condition.
        • SQL is declarative even though an optimizer later chooses a procedural execution plan.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB37 Transactions and the ACID properties

      • A transaction groups operations into one logical unit.
        • Atomicity applies all its effects or none.
        • Consistency means a correct transaction preserves declared invariants.
        • Isolation controls interference between concurrent transactions; serializable isolation provides behavior equivalent to some serial execution.
        • Durability preserves committed effects after a crash, typically through durable logging rather than forcing every data page immediately.
      • For a transfer, subtracting 100 from one balance and adding 100 to another must commit together; losing either half violates atomicity and may violate the total-balance invariant.
        • BEGIN starts work, COMMIT completes it, ROLLBACK undoes uncommitted work and SAVEPOINT marks an intermediate rollback point.
        • A failed transaction may roll back while other users' committed transactions remain.
        • SQL transaction syntax and error-handling constructs differ by DBMS; @@ERROR/IF in the short note is SQL Server-specific.
      • References: FDB-MOD, FDB-NOTE

    • FDB38 Choose a design technique from the requirement

      • Normalization reduces dependency-driven anomalies.
        • Indexing supplies search paths.
        • Denormalization deliberately repeats or precomputes facts to reduce selected read costs, increasing maintenance work.
        • Partitioning divides rows or columns; replication creates copies to improve locality or availability while complicating updates.
        • These techniques can coexist.
        • An e-commerce or gaming label alone does not select one.
      • Privacy requires a threat model.
        • Authentication verifies identity; role-based authorization limits allowed records/actions; encryption protects data at rest or in transit; auditing records activity.
        • Both encryption and access control can protect patient data.
        • Scalability, availability, fast retrieval, redundancy control and security are all reasonable design considerations.
        • Functional requirements describe behavior; nonfunctional requirements quantify qualities such as 99.9% uptime or response time.
        • Authentication and encryption mechanisms alone do not uniquely establish that distinction.
      • In a CMS, tags/categories describe meaning, while foreign keys preserve valid references between content and tags.
        • A ContentTag(ContentID,TagID) association models multiple tags per item; these functions complement each other.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB39 Integrated design: student registration and dormitory allocation

      • State the rules first: each student belongs to one department, may enroll in many courses, and has at most one current dorm assignment.
        • Each course accepts many students; each dorm holds at most six students.
        • Identify Department, Student, Course and Dorm entities; Enrollment is the M:N relationship with Grade.
      • Use Department(DeptID,Name), Student(SID,Name,DeptID,DormID), Course(CID,Title), Enrollment(SID,CID,Grade) and Dorm(DormID,FloorNumber).
        • Declare all entity IDs primary keys; Student.DeptID and Student.DormID reference their parents; Enrollment has composite key (SID,CID) and both references.
        • Make DormID nullable until assignment.
        • Separate StudentPhone(SID,Phone) for multiple contacts.
        • Normalize repeated department/course facts into their owning tables.
        • A simple foreign key does not enforce the six-student capacity; use a concurrency-safe trigger, allocation transaction or explicit slot design with six unique slots per dorm.
      • Worked example
        • Complete the reference as FOREIGN KEY (DormID) REFERENCES Dorm(DormID). STUDENT is the referencing child; DORM is referenced. Consistent names and an added Student.DormID column are required before execution.
      • References: FDB-MOD

    • FDB40 Resolve malformed and overlapping questions

      • Treat a supplied key as a claim to check.
        • Owner and strong entity can both fit the weak-entity question; row and record are synonyms in a relational table; difference and set-difference are the same operator.
        • A negative DROP question admitting DELETE, UPDATE and an invalid REMOVE has several answers.
        • Do not select one merely because it was highlighted.
      • For malformed SQL, identify the damaged token and show the corrected form without accepting the printed text.
        • For unsupported cardinalities, request business rules and direction.
        • For best/efficient/important questions, specify workload, quality goal or comparison baseline.
        • A diagram-dependent conclusion needs the missing diagram or an explicit description of its relevant symbols.
        • The question index records these local exceptions and the minimal clarification; the teaching remains useful even where the original item cannot support one answer.
      • References: FDB-MOD

  • Advanced Database Systems

    • Use object semantics, recovery algorithms, distributed design and explicit query costs to reason about system behavior.
      • Worked traces and assumptions extend the brief module where its object-model coverage and the banks are incomplete.
    • For each schedule, mark conflicting items and build the precedence graph; test commit dependencies separately.
    • For recovery, write the durable commit set, buffer policy and checkpoint/ARIES assumptions before choosing undo or redo.
    • Compare equivalent plans with stated page counts, memory and network bytes; show the arithmetic rather than memorizing a preferred join.
    • Construct one homogeneous and one heterogeneous distributed design, including ownership, reconstruction, replication and failure behavior.
    • Review OID versus values, encapsulation versus abstraction, 2PL versus 2PC and rollback versus redo through short examples.

    • ADB01 Objects, identity, classes and persistence

      • An object combines identity, state and behavior.
        • A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance.
        • The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime.
        • Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.
      • Persistence lets an object survive beyond the program execution that created it.
        • An OODBMS adds durable storage, transactions, querying and controlled sharing to object concepts.
        • It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables.
        • An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.
        • These three approaches differ.
        • Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.
      • References: ADB-NOTE, ADB-OO

    • ADB02 Encapsulation, abstraction and object associations

      • Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details.
        • Account.withdraw(amount) can enforce a balance rule while hiding its storage.
        • Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented.
        • These ideas overlap in information hiding, but combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.
      • An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects.
        • It is different from inheritance, which means an is-a relationship between types.
        • Methods can invoke operations on other objects, supporting collaboration.
        • A class defines structure and behavior; an attribute describes state; a method implements an operation.
        • Do not treat each of these as an interchangeable name for the whole object.
      • References: ADB-NOTE, ADB-OO

    • ADB03 Inheritance, polymorphism and safe substitutability

      • Inheritance derives a subtype from a superclass, reusing applicable attributes and behavior.
        • GraduateStudent is a Student; association instead says Student belongs to Department.
        • EER teaches inherited attributes and relationships, while a programming object model also specifies behavior.
      • Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses.
        • The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object.
        • This is not arbitrary conversion of an object into an unrelated class, nor dynamic class mutation.
