        • Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship; polymorphism uses that relationship through a common interface.
        • If a question asks whether treating subclasses as a superclass is inheritance or polymorphism, clarify whether it asks about the structural prerequisite or the runtime use.
      • References: ADB-NOTE, ADB-POLY

    • ADB04 Object type constructors

      • In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state).
        • An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string.
        • A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B').
        • It is not a collection of records.
      • A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions.
        • Constructors can be nested to represent complex objects, such as a tuple with a set of phone numbers.
        • An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable.
        • A type constructor defines the shape of a value; it is not the same as an executable constructor operation that creates a new object.
      • References: ADB-CONSTRUCT

    • ADB05 ODL, OQL and inverse relationships

      • Object Definition Language (ODL) is the ODMG schema-definition language for object databases; it describes interfaces/classes, attributes, operations and relationships.
        • Object Query Language (OQL) expresses queries.
        • Host-language bindings connect these definitions and operations to languages such as Java or C++.
        • Defining a logical schema is different from implementing its storage.
      • An inverse declaration pairs opposite directions of the same relationship.
        • Conceptually, Department.employees is inverse to Employee.department: when an employee belongs to department D, the corresponding employee appears in D's collection.
        • The declaration expresses relationship consistency; it is not an inheritance keyword or an ordinary scalar attribute.
        • An MCQ calling ODL both a DDL and a language for developing logical schemas offers overlapping true descriptions, so its exact wording matters.
      • References: ADB-ODL

    • ADB06 Transactions, ACID and state transitions

      • A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work.
        • Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.
        • A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.
      • Active means operations are executing.
        • Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.
        • Committed means commitment succeeded.
        • A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt.
        • Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability.
        • Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.
      • Worked example
        • A=5,000 and B=8,000 become 4,250 and 8,750 after transferring 750 from A to B. Both balances total 13,000. Unchanged or reverse-transfer balances can also preserve that sum; only the requested debit/credit implements the specified successful transfer.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB07 Read/write operations, buffers and log records

      • read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable. write_item(X) copies the new program value into the buffered page, marking it dirty.
        • Writing that page to disk can occur later according to the buffer policy; write_item is not inherently an immediate disk flush.
        • Insert and delete also modify data; sorting is a query-processing operation rather than a primitive item update.
      • A conceptual log can contain START, UPDATE(T,X,old,new), COMMIT, ABORT and END records.
        • Before-images support undo; after-images support redo.
        • Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read.
        • COMMIT records successful completion; an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB08 Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

      • Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600.
        • Correct serial execution yields 800.
        • Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered.
        • Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.
      • Nonrepeatable read means a repeated read of one row sees a committed change.
        • A phantom means repeating a predicate query finds a changed qualifying set after another transaction inserts, deletes or changes matching rows.
        • Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.
        • A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB09 Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

      • A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively.
        • A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions.
        • Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide.
        • Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes.
        • Read/read pairs do not conflict.
      • For conflict serializability, make one graph vertex per transaction.
        • For every earlier conflicting operation of Ti and later operation of Tj, add Ti→Tj.
        • Acyclic means conflict-serializable; a topological ordering gives a valid serial order.
        • Cyclic means not conflict-serializable.
        • This test is stronger than view serializability, which also compares read-from relationships and final writers and may permit some schedules with blind writes.
      • Worked example
        • r1(X), w2(X), r2(Y), w1(Y) gives T1→T2 on X and T2→T1 on Y, a cycle. r1(X), w1(X), r2(X), w2(X) gives only T1→T2 and is conflict-serializable.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB10 Recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules

      • Recoverable means if Tj reads Ti's value, Tj cannot commit before Ti commits.
        • Otherwise Ti might abort after Tj already committed dependent work.
        • Cascadeless means a transaction reads only values written by committed transactions, avoiding cascading aborts.
        • Strict means no other transaction reads or overwrites an item written by an uncommitted transaction.
        • Strict ⇒ cascadeless ⇒ recoverable.
      • For w1(X), r2(X), c2, a1, T2 committed a dirty dependency, so the schedule is unrecoverable.
        • Moving c2 after c1 makes that dependency recoverable, but the earlier dirty read still makes it not cascadeless.
        • Serializability and recoverability are separate tests: one concerns equivalent transaction order and the other safe commit/rollback dependencies.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB11 Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

      • A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist.
        • An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item.
        • Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive.
        • These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.
      • A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.
        • S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.
        • X→S is a downgrade.
        • The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests.
        • One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.
        • No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.
      • Held / requestedSX
        SCompatibleConflict
        XConflictConflict
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB12 Two-phase locking and its variants

      • Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them.
        • Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired.
        • The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.
      • Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.
        • Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point.
        • Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.
        • It requires knowing the lock set and can reduce concurrency.
        • Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB13 Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

      • Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj.
        • A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model.
        • Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain.
        • Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.
      • Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles.
        • A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.
        • A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.
        • Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.
        • Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB14 Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

      • A smaller timestamp means an older transaction.
        • In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself.
        • In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder.
        • Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.
      • Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.
        • Starvation avoidance additionally assumes holders eventually finish and scheduling is fair.
        • The new guides reverse wait–die in several explanations; younger waits and older dies is incorrect for wait–die.
        • Deadlock-prevention priority rules are also different from basic timestamp ordering's read/write validity tests.
      • Requester relative to holderWait–dieWound–wait
        OlderWaitAbort younger holder
        YoungerAbort requesterWait
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-DEADLOCK

    • ADB15 Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

      • Assign each transaction TS(T).
        • For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer.
        • A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS.
        • A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS.
        • These tests preserve timestamp order.
      • For TS(T)=10 and write_TS(X)=20, T cannot read X: it would observe a logically later write.
        • Thus the transaction aborted can be older, contrary to the guides' blanket younger-always-aborts claim.
        • The Thomas write rule can ignore an obsolete write instead of aborting in one case, but that is a different protocol and must be stated.
        • Basic timestamp ordering avoids lock-wait deadlocks but may cause repeated restarts.
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-TIMESTAMP

    • ADB16 Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

      • Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.
        • It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.
        • Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot.
        • Snapshot isolation is not automatically serializable: concurrent writes to different rows can violate a shared invariant.
      • Fine-grained row locks permit more independent operations but require tracking many locks.
        • Coarse table/database locks simplify management but block unrelated rows and reduce concurrency.
        • Intention locks advertise planned descendant locks in a hierarchy; escalation replaces many small locks with a coarser one.
        • Small granularity does not inherently cause more logical conflicts.
        • Choose granularity from contention and management overhead, not a universal rule.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB17 Query processing: representation before execution

      • Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions.
        • Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree.
        • Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods.
        • Evaluation executes that plan and returns results.
        • Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.
      • A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates.
        • A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms.
        • Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.
        • DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB18 Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

      • Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile.
        • Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input.
      • Semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, such as a key proving a join cannot multiply matching rows.
        • Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone.
        • Outer joins, NULLs, duplicates and aggregation restrict equivalences: moving a right-table filter from ON to WHERE after a left join may delete its preserved unmatched rows.
        • Fewer intermediate rows is a useful heuristic, not proof of minimum runtime.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB19 Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

      • A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.
        • Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions.
        • Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows.
        • For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger.
        • Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero.
        • Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.
      • For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.
        • Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms.
        • Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans.
        • State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.
      • References: ADB-MOD, PRIMARY-CMU-INCLUSION, PRIMARY-JOB

    • ADB20 Join algorithms and access-path tradeoffs

      • Tuple nested loops scan the inner relation for each outer tuple.
        • Page nested loops approximately cost B(R)+B(R)×B(S) page reads.
        • With M buffers, block nested loops can cost B(R)+ceil(B(R)/(M−2))×B(S), reserving an inner and output buffer.
        • Try both outer choices.
      • An indexed nested-loop join probes an inner index for each qualifying outer tuple; it suits a small outer result and a useful index.
        • Sort-merge joins sorted join keys and must include any sorting cost.
        • Hash join partitions/builds a hash structure and probes it; equality joins suit it, ranges generally do not.
        • A one-pass in-memory hash join can read each input once when the build side fits.
        • Include output/materialization cost if the exercise requires it.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB21 Compare actual query strategies

      • Compare only plans returning the same result under the same assumptions.
        • Add scans, probes, sorting, intermediate writes and communication as applicable; do not count an omitted cost in only one plan.
        • Record memory limits and whether inputs are already ordered.
        • Choose the lowest estimated cost for the specified objective, then test estimates against actual execution.
      • Example: R has 100 pages, S has 1,000 pages and M=12 buffers.
        • Block nested loops with R outer cost 100+ceil(100/10)×1,000=10,100 reads; S outer costs 1,000+ceil(1,000/10)×100=11,000.
        • If a selective R index costs 3 reads and returns 20 outer tuples, with each S index probe costing 4 reads including matches, indexed nested loops cost 3+20×4=83 reads.
        • That wins under these supplied assumptions; it is not a universal join ranking.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB22 Pipelining, parallelism and caching

      • Materialization stores an intermediate result before the next operator consumes it.
        • Pipelining passes tuples as they become available, overlapping producer and consumer work and reducing temporary I/O. A sort is normally blocking; a hash join must build its hash table before probing can output, though later probe/output can stream.
        • Pipelining does not require separate CPUs.
      • Parallel execution uses multiple workers, for example partitioned scans/joins, independent subplans or operator pipelines.
        • Interleaving on one CPU is concurrency; simultaneous cores provide parallelism.
        • Result caching reuses answers and needs invalidation when underlying data changes.
        • Plan caching reuses an execution strategy, not the rows returned.
        • Buffer caching keeps data pages; materialization retains intermediate rows.
        • A vague query caching question must specify which of these it means.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB23 Indexes, statistics and re-optimization

      • B/B+ tree indexes support ordered and range predicates; hash indexes target equality; bitmap indexes can help some analytic selections.
        • Clustered storage keeps related rows close.
        • An index may reduce reads but adds space and update work; scanning can be faster when most rows qualify.
        • Commonly useful is not a unique property of one index type.
      • Re-optimization chooses a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest the old plan is unsuitable.
        • Updating statistics does not itself execute the query.
        • Use EXPLAIN and measured execution to compare estimates, spills, scans and join choices.
        • Avoid universal rules that joins always beat subqueries, functions can never use indexes or more indexes always improve performance.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB24 Security, integrity and inference control

      • Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions.
        • Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions.
        • A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges.
        • A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.
      • Inference control concerns learning protected individual facts indirectly from allowed aggregate answers.
        • Releasing SUM for a group and SUM for the same group excluding one known person may disclose that person's value by subtraction.
        • Suppressing individual rows alone is insufficient; protections may restrict queries, aggregate sizes or add appropriately designed noise.
        • If a question merely says aggregates visible and details hidden, access-restricted views also fit; explicitly mention prevention of indirect disclosure to identify inference control uniquely.
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-INFERENCE

    • ADB25 GRANT, REVOKE and privilege scope

      • GRANT SELECT ON Catalogue TO Mohammed; permits reads.
        • REVOKE DELETE, UPDATE (Price,Year) ON Catalogue FROM Mohammed; removes the specified table deletion and column update grants in SQL dialects supporting that form.
        • DELETE applies to rows/table access rather than particular columns; UPDATE can be column-scoped.
        • REVOKE removes permission, whereas GRANT gives it.
      • Roles group privileges.
        • WITH GRANT OPTION permits a recipient to grant a privilege onward; removing an upstream grant can cascade or be restricted according to the chosen command and DBMS.
        • Removing one direct grant may leave effective access through another role or grant path.
        • A view is a stored query definition, not encryption.
        • Least privilege assigns only the access needed for the task.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB26 Classify failures and choose the starting resource

      • Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.
        • Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure.
        • A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive.
        • Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs.
        • Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.
      • Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
        • Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy.
        • These are cooperating mechanisms, not four mutually exclusive complete alternatives.
        • Buffer management is not durable backup.
        • Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification.
        • A full backup copies the database to separate storage; scheduled backups plus archived logs support restoration to a chosen recoverable point.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB27 WAL, undo and redo

      • Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.
        • To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage.
        • A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.
      • Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.
        • Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.
        • Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.
        • In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners.
        • ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB28 Steal and force determine recovery work

      • Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo.
        • No-steal prevents those uncommitted effects reaching the persistent database.
        • Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo.
      • For the conventional page/log model: steal/no-force needs undo and redo; steal/force needs undo but no redo; no-steal/no-force needs redo but no undo; no-steal/force needs neither data-page undo nor redo after a system crash.
        • Logging/atomic commit machinery may still be necessary.
        • These policies are independent of whether an update overwrites an old page or uses a separate location.
        • Immediate update alone does not uniquely specify every recovery requirement.
      • Buffer policyForceNo-force
        StealUNDOUNDO + REDO
        No-stealNeither data-page UNDO nor REDOREDO
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB29 Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

      • Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.
        • Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers.
        • Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.
      • In-place update overwrites the original location.
        • Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.
        • Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.
        • Before commit, a crash uses the old map.
        • It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB30 Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

      • A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.
        • In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo.
        • Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo.
        • Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.
      • A fuzzy checkpoint permits ongoing transactions and records active-transaction and dirty-page information without forcing all pages simultaneously.
        • Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.
        • A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions.
        • Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB31 ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

      • ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.
        • Analysis reconstructs active/loser transactions and dirty-page information.
        • Redo repeats history, starting from the relevant earliest dirty-page update; pageLSNs help skip already-installed actions.
        • Undo reverses loser transactions.
      • Compensation log records (CLRs) describe undo actions and their continuation information.
        • They can be redone but are not themselves undone.
        • This makes recovery restartable: after a second crash, durable undo progress need not be undone again as if no progress occurred.
        • Absence of checkpoints alone does not imply identical undo/redo lists.
        • State the recovery algorithm, durable logs/page state and progress before predicting repeated-crash behavior.
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-RECOVERY

    • ADB32 Execute a small recovery problem

      • Assume steal/no-force, durable WAL and a simple undo/redo method.
        • Initially X=100,Y=50.
        • The durable log contains START T1; UPDATE T1 X 100→120; COMMIT T1; START T2; UPDATE T2 Y 50→70; crash.
        • T1 is a winner and T2 a loser.
        • Redo X=120 if needed; undo Y=50 if T2's change reached disk.
        • Under no-steal, Y never reached the persistent database, so no undo of it is needed.
      • To solve larger cases, list transactions and durable commit status, identify the checkpoint type and buffer policy, select the algorithm, apply redo/undo in its required order and recompute final values.
        • Transactions active at failure are not automatically restarted and committed.
        • Business-level retries require a new controlled attempt; idempotency prevents duplicate effects when the client is unsure whether a commit succeeded.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB33 Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

      • A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system.
        • A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces.
        • Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction.
        • Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.
      • Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics.
        • ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction.
        • Locality, expansion and replicated availability are potential benefits.
        • Distribution adds communication, coordination and security costs; a site outage can still make needed data unavailable if no usable replica exists.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB34 Architectures and local autonomy

      • In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules.
        • In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions.
        • Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers.
        • These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.
      • A tightly integrated distributed system can present one global schema and shared control.
        • A federation integrates autonomous databases through mappings; a loosely coupled multidatabase system may preserve more independence without one complete global schema.
        • State how much schema, transaction and administrative autonomy local sites retain.
        • Calling a system heterogeneous does not require all sites to surrender autonomy or to copy every row everywhere.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB35 Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

      • Location transparency hides which site holds a named object.
        • Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation.
        • Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained.
        • The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.
      • If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent.
        • Thus a stem saying access a specific fragment without knowing its distribution needs clarification.
        • Column subsets define vertical fragmentation, not a type of transparency.
        • Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB36 Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

      • Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation.
        • Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended.
        • Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed.
        • Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.
      • Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.
        • Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.
        • A full outer join is not universally required.
        • Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.
        • Losing the only site containing a fragment makes that fragment unavailable, even while other sites continue.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB37 Replication policies and their costs

      • Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.
        • Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation.
        • They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.
      • Eager/synchronous replication coordinates propagation before the specified commit/acknowledgment point, increasing update latency.
        • Lazy/asynchronous replication propagates later and may expose stale reads or need conflict resolution.
        • Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes.
        • These dimensions can coexist, so commonly used does not identify one unique policy.
        • Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB38 Distributed query plans and semijoin arithmetic

      • Distributed processing decomposes a logical query, localizes referenced relations to fragments/replicas, chooses global placement/order and optimizes local subplans.
        • Include bytes moved, message latency, bandwidth and local work.
        • Apply filters and projections before shipping when equivalent.
        • A semijoin retains only rows of one input that have a match in the other, returning that input's attributes.
      • Suppose R at A occupies 100 MB and S at B 20 MB; compute the result at A. Shipping all S costs 20 MB.
        • A semijoin can send 0.2 MB of distinct R join keys to B, then return 1 MB of matching S rows: 1.2 MB before other costs.
        • It wins on transferred bytes, but extra messages may dominate on high-latency links.
        • If nearly all S matches, key shipping may not help.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB39 Distributed atomic commit and Oracle commit points

      • Two-phase commit (2PC) first asks participants to prepare and durably promise they can commit.
        • If all vote yes, the coordinator records commit durably and tells participants; otherwise it decides abort.
        • A prepared participant must retain enough state to obey the final decision.
        • Coordinator/communication failure can leave it in doubt and block progress until the decision is learned.
        • Timeout after preparation is not permission to invent a commit or abort.
      • 2PC coordinates atomic outcome; locking/other concurrency protocols provide isolation.
        • Oracle's COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH helps choose the commit point site in its distributed transaction mechanism, with higher eligible strength preferred.
        • This is an Oracle-specific 2PC role rule, not a lock phase or checkpoint setting.
        • The transaction coordinator coordinates decisions rather than physically storing every site's rows.
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-ORACLE

    • ADB40 Construct homogeneous and heterogeneous designs

      • For a bank using one compatible DBMS at three branches, horizontally fragment branch accounts by BranchID; keep each account at its home branch and replicate selected read-mostly reference data.
        • For cross-branch transfers, use global identifiers, coordinated commit and a stated isolation policy.
        • Choose replica placement so the required service remains available after the specified failure.
        • Verify reconstruction, capacity, latency and recovery procedures.
      • For a merger retaining different branch DBMSs, add mappings for AccountID, currency, time zones and numeric precision, plus middleware/gateways for supported operations.
        • Decide whether all engines support atomic distributed commits; if not, define an explicit compensating workflow and its intermediate-state limits.
        • Compare retaining autonomy against coordination and availability requirements.
        • A good design answers who owns each fact, where copies live, what a failed link permits and how conflicting writes are resolved.
      • References: ADB-MOD

    • ADB41 Warehouses, OLTP, OLAP and columnar storage

      • OLTP handles frequent operational transactions, such as account updates; OLAP scans and summarizes large datasets for analysis.
        • A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading.
        • These are workload tendencies: OLTP can retain history and warehouses can be updated.
      • A star schema places measurements at a declared grain in a fact table linked to descriptive dimensions, such as time, product and store.
        • A snowflake normalizes dimension structure further.
        • Columnar storage groups values by column, reducing unnecessary column reads and aiding compression in scans; row-oriented storage groups each record's fields.
        • Neither physical layout alone determines whether the logical model is relational.
        • Indexes and denormalization choices depend on workload.
      • References: ADB-MOD, ADB-NOTE

    • ADB42 NoSQL families, wide columns and CAP

      • Key-value stores retrieve values by key; document stores hold structured documents; wide-column/column-family systems organize sparse rows and related column families; graph systems model nodes and edges for relationship traversal.
        • Wide-column systems such as Cassandra are not simply interchangeable with analytic columnar relational engines.
        • Flexible schema does not mean no schema rules, and NoSQL does not imply no transactions.
      • CAP states that under a network partition, a distributed service cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request at nonfailed nodes.
        • It is not a universal menu saying casually pick any two forever.
        • Systems choose failure behavior and may vary it by operation.
        • CAP consistency is a single-copy visibility/order property, distinct from ACID consistency's preservation of application invariants.
      • References: ADB-NOTE, ADB-CAP

    • ADB43 Data sources and association rules

      • Structured data follows explicit fields, such as a registrar's relational tables.
        • Unstructured data includes free text, images and audio; web/search collections can include these alongside structured content.
        • A DBMS can also store text or BLOBs, so a storage product does not prove all its contents are structured.
      • An association rule X⇒Y describes co-occurrence.
        • Support=count(X and Y)/N; confidence=count(X and Y)/count(X)=P(Y|X).
        • If 75 of 100 shoe purchases include socks, confidence(shoes⇒socks)=0.75.
        • This does not prove causation or specify support without total transaction count.
        • Clustering groups similar cases without target labels; classification predicts categories and regression predicts numeric outcomes.
        • Purchasing co-occurrence is association mining even when its result informs store layout.
      • References: ADB-MINING

    • ADB44 Data-mining workflow and evaluation

      • CRISP-DM starts with business understanding: define the decision and success criteria.
        • Then understand data, prepare it, model, evaluate and deploy; the process is iterative.
        • Cleaning, integration and feature selection occur during preparation, not before the business problem exists.
      • Within modeling, split data appropriately, train on training data, tune using validation and evaluate once on a held-out test set before deployment.
        • Testing and evaluation are sometimes overlapping labels rather than universally distinct sequential phases.
        • If an MCQ asks training→testing→evaluation→deployment, state that convention; another valid workflow can evaluate during model selection before final testing.
        • Deployment includes monitoring and may trigger another preparation/modeling cycle.
        • Do not leak future or test outcomes into training.
      • References: ADB-CRISP

    • ADB45 Repair source wording before trusting a key

      • Some questions classify overlapping mechanisms as exclusive: ARIES and deferred update can both be log-based; restart recovery can use checkpoints, rollback and redo; NO-UNDO/REDO equals redo-only.
        • Questions using best, important, common or faster need a workload and comparison criterion.
        • Read the literal scope rather than treating one familiar term as automatically unique.
      • State the minimum missing information: exact DBMS/version for vendor behavior; OID/type convention for object constructors; requester/holder ages for waiting; durable log, page state and policy for recovery; fragment definitions and network cost for distribution.
        • Retain genuine ambiguity when multiple offered descriptions remain true.
        • The index provides question-specific clarifications and checked corrections without reproducing whole questions in the teaching prose.
      • References: ADB-MOD

  • Object Oriented Programming

    • Design with objects, then trace the Java rules that make the design run.
      • Java17 is the baseline for traditional bank examples; modern interface and Java25 constructor differences are explicitly explained.
      • The official allocation is six items.
    • Draw separate boxes for reference variables and objects, then trace constructor and field state changes.
    • For a call, check visibility and declared type first, overload selection second, runtime overriding third.
    • Practice one small interface hierarchy with valid implementations, a checked exception and a safe downcast; repair compiler errors before predicting output.
    • Sections in this course
      Objects, classes and responsibilitiesFour principles and the difference between hiding and abstractionCreate objects and distinguish references from instancesUML class and instance notationVariables, defaults, scope and initializationPrimitive types, literals and conversionsStatic members, static blocks and finalAccess control and package boundariesConstructors and missing default constructorsConstructor chaining and initialization orderMethods, getters and settersMethod overloading and compile-time selectionInheritance and useful relationshipsOverriding and restrictionsDynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual typethis, super, fields and static hidingC++ this and language-specific assumptionsAbstract classes and concrete implementationsInterfaces: contracts and modern JavaConflicting interface methods and abstract class choiceCasts and instanceofIdentity, equals, toString and immutable stringsExpressions: numbers, bits and text outputIncrement order and the character-space trapControl flow traces and exact printingArrays: creation, bounds and ragged rowsArray algorithms, sort and copy APIsPackages, imports and command-line toolsException hierarchy and checked obligationsthrow, throws and catch selectionfinally, cleanup and diagnostic informationStreams, GUI events and JDBC practiceJDBC flow from user action to databaseLegacy applets and lifecycle questionsAndroid Activity, Intent, manifest and layoutsAndroid app declarations and packagingResolve defective wording and syntax before tracingAmbiguities that require a stated interpretationLanguage classifications and portability in the bank

    • OOP01 Objects, classes and responsibilities

      • An object has identity, state and behavior.
        • State is stored in fields; behavior is provided by methods.
        • A Rectangle object may hold width and height and answer getArea() or getPerimeter().
        • Two objects can have equal fields and still be distinct objects.
        • A class defines their common structure and behavior; an object is a particular instance.
      • Choose classes around responsibilities: an account controls its own balance, a transaction records a payment, and a service coordinates them.
        • Objects send messages through method calls such as obj.add().
        • They can delegate work to other objects; saying that objects cannot manage their own state is misleading.
        • Procedural and object oriented designs both support reuse; global shared data is not compulsory in procedural programming.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP02 Four principles and the difference between hiding and abstraction

      • Encapsulation groups related state and operations and controls access.
        • Information hiding keeps implementation decisions behind a stable interface.
        • Abstraction presents the essential operations while omitting details irrelevant to the caller.
        • These ideas overlap: a private balance plus deposit(amount) can demonstrate all three, depending on what the question emphasizes.
      • Inheritance forms a subtype relationship and may reuse implementation.
        • Polymorphism lets code using a common type invoke behavior appropriate to different concrete objects.
        • Prefer a precise mechanism over a vague slogan: wrapping fields and methods points to encapsulation; showing what an operation does while hiding how points to abstraction.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP03 Create objects and distinguish references from instances

      • Student s; declares a reference variable; it creates no Student object.
        • Student s=new Student(); allocates and initializes an instance.
        • Member access uses s.name or s.study(), subject to visibility.
        • Assignment t=s copies a reference, so both can refer to the same object; changing that object through t is observable through s.
      • Java passes all arguments by value.
        • Passing a reference copies it: a method may modify the shared object, but assigning its parameter to a new object does not reassign the caller’s reference.
        • The runtime may reclaim unreachable objects; collection timing is unspecified.
        • Reachable object cycles can matter for retention, but an unreachable cycle can be collected.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP04 UML class and instance notation

      • A UML class box normally contains name, attributes and operations.
        • Visibility uses + public, - private and # protected.
        • A field can be written name:String and an operation getName():String.
        • A constructor Student(String,String,String,int) requires three strings and an integer, so an age argument "25" has the wrong type.
      • An instance is conventionally labeled with an underlined instanceName:ClassName, such as sara:Student.
        • Class notation describes a type; instance notation describes one particular object and may show its slot values.
        • Underlining static class features has a different purpose; read the whole notation rather than assuming every underline means the same thing.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP05 Variables, defaults, scope and initialization

      • The introductory three-way grouping is local, instance and class/static variables.
        • Locals occur in methods, constructors or blocks; they must be definitely assigned before use and cannot have public/private/protected modifiers.
        • Fields occur in a class outside method bodies; non-static fields belong to each instance, while static fields belong to the class.
        • Declaration location alone does not distinguish instance and static fields.
      • Java fields and array elements receive defaults: numeric zero, char '\u0000', boolean false and references null.
        • A local int t; followed by printing t is a compilation error.
        • Initializers such as int a=10,b=10; assign initial values.
        • A final local is permitted; final is not an access modifier.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP06 Primitive types, literals and conversions

      • Java has byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean.
        • Signed integer widths are 8,16,32,64 bits respectively. byte ranges from -128 to 127; short from -32768 to 32767. char is an unsigned 16-bit UTF-16 code unit and can hold a digit, letter or symbol, not a whole String. enum and String are reference types.
      • A compatible widening conversion often needs no cast; narrowing usually needs an explicit cast and may lose information.
        • Widening an int to float can lose precision, so “widening never loses information” is false.
        • Arithmetic promotes char, byte and short to int in many expressions. boolean does not convert to or from numeric truth values; if(0) and for(...;0;...) are invalid.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP07 Static members, static blocks and final

      • static gives one field per loaded class, shared by its instances.
        • If count starts at zero and every constructor increments it, three creations leave count=3.
        • Prefer ClassName.count and ClassName.utility().
        • A static method has no current instance, but can still use instance members through an explicit object reference.
      • A static initializer runs during class initialization, before the class’s first relevant active use, not simply whenever a file is loaded. final prevents reassignment of a variable, overriding of a method or extension of a class.
        • A final reference may still refer to a mutable object.
        • A shared mathematical PI is a good static final candidate; a student name normally belongs to an instance.
        • A calculation using only parameters may be static.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP08 Access control and package boundaries

      • For ordinary members: private restricts access to the declaring class/nest; no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access; public is widest, provided the declaring type itself is accessible.
        • Top-level classes/interfaces may be public or package-private, not protected/private.
        • Member types have additional visibility possibilities.
      • Across packages, a subclass accessing a protected instance member must do so through its own inherited context or an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, not any arbitrary superclass object. protected therefore does not mean “subclasses only”: unrelated classes in the same package also have access.
        • A class’s own main method can access private fields of an instance of that class.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-G, OOP-A

    • OOP09 Constructors and missing default constructors

      • A constructor has the class’s exact name and no return type, not even void.
        • It initializes the new object and can be overloaded or private.
        • A private constructor can support a factory or controlled singleton creation; it does not mean the class can never create an object internally.
      • If a class declares no constructor, Java supplies a default constructor.
        • If Circle(double r) is declared, new Circle() fails unless a no-argument constructor is also declared.
        • Constructors are not inherited or overridden.
        • They may contain return; but cannot return an expression.
        • Fields get their default values before ordinary constructor initialization, rather than receiving defaults only because a default constructor was generated.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP10 Constructor chaining and initialization order

      • Under the Java 17 rules used for the bank’s ordinary examples, an explicit this(args) or super(args) invocation must be the first constructor statement. this invokes another constructor in the same class; super invokes the immediate superclass constructor.
        • A constructor cannot explicitly invoke both.
        • If there is no explicit delegation, an implicit super() is inserted; a matching accessible no-argument parent constructor must exist.
      • Trace parent construction first, then subclass field initializers and instance blocks in order, then the relevant subclass constructor body.
        • In the repaired FinalExam example, the parent sets num1=4, the subclass initializes num=3, this(5) sets num=25, and the no-arg body sets num1=num, leaving 25.
        • Java 25 permits restricted statements before explicit constructor invocation; the older first-statement rule must be version qualified.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-V

    • OOP11 Methods, getters and setters

      • A method has modifiers, return type, name, parameter list and body: public int getAge(){return age;}.
        • A void method returns no value.
        • Parameters name the inputs in the declaration; arguments supply values at a call.
        • An instance method can be invoked as object.method(), or with an implicit this inside suitable instance context.
      • An accessor/getter returns information; a mutator/setter changes state.
        • Encapsulation does not require blindly generating setters for every field: validate changes and expose only useful operations.
        • For a bank account, deposit must reject negative amounts.
        • A private field cannot normally be accessed directly by a separately declared subclass, even with this.field; use a permitted parent operation.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP12 Method overloading and compile-time selection

      • Overloaded methods share a name but have different parameter types, counts or type order.
        • Return type alone is insufficient in Java and C++.
        • Overloads can also arise through inherited methods; “same class only” is a teaching simplification. f(int), f(double) and f(int,int) are distinct, but changing a parameter name does not create an overload.
      • The compiler selects the applicable signature from the declared argument types and conversions. int arguments usually choose an exact int overload rather than a wider double overload.
        • A return type is not part of an ordinary Java method signature.
        • Distinguish a different signature from overriding an inherited signature.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP13 Inheritance and useful relationships

      • class Dog extends Animal declares a subclass/derived/child of a superclass/base/parent.
        • A class extends one direct class and can implement multiple interfaces.
        • Single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance mean one parent, a chain, and several children of one parent.
        • Java does not permit class Dog extends Animal,Mammal.
      • Use inheritance when a subtype can satisfy the parent’s contract: Dog is an Animal.
        • For shared Pet.name and speak(), put common state/contract in Pet, specialized fetch() in Dog, and appropriate speak() implementations in Dog and Cat.
        • Composition represents has-a, such as Car containing Engine.
        • Reuse alone does not justify an invalid is-a relationship.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP14 Overriding and restrictions

      • A subclass overrides an eligible inherited instance method with the same signature and a compatible return type; a covariant reference return may be a subtype.
        • Visibility cannot become more restrictive, and checked exceptions cannot be broadened incompatibly. @Override requests compiler checking; Java has no override keyword.
        • Constructors, final methods, static methods and private parent methods are not overridden.
      • A same-signature child method matching a private parent method is an independent declaration, not runtime overriding and not ordinary static-method hiding.
        • An abstract inherited method is implemented by an overriding method in a concrete subclass.
        • Merely reusing a name in two unrelated classes does not establish overriding.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP15 Dynamic dispatch: declared type versus actual type

      • For Animal a=new Dog(), Animal is the declared type and Dog the actual type.
        • The declared type determines which member operations compile.
        • If fetch() exists only in Dog, a.fetch() fails compilation.
        • For an eligible overridden sound(), a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() at runtime.
      • To solve dispatch questions: check the declaration and visibility, determine the compile-time signature, then identify the object’s runtime class and its most specific override.
        • An array Animal[]{new Dog(),new Cat()} can call speak() on each using one loop.
        • New subclasses can supply behavior without rewriting this generic loop, which is the practical meaning of extensibility.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP16 this, super, fields and static hiding

      • Java this denotes the current object; this.name=name distinguishes a field from a parameter. super.name selects a hidden superclass field; super.sound() directly requests the parent implementation.
        • It does not create a second parent object.
        • An unqualified instance call may dispatch dynamically; an explicit super call is different.
      • Fields are hidden rather than dynamically overridden, and same-signature static methods hide rather than override.
        • With Animal a=new Dog(), a.staticMethod() resolves using Animal’s compile-time type.
        • Prefer Animal.staticMethod() for clarity.
        • Java this and super are unavailable as current-instance references in static context.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP17 C++ this and language-specific assumptions

      • In ordinary C++17 non-static member functions, this is a pointer to the object on which the function is called; this->field selects a member.
        • It is often explained as an implicit object argument to a member function call.
        • It is not an argument passed to member variables, and a static member function has no this pointer.
      • C++ runtime polymorphism requires a virtual function when calling through a base pointer/reference.
        • C++ may inherit multiple classes; Java permits multiple interface types instead.
        • C++ object-value assignment can copy an object, whereas assigning Java class variables copies references.
        • Never transfer Java dispatch or memory-management assumptions to a C++ question without checking the code.
      • References: OOP-T, OOP-M

    • OOP18 Abstract classes and concrete implementations

      • An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated but can define fields, constructors, abstract methods and concrete methods.
        • It need not contain an abstract method.
        • An abstract method has no body; abstract and final conflict because an operation cannot require overriding while forbidding it.
      • A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of all required abstract methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract.
        • If parent declares abstract String welcome(), a String welcome() implementation is required; int welcome() is incompatible, and welcome(int) merely adds an overload.
        • A valid class can contain both the required implementation and an unrelated overload.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP19 Interfaces: contracts and modern Java

      • interface Payable{double getPaymentAmount();} declares an abstract public operation. class Invoice implements Payable must provide public double getPaymentAmount(), perhaps returning getQuantity()*getPricePerItem().
        • A class can extend a superclass and implement zero or more interfaces.
        • An interface can extend several interfaces.
        • No interface instance fields or constructors exist; fields are implicitly public static final.
      • A method declaration without private, default or static is implicitly public abstract.
        • Modern interfaces may also have default/static method bodies, and Java 9+ private helper methods.
        • The module’s claim that every interface method lacks a body is outdated.
        • Implementations must satisfy all inherited abstract contracts; they may inherit suitable public implementations.
        • Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly, but references may hold implementing objects, anonymous implementations or suitable functional-interface lambdas.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G, OOP-I

    • OOP20 Conflicting interface methods and abstract class choice

      • Use an abstract class for shared state, construction and common implementation; use an interface for a capability across unrelated classes and multiple type inheritance.
        • A concrete inherited class method takes precedence over an interface default.
        • An inherited abstract class declaration can require a concrete subclass to implement the operation rather than silently adopting a default.
      • Unrelated interfaces providing conflicting defaults require an explicit resolution; interfaces do not remove every diamond ambiguity.
        • If two compatible interfaces merely declare the same abstract signature, one public implementation can satisfy both.
        • If return types or other contracts conflict, additional declarations may still be impossible.
        • The answer to “same method in abstract class and interface” depends on whether each is abstract or implemented and whether their signatures are compatible.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-I

    • OOP21 Casts and instanceof

      • Upcasting a subclass reference to a superclass is implicit and does not change the object.
        • A downcast may pass compile-time type checks yet fail at runtime.
        • Car a=new Car(); Ferrari f=(Ferrari)a; throws ClassCastException before subsequent drive() or brake() calls.
        • It does not turn a plain Car into a Ferrari.
      • Use if(a instanceof Ferrari) before narrowing when the dynamic type is uncertain. null instanceof Ferrari is false; casting null yields null, although dereferencing it fails.
        • For Object obj="Hello", (String)obj succeeds and (Integer)obj throws ClassCastException.
        • A literal 'Hello' is invalid Java syntax, so the bank’s single-quoted version must be clarified first.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP22 Identity, equals, toString and immutable strings

      • For object references, == tests identity; equals invokes the class’s equality policy.
        • Object.equals uses identity unless overridden; String.equals compares character content.
        • Equal objects must have equal hashCode values when that contract is implemented. toString gives a textual representation, not an equality test.
      • Java String objects are immutable. text += " World" assigns a reference to a new concatenated result and can print Hello World without mutating the original String object. final class String prevents subclassing; final alone does not make arbitrary objects immutable. charAt(index) returns a char; length() counts UTF-16 units; substring(begin,end) excludes end.
        • Character.toUpperCase(ch) converts a character, and matches(String regex) takes a regular-expression parameter named regex.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP23 Expressions: numbers, bits and text output

      • Java evaluates operands left to right while respecting precedence.
        • With n=6,m=15,p=3, n-=m then n*=p leaves -27. 6-2+10%4+7 is 13.
        • In 8-2*5*(3+9/3)+6/3, the result is -50.
        • Integer 6/4 is 1; double 6.0/4 is 1.5.
        • Unlike C++, Java % also accepts floating-point operands.
      • For bitwise values, write binary columns: 11&9=9; 9^3=10; 10|12=14. && and || short circuit Boolean operands; & and | can also operate on Boolean values without short circuiting.
        • Printing Boolean true gives lowercase true, not 1 or uppercase TRUE.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP24 Increment order and the character-space trap

      • Starting x=5, printing x++ then ++x gives 5 then 7.
        • For int y=++x*x--, Java uses 6*6=36 and leaves x=5.
        • System.out.println(x + ' ' + y) then adds char space’s numeric value 32, so it prints 73.
        • To print separated values, use x + " " + y instead.
      • Once a String operand is encountered, + concatenates in left-to-right groups: 1+2+"x" gives "3x", while "x"+1+2 gives "x12".
        • Do not describe intended separated output as the output of a single-quoted character expression.
        • This correction directly addresses the new guide’s incorrect key.
      • References: OOP-G, OOP-X

    • OOP25 Control flow traces and exact printing

      • while and for pre-test and may execute zero times; do-while post-tests and executes once. break exits the loop; continue skips its remaining body and then runs a for update.
        • Traditional colon-style switch labels fall through without break.
        • Choice 1 printing Hello then case 2 printing you and breaking is followed by Goodbye outside the switch; default is skipped.
      • Count executions independently from printing.
        • For i=0..4, if(i%2==0) print(i+" "); followed unconditionally by print(i+1); produces "0 122 344 5".
        • A loop summing j=1..10 yields 55.
        • In if(a)... else if(a&&b)..., the second condition can never be true on a path reaching it because a is already false.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP26 Arrays: creation, bounds and ragged rows

      • int[] a=new int[5]; and int a[]={1,2,3}; are valid. int[] a={}; creates a zero-length array; explicit new is unnecessary in a declaration initializer. int a[],b; makes only a an array; int[] c,d; makes both arrays.
        • Array objects have fixed length after creation, although the reference may be reassigned.
        • Elements have a declared common component type, which may be a superclass/interface.
      • Valid indices are 0..a.length-1; an invalid access throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
        • Java two-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays and may be ragged: {{12,-9,8},{7,14},{-32,-1,0}} has row lengths 3,2,3.
        • Java does not expose a portable physical contiguity guarantee, so a language-level answer should not rely on raw addresses.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP27 Array algorithms, sort and copy APIs

      • For int[] a=new int[4], setting a[i]=i*3 and accumulating yields 0+3+6+9=18.
        • To average an array, sum every element and divide by its length using floating arithmetic; handle zero length separately.
        • Floating representations and printing can differ from a rounded mathematical result.
        • The six-value bank average is mathematically 98.8/6, approximately 16.46666667, not an exact assertion about the printed string.
      • java.util.Arrays.sort(a) sorts in place.
        • System.arraycopy(src,srcPos,dst,dstPos,length) copies into an existing array; its exact spelling uses lowercase c. Arrays.copyOf(a,n) creates a copy. a=b merely aliases the same array.
        • Random access is the reliable array advantage; size is bounded by implementation/resources, not unlimited.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP28 Packages, imports and command-line tools

      • package p; precedes imports; imports precede top-level type declarations. import p.*; imports accessible types from p as needed, not types in p.sub automatically.
        • Packages organize names and control access; hierarchical spelling does not grant special access between a package and its subpackages. java.lang is implicitly imported; java.util supplies utilities; java.io supplies I/O; java.awt includes Button and Checkbox.
      • Ordinary compilation uses javac Test.java, producing bytecode, then java Test launches the class.
        • Modern Java can also launch a source file using java Test.java, so an unrestricted run-command question can have multiple answers.
        • For ordinary public top-level types, filename and type name match.
        • Capitalized class names and lowercase method names are conventions, not universal syntax requirements.
        • Java identifiers are case sensitive; $ is allowed but @ is not an identifier character.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP29 Exception hierarchy and checked obligations

      • Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches.
        • RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked; other throwable classes are checked.
        • IOException, FileNotFoundException and SQLException are standard checked examples.
        • ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked.
        • A missing semicolon or undeclared variable is a compile-time source error, not a checked exception.
      • Checked does not mean the exception occurs at compile time: the compiler checks an obligation to catch or declare it, while an actual throw occurs at runtime.
        • A custom exception can extend Exception or RuntimeException.
        • Error normally signals serious conditions for which routine recovery is inappropriate; it is not technically impossible to catch an Error.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-G, OOP-E

    • OOP30 throw, throws and catch selection

      • throw new IOException("message") actively throws a value; throws IOException in a signature declares a possible checked exception.
        • A caller must handle or propagate checked obligations. try encloses guarded operations; a matching catch handles the thrown type or a subtype.
        • Execution skips the remainder of the try when a throw occurs.
      • Catch blocks are considered in source order.
        • Place FileNotFoundException before IOException and IOException before Exception; a general catch before a subtype catch makes that later handler unreachable and prevents compilation.
        • If no catch matches, the exception propagates outward and an uncaught exception terminates its thread.
        • Multiple catch blocks are allowed; catch(IOException | SQLException e) handles alternatives, which must not be related by subclassing.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-G, OOP-E

    • OOP31 finally, cleanup and diagnostic information

      • finally normally executes after try and any selected catch, including when leaving by return or propagating an exception.
        • It is not guaranteed if the process/JVM exits or crashes, or control never leaves the try.
        • A return expression is evaluated before finally; a finally return overrides the pending return and can suppress an exception, so avoid that pattern.
      • try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources even on exceptional exit. getMessage returns the message, toString normally includes type and message, and printStackTrace shows exception information and recorded call frames for diagnosis.
        • Tests should cover expected success, caught failures and propagation.
        • Exception handling does not replace validation or correct an algorithm’s logic automatically.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-G, OOP-C

    • OOP32 Streams, GUI events and JDBC practice

      • InputStream/OutputStream read and write bytes; Reader/Writer handle text characters through an encoding.
        • Close resources deterministically.
        • A read returning -1 signals end-of-stream.
        • A GUI event source notifies registered listeners; a button can call an ActionListener’s actionPerformed method.
        • In Swing, update components on the event dispatch thread and keep handlers short so the interface remains responsive.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-UI

    • OOP33 JDBC flow from user action to database

      • A JDBC operation obtains a Connection, prepares SQL, binds values, executes and processes results, then closes resources.
        • For PreparedStatement ps=con.prepareStatement("SELECT name FROM Student WHERE id=?"), ps.setInt(1,id) binds the first parameter. executeQuery returns a ResultSet; rs.next() moves to each row before reading columns. executeUpdate returns an affected-row count for updates.
      • Parameter binding keeps values separate from SQL syntax.
        • Catch or declare SQLException.
        • When several writes form one operation, disable auto-commit, commit on success and roll back on failure.
        • A GUI handler should delegate a slow database operation away from its UI thread, then display the result through the appropriate UI mechanism.
      • References: OOP-J

    • OOP34 Legacy applets and lifecycle questions

      • In the historical applet model, Java code was embedded in an HTML document and executed by a compatible JVM host/plugin or applet viewer. init initializes once; start follows initialization and resumes activity; stop suspends activity when the host deactivates it; destroy performs final cleanup before unloading. paint draws content and is not a constructor.
      • Treat these as historical bank concepts, not instructions for modern browser deployment. destroy is not defined exclusively as “browser shuts down”: the host may destroy an applet on unloading, and abrupt process termination does not guarantee cleanup.
        • A JVM alone is also not the complete browser embedding environment.
      • References: OOP-L

    • OOP35 Android Activity, Intent, manifest and layouts

      • An Android Activity is a component providing an entry point for user interaction, often corresponding to a screen.
        • An Intent describes a requested action or explicit target; extras carry values between activities.
        • For example, putExtra("id",17) attaches an ID for the destination to read.
        • A content provider shares structured data, while a broadcast receiver handles broadcast messages; neither is the ordinary answer for starting an activity with parameters.
      • References: OOP-D1, OOP-D2

    • OOP36 Android app declarations and packaging

      • AndroidManifest.xml declares essential app metadata such as components, permissions and intent filters.
        • It is not executable code and does not contain all source or layout details.
        • Traditional view-based layout containers such as LinearLayout and RelativeLayout derive from android.view.ViewGroup, which contains child views.
      • An .apk is an Android package archive used for installation and runtime contents. “Android Package Kit” is a common exam expansion; Android’s documentation calls it an Android package.
        • A manifest describes the package, while layout resources describe views.
        • These distinctions explain the old bank’s Android questions outside the main Java module.
      • References: OOP-D3, OOP-D4, OOP-D5

    • OOP37 Resolve defective wording and syntax before tracing

      • Source OCR sometimes changes extends to Extends, println to printIn/printin, constructor class names, braces, or operators such as <= and ==.
        • Java is case sensitive: the literal malformed program may not compile even when an intended trace is easy to infer.
        • For the repaired even-i loop with i=2,4,6,8,10 and i%4==0, only 16 and 64 print; an offered output that adds other values is wrong.
      • For the corrupted SS118 options, the recovered source’s valid block implements public String welcome() and additionally overloads welcome(int).
        • The current A–D labels are fragments and cannot identify that block reliably.
        • Report the required signature, not a fabricated letter.
        • Likewise a numeric mean rounded in choices is not necessarily the exact Java printed output.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP38 Ambiguities that require a stated interpretation

      • The single-choice bank sometimes supplies multiple valid statements: a static constant and a parameter-only utility may both be suitable static members; multiple array declarations/initializers can be legal; an abstract class may contain a complete interface implementation.
        • Encapsulation and abstraction overlap, so choose only when the requested emphasis is specific.
      • An interface supports multiple type inheritance and abstraction, making broad purpose options overlap. “All methods are public abstract” needs a restricted abstract-declaration or legacy interpretation. “Only subclasses” cannot be enforced by Java protected because the same package also has access.
        • No keyword implements overriding: it is recognized from compatible declarations, and @Override is an annotation.
        • For C++ this, replace erroneous “variables receive the hidden argument” with “ordinary non-static member functions have an implicit object”.
      • References: OOP-M, OOP-N, OOP-G

    • OOP39 Language classifications and portability in the bank

      • Under the conventional introductory generation taxonomy, general-purpose high-level languages such as C++, Java, Python and Perl are third generation.
        • The taxonomy is separate from object orientation and from compilation versus interpretation.
        • Java source normally compiles to JVM bytecode, and a compatible JVM plus libraries supports portability across systems.
      • Portability still depends on compatible APIs, versions and environment assumptions; it is not an unconditional guarantee for any program on any device.
        • Java supports objects and classes but also primitive values. “Difficult to learn” is a subjective judgment rather than a technical language property.
