        • Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.
      • To display or count nodes, follow next from head until null, processing each node.
        • Counting is Theta(n) unless size is maintained.
        • An array-linked list still follows links unless separately position-indexed.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA09 Update links without losing the rest of the list

      • Prepend with new.next=head; head=new.
        • To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new.
        • Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it.
        • Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.
      • Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known.
        • Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null.
        • To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation.
        • Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.
      • Reverse a chain with prev=null, cur=head: save next=cur.next; set cur.next=prev; advance prev=cur and cur=next; finish with head=prev.
        • This is linear time and constant extra pointers.
      • Work it through
        • For 3→7→9, insert 5 after 3: first point 5 at 7, then 3 at 5. Reversing those assignments can lose access to 7→9.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA10 Doubly linked, circular and practical list choices

      • Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends.
        • Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor.
        • A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.
      • Lists suit changing sequences when references to insertion positions are already available.
        • Finding a position is still linear.
        • Lists can hold polynomial terms (coefficient, exponent), directory or block links, child lists in nonbinary trees, and hash chains.
        • Browser history can use a doubly linked cursor.
        • A playlist may be circular; airline seat lookup requires a specified seat-record model, not an automatic linked-list answer.
      • OperationArraySingly linked list
        Access index iO(1)O(n) worst
        Insert at frontO(n) shiftsO(1)
        AppendO(1) with spare capacityO(1) with tail; O(n) head only
        Delete tailO(1)O(n), predecessor needed
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA11 Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

      • Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO.
        • Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.
        • With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full.
        • Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].
      • A count-based alternative uses size=0 and A[size++]=x. Do not combine its empty/full tests with the top-index convention.
        • Fixed-array push/pop are constant time.
        • Linked stacks achieve constant time by inserting and deleting at the head; using a singly linked tail for pop would require a predecessor traversal.
      • Exam trap
        • Overflow is an attempted insertion into full storage; underflow is an attempted removal from empty storage. Merely checking isEmpty does not underflow.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA12 Trace stack operations and reversible actions

      • Write the stack bottom-to-top after every instruction and record popped values separately.
        • Push 1, push 2, pop emits 2 and leaves [1].
        • Push 1, push 2, pop, pop, pop then emits 2,1,1; push 2, pop emits 2.
        • The complete output is 2,2,1,1,2.
      • Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first.
        • Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top.
        • Reversal pushes input then pops it.
        • Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back.
        • A new edit after undo normally clears redo.
        • DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA13 Infix, postfix and prefix expressions

      • Infix places an operator between operands and uses precedence and parentheses.
        • Prefix places it first; postfix places it last.
        • Their fixed operator arity determines grouping.
        • To convert infix to postfix, output operands immediately and hold operators on a stack.
        • Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new operator; also pop equal precedence for left-associative operators.
        • Parentheses temporarily override this order.
      • To evaluate postfix, push operands.
        • At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right.
        • Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.
      • Work it through
        • A+B*C-D/E becomes ABC*+DE/-. For 8 3 -, pop 3 then 8, producing 5. (A+B)*C becomes AB+C* and prefix *+ABC.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT, DSA_PREFIX

    • DSA14 Queues preserve arrival order

      • An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front.
        • This is FIFO or first-come, first-served.
        • A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head.
        • The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both.
        • With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.
      • FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration.
        • A play sequence can also use a queue.
        • Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.
      • Work it through
        • Enqueue 4,8; peek is 4, so a conditional removal only if peek>5 does nothing. Enqueue 1,6 then dequeue: [8,1,6].
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA15 Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

      • A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front.
        • A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic.
        • Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.
      • Dequeue reads A[front], sets front=(front+1)%C and decreases size.
        • An alternative reserves one unused slot and uses next(rear)==front for full; its empty test and capacity differ.
        • State the convention before tracing.
      • Work it through
        • Full capacity-six [11,13,15,17,19,21], front=0: remove 11, then enqueue 9 into slot 0. Physical array: [9,13,15,17,19,21]; logical front-to-rear queue: [13,15,17,19,21,9]. A noncircular version can instead overflow.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA16 Deques, merging and splitting queues

      • A deque permits both-end insertion/removal without guaranteeing middle access.
        • Endpoint-linked operations are constant but middle indexing is linear.
        • A circular-array deque may support indexed access.
        • Dequeue names removal; deque names the structure.
      • Merging FIFO queues needs an explicit policy: append one sequence after another or alternate their fronts.
        • Splitting by a predicate preserves each subgroup’s original order if each removed item is appended to its matching output queue.
        • A fixed-capacity buffer also needs a full-policy choice: reject, block or overwrite.
        • Capacity alone does not choose a policy.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA17 Priority queues serve by priority, with an explicit tie rule

      • A priority queue returns the smallest or largest priority key under its convention.
        • Urgent patients may precede earlier arrivals.
        • Insertions and extractions can interleave.
        • Binary heaps support constant peek and logarithmic insert/extract.
      • Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff.
        • Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee.
        • If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter).
        • Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing.
      • Exam trap
        • The new guide assumes FIFO ties without defining stability. That is an additional policy, not a universal priority-queue rule.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_PQ

    • DSA18 Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

      • A rooted tree has one parentless root and one parent per other node.
        • It is connected and acyclic, has n-1 edges, and one path between any pair.
        • Depth counts root-to-node edges; height is maximum depth.
        • A single-node tree therefore has height zero.
        • Leaves have no children.
      • Binary means at most two children.
        • Full means each node has zero or two children.
        • Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left.
        • Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children.
        • Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA19 BST search follows a global ordering invariant

      • With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.
        • Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction.
        • Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.
      • Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null.
        • Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf.
        • Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain.
        • Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit.
        • An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.
      • Standard optimal-BST dynamic programming tries each possible root for each key interval: O(n²) intervals times O(n) roots gives O(n³) construction.
        • It minimizes probability-weighted search depth, not necessarily worst-case height.
      • Work it through
        • Insert 40,20,50,10,30,60: root children are 20 and 50; 20 has 10,30; 50 has right child 60. Height is two edges. Sorted insertions 1,2,3,4,5 instead form a right chain.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT, DSA_OBST

    • DSA20 Tree traversal is a rule you can execute

      • Preorder visits node,left,right; inorder left,node,right; postorder left,right,node.
        • Apply recursively; null children do nothing.
        • Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST.
        • Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue.
      • For root 4, children 2 and 6, and leaves 1,3,5,7: preorder is 4,2,1,3,6,5,7; inorder is 1,2,3,4,5,6,7; postorder is 1,3,2,5,7,6,4.
        • Level order is 4,2,6,1,3,5,7.
        • Randomized visitation is possible; it is simply not one of these standard named depth-first orders.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA21 BST deletion preserves every subtree restriction

      • A leaf can be detached by clearing its parent link.
        • For one child, make the parent bypass the node and point to the child.
        • For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location.
        • That second deletion has at most one child.
      • Deletion by merging is another approach.
        • Promote the right subtree and attach the entire old left subtree to the minimum node in the promoted right subtree; or use the symmetric left promotion.
        • Update root itself when deleting root.
        • Copying values and reconnecting subtrees can yield different valid shapes, so a trace must name its deletion method.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA22 Balanced trees prevent the sorted-input chain

      • AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1.
        • After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary.
        • LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric.
        • Rotations preserve inorder key order.
      • Inserting 30,20,10 triggers LL repair: 20 becomes root with children 10,30.
        • Red-black colouring rules provide another logarithmic-height discipline.
        • Both prevent linear worst-case search; balanced trees also support ordered ranges unlike ordinary hashing.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_BAL

    • DSA23 A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

      • A binary max-heap is complete with each parent at least its children; a min-heap reverses this order.
        • Unlike BSTs, heaps do not order entire subtrees.
        • The root is maximum.
        • If all keys are distinct, the second largest is a root child.
        • With duplicate maxima, the second largest distinct value may be deeper: [9,9,9,8,7,6,5] is a valid max-heap and that value is 8 at index 3.
        • The minimum may be any leaf, requiring linear worst-case scanning.
      • Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0.
        • One-based representation uses children 2i,2i+1 and parent floor(i/2).
        • A child exists only if its index is inside the current heap size.
      • Exam trap
        • A question offering right child 2i+1 assumes one-based indexing. It conflicts with the original module’s zero-based convention unless that convention is changed.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA24 Restore a heap after insertion or removal

      • Insert at the next complete-tree position and swap upward while parent order is violated.
        • To remove the root, move the final element to root, reduce heap size, then swap downward with the more dominant child until order holds.
        • Each path has logarithmic length.
        • Building bottom-up by sinking internal nodes takes linear total time; repeated independent insertions give an O(n log n) construction bound.
      • Work it through
        • Max-heap [10,8,6,2,1,4,5]: remove 10, move 5 to root and sink, giving [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8, move 4 up then exchange with 6: [6,5,4,2,1].
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_PQ

    • DSA25 Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

      • Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots.
        • A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity.
        • With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.
      • Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function.
        • Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly.
        • Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup.
        • Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_UNIV

    • DSA26 Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

      • Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list.
        • Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases.
        • Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.
      • Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5.
        • Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots.
        • Neither method guarantees no collisions.
        • Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.
      • At h(k)=3 in a seven-slot linear-probing table, addresses wrap 3,4,5,6,0,1,2.
        • A home address is not guaranteed to remain the final slot.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_HASH

    • DSA27 Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts

      • A map associates unique keys with values; different keys may share values, and entries can be traversed.
        • A set forbids duplicate elements.
        • Null and iteration-order policies depend on implementation.
        • Lists preserve positions and generally allow duplicates; Java LinkedList also permits null.
      • A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering.
        • A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list.
        • Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full.
        • No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.
      • References: DSA_MAP, DSA_SET, DSA_JAVA, DSA_SHORT, DSA_CACHE

    • DSA28 Linear search: a scan with an early stop

      • Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted.
        • Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too.
        • A first-element match costs Theta(1).
        • An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time.
        • Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.
      • For a single unsorted query, sorting first is rarely justified.
        • Small lists may favour scanning because setup matters.
        • Sorting does not avoid examining all values for mean, variance or arbitrary parity counts.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA29 Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

      • On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1.
        • Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2.
        • Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1.
        • Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi.
        • Reverse comparisons for descending order.
        • Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.
      • Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.
        • Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth.
        • Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time.
        • Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.
      • Work it through
        • Find 19 in [11,13,15,17,19,21]: mid=2 gives 15; search indices 3..5; mid=4 gives 19. Binary debugging needs an ordered good/bad boundary, not arbitrary fault locations.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA30 Search variants need their own assumptions

      • Interpolation search estimates the index from numeric values: lo+(hi-lo)×(key-A[lo])/(A[hi]-A[lo]), rounded to a valid index.
        • Guard equal endpoints and out-of-range targets.
        • On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time.
        • Binary search gives a logarithmic worst bound without that distribution assumption.
      • Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic.
        • Jump search probes block boundaries then scans within a block.
        • Regular intervals could mean unit-step scanning or larger jumps.
        • Interpolation also needs sortedness, so prerequisite questions can overlap binary search.
      • References: DSA_INTERP, DSA_SEARCH, DSA_JUMP

    • DSA31 Compare sorting rules, not just algorithm names

      • Stable sorting preserves the input order of equal keys.
        • An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested.
        • There is no single algorithm identified by stable or in-place alone.
        • State the implementation, input case and resource being compared.
      • MethodBest / average / worst timeExtra storage; usual stability
        Bubble with early stopn / n² / n²constant; stable
        Selectionn² / n² / n²constant; unstable
        Insertionn / n² / n²constant; stable
        Quicksortn log n / n log n / n²stack usually log n average, n worst; unstable
        Ordinary array mergesortn log n in all caseslinear; stable with left-first ties
        HeapsortO(n log n) bound in all casesconstant with iterative sink; unstable
      • Exam trap
        • Big-O bounds can overlap. n log(n²)=2n log n, so it has the same growth as n log n, unlike n(log n)².
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA32 Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

      • For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right.
        • The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass.
        • Shrink the next pass by one position.
        • Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.
      • Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes.
        • A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic.
        • Strict swaps preserve equal-key order.
        • Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.
      • Work it through
        • [4,1,3,2] → [1,4,3,2] → [1,3,4,2] → [1,3,2,4] after the first pass.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA33 Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

      • At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].
        • There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order.
        • At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed.
        • A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.
      • Selection suits expensive record moves with cheap key comparisons, not every large dataset.
        • It is unstable: exchanging first 2a with 1 in [2a,2b,1] gives [1,2b,2a].
        • Constant extra element storage is shared by several sorts.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA34 Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

      • Begin with the first element already sorted.
        • For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.
        • That gives n-1 insertion passes.
        • On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time.
        • Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.
      • Few inversions mean few shifts, favouring insertion for nearly sorted or small arrays.
        • Shift only strictly larger keys for stability.
        • A linked implementation saves array shifts but still must locate each insertion position.
      • Work it through
        • Insert 2 into prefix [1,4,7]: save 2, move 7 then 4 right, and write 2 after 1. The sorted prefix becomes [1,2,4,7].
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA35 Shell sort: insertion across decreasing gaps

      • Choose a sequence of positive gaps ending at 1.
        • For each gap h, insertion-sort each subsequence of positions h apart.
        • The final h=1 pass finishes ordinary sorting after earlier long moves have reduced disorder.
        • An h-sorted array satisfies A[j]≤A[j+h] wherever both indices exist.
      • The O(n^(3/2)) bound depends on gaps; Knuth increments 1,4,13,… have that worst order.
        • Shell sort is generally unstable because distant moves can reorder ties; extra element storage is constant.
      • Work it through
        • For [5,4,3,2,1], gap 3 sorts positions (0,3) and (1,4), giving [2,1,3,5,4]. Gap 1 then produces [1,2,3,4,5].
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_SHELL

    • DSA36 Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

      • Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces.
        • Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work.
        • Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model.
        • Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.
      • A final pivot 5 in the bank’s ten distinct values has five smaller values before it and four larger after it.
        • Internal orders depend on the partition algorithm; several candidate arrays can satisfy the invariant.
        • State the algorithm before predicting one exact array.
        • Quicksort normally rearranges in the same array but recursive storage can be linear in the worst case.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_NEW, DSA_SHORT

    • DSA37 Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

      • Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front.
        • With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order.
        • Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer.
        • There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
      • Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively.
        • In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant.
        • Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory.
        • External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_EXTERNAL

    • DSA38 Heapsort: repeatedly place the extreme at the end

      • For ascending in-place heapsort, build a max-heap over the array.
        • Exchange root with the final active element, shrink the active heap, and sink the new root.
        • The removed maximum now belongs in the sorted suffix.
        • Repeat until one active item remains.
      • Building with bottom-up sinking is linear; repeated extraction gives O(n log n) worst time.
        • Iterative sinking needs constant auxiliary storage.
        • The method is generally unstable because long root-to-end exchanges can reorder equal keys.
        • It is not uniquely the method for sorting by priorities: any comparison sort can compare a priority field.
        • Heap extraction is its distinctive mechanism.
      • References: DSA_MOD

    • DSA39 Radix sorting uses key digits, not arbitrary magic

      • LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left.
        • Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits.
        • With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
      • MSD begins at leading digits and subdivides equal-prefix groups.
        • Strings are lexicographically comparable.
        • Radix methods require accessible digits and length/signed-value conventions, not arbitrary unstructured keys.
        • Large radix, long keys or small n may favour comparison sorting.
      • References: DSA_RADIX

    • DSA40 Graphs: represent the relationships you actually need

      • A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships.
        • Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected.
        • Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges.
        • DAG expands to directed acyclic graph.
        • Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.
      • A matrix uses Theta(V²) space and constant edge lookup.
        • Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours.
        • Dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts.
        • Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.
      • References: DSA_SHORT

    • DSA41 BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

      • Mark the source when enqueuing it.
        • Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it.
        • Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed.
        • FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.
      • BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.
        • With adjacency lists it costs O(V+E); scanning a matrix costs O(V²).
        • To traverse a disconnected graph, restart from each unvisited vertex.
        • Neighbour order affects tied traversal order but not minimum distances.
      • Work it through
        • Edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D; alphabetical neighbours: queue [A] → [B,C] → [C,D] → [D] → []. Discovery order A,B,C,D; D has distance two.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_GRAPH

    • DSA42 DFS: finish a branch before returning

      • Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours.
        • An explicit stack can store pending work instead.
        • Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.
        • Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.
      • Using the same graph and alphabetical neighbours, recursive DFS can discover A,B,D,C. Its path is a valid reachability witness but not necessarily shortest.
        • Adjacency-list cost is O(V+E), with O(V) visited state and possible stack depth.
        • DFS supports cycle and connectivity analysis; a directed cycle test distinguishes active recursion vertices from already completed ones.
      • References: DSA_SHORT

    • DSA43 Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives

      • For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)).
        • A min-priority queue supports the next choice.
        • BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.
      • An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph.
        • Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex.
        • Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected.
        • An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs.
      • Work it through
        • Triangle weights AB=1, BC=2, AC=10: Prim or Kruskal selects AB,BC, total 3. Dijkstra from A gets B=1 and improves C from 10 to 3 through B.
      • References: DSA_SHORT, DSA_SP, DSA_MST

    • DSA44 Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

      • Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.
        • For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending).
        • It is linear time with constant working storage.
        • Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case.
      • Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text.
        • Preprocess the pattern’s longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
        • After mismatch, fall back using those prefix lengths rather than restarting comparisons from the beginning; the text pointer need not move backward.
        • Pattern preprocessing plus scanning takes O(pattern length+text length).
      • Work it through
        • For [-2,3,-1,4,-5], Kadane ending values are -2,3,2,6,1, so best is 6 from [3,-1,4]. Pattern ABAB has prefix lengths [0,0,1,2].
      • References: DSA_KADANE, DSA_KMP

    • DSA45 Handle missing data and misleading labels explicitly

      • A trace needs the complete operation sequence, initial state, capacity and output orientation.
        • State these assumptions before calculating.
        • A highlighted key never removes overlapping valid choices.
      • Specify whether a question asks which structure can implement something or which is best under stated costs.
        • ADTs do not force one representation, and serial-access memory is not inherently LIFO.
        • A heap file is an unordered database record file, unrelated to a binary heap: insertion uses available space, scanning can find records, and ordered output requires sorting or an index.
        • It need not insert at the beginning.
      • References: DSA_MOD, DSA_DB

  • Web Programming

    • Build a connected model of browser markup, CSS, JavaScript, server processing and persistent data.
      • Read code literally before tracing it.
      • Unless a section explicitly discusses legacy syntax, JavaScript means modern ECMAScript in a browser and PHP means PHP 8.x; database examples use MySQLi or PDO with a configured MySQL connection.
    • Trace input → request → server validation → database → response → DOM update, including failures and permissions.
    • Practise CSS winner/box calculations and small JS/PHP traces; record values and types after every statement.
    • Compare GET/POST, browser/server state, callbacks/concurrency and parameterization/output encoding.
      • Repair a malformed task before trusting its key.
    • Sections in this course
      Browser, server and technology rolesHosting, URLs and static versus dynamic contentRead an HTTP/1.1 exchangeMethods, status and GET/POST reasoningHTTPS and resource-oriented APIsHTML document, text and metadataLinks, images and accessible meaningLists, tables and navigationForm controls and successful submissionFrames, media and graphicsCSS attachment and selector meaningResolve cascade, specificity and inheritanceStyle properties and box calculationsLayout, alignment and responsive designJavaScript syntax, inclusion and declarationsTypes, conversions and missing valuesTrace assignments, comparisons and postfix updatesMath, string and array API microtracesControl flow, functions and errorsDOM selection, creation and safe updatesEvents and validated submissionWindow, dialogs and browser propertiesPHP syntax, names and typesPHP output, strings and comparisonsPHP scope, parameters and persistent localsPHP arrays, loops and callable behaviorRequest data, server validation and injectionCookies and browser storageServer sessions and the authorization trust pathUploads, files and storage safetyDatabase connections, TLS and actual APIsSQL operations, result rows and safe renderingPHP includes, objects and datesAJAX and response handlingPolling, WebSockets and data formatsNode server, event loop and scalingRaces, locks and transaction invariantsFrameworks and version-aware setupManage content, performance and revisionsAssemble and evaluate an end-to-end featureLiteral code defects and answerability limits

    • WEB01 Browser, server and technology roles

      • The Internet connects networks; the Web is a resource system commonly using HTTP.
        • A browser/user agent requests resources and renders HTML/CSS, then runs permitted JavaScript.
        • A web/HTTP server receives requests and returns representations, sometimes invoking application code.
        • Client and server are roles and can run on the same machine.
      • HTML supplies structure/meaning; CSS controls presentation; JavaScript supplies programmable interactivity.
        • PHP, Python, JSP/Java and ASP.NET applications generate server responses and access databases; C# is commonly used with ASP.NET.
        • Node.js is a JavaScript runtime, not a separate language.
        • JavaScript can run on either side.
        • Browser scripts are sandboxed, but may access selected files/devices through permission-based APIs.
        • They are not inherently limited to trivial programs, nor can they freely access arbitrary client hardware.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB02 Hosting, URLs and static versus dynamic content

      • Hosting supplies an environment where a site is served; domain registration reserves a name, and DNS maps names to network records.
        • An ISP provides connectivity.
        • A URL identifies scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment; the host identifies the machine/service name, while a fragment selects a local document location.
      • A basic static server returns stored files; dynamic processing constructs a representation from logic, requests or data.
        • Static pages can still run interactive browser scripts, and dynamic generation need not change visible text every time.
        • A website groups resources; a page is one document/resource.
        • Open standards do not guarantee identical support for every feature in every browser.
        • Historical editor-name items refer to Microsoft FrontPage and Macromedia HomeSite5, not languages or required modern tools.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-HOMESITE, WEB-FRONTPAGE

    • WEB03 Read an HTTP/1.1 exchange

      • An HTTP/1.1 request begins with method, request-target and version, followed by header fields, a blank line, and an optional body.
        • For example, GET /courses?id=7 HTTP/1.1 followed by Host: example.edu and a terminating blank line can have no body.
        • A response begins with version, status code and optional reason phrase, then headers, blank line and permitted content.
        • Request lines are not response status lines.
      • Content-Type describes representation format; Content-Length or transfer framing establishes message boundaries when applicable.
        • HTTP is stateless in its request semantics, but applications maintain state through sessions/databases.
        • HTTP2/3 encode messages differently, so an “always contains a request line” question needs HTTP/1.x context.
        • Asynchronous use is a client programming choice, not proof that HTTP has no responses.
      • References: WEB-N, WEB-H1

    • WEB04 Methods, status and GET/POST reasoning

      • GET retrieves a representation with safe semantics; do not implement an intentional state-changing action as a GET link.
        • POST asks the target to process supplied content.
        • PUT creates/replaces the identified resource representation; DELETE requests removal of its association.
        • Safe describes intended state effects; idempotent means repeating the same request has the same intended effect, not necessarily the same response.
        • GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent; arbitrary POST is not.
      • 200 indicates success, 201 creation, 204 success without content, 301 permanent redirection, 400 malformed request, 401 missing/invalid authentication, 403 refusal, 404 unavailable/not found, and 500 an unexpected server failure.
        • GET forms usually put name/value pairs in the URL query; POST forms put them in the body.
        • Neither method encrypts data.
        • POST bodies are visible to developer tools and subject to server/configured size limits.
      • References: WEB-N, WEB-HTTP

    • WEB05 HTTPS and resource-oriented APIs

      • HTTPS uses HTTP over TLS, protecting channel confidentiality/integrity and authenticating the server under certificate checks.
        • It does not make unvalidated input safe or guarantee a trustworthy merchant.
        • A RESTful API follows constraints such as client/server separation, stateless requests, cacheability and a uniform resource interface.
        • Resources have identifiers and representations; JSON is common but not required.
        • Merely returning JSON does not prove REST.
      • For a resource /students/7, GET reads it, PUT can replace it, and DELETE requests removal, subject to authentication/authorization and validation.
        • Represent errors consistently and evaluate retry safety before repeating a request.
        • Store durable application facts server-side; stateless API requests can still operate on persistent database state.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB06 HTML document, text and metadata

      • HTML means HyperText Markup Language. <!DOCTYPE html> selects modern standards mode; <html> is the document root, <head> holds metadata, and <body> contains document content. <title> supplies the page/tab title.
        • Meta charset declares encoding; description summarizes the page; viewport controls mobile viewport behavior.
        • Heading levels h1–h6 express hierarchy, with h6 conventionally smallest in default styling, not a mandatory CSS size.
      • <p> marks paragraphs; <br> is a line break and <hr> a thematic break. <pre> preserves source whitespace; <code> marks code. <strong> indicates importance and <em> stress; <b>/<i> have other text semantics and are not identical to importance/emphasis. <sub>/<sup> mark sub/superscripts. <!-- comment --> is not displayed but remains visible in source.
        • Entities include &copy;, &lt;, &gt; and &amp;.
        • Tags mark boundaries; an element includes content and attributes, or is a void element such as img.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB07 Links, images and accessible meaning

      • Use <a href="page.html">Read</a> for a link; href is the destination, not url/link.
        • A fragment such as href="#details" links to an element with id="details". target="_self" uses the current context, _blank a new context, _parent its parent and _top the top-level context.
        • Browser preferences determine tab versus window.
      • <img src="photo.jpg" alt="Students in a lab"> supplies source and alternative text.
        • Use empty alt for purely decorative images; informative images need meaningful alternatives.
        • Width/height reserve dimensions; title is not a replacement for alt.
        • An anchor may wrap an image.
        • Give controls programmatic labels, clear link text and keyboard access; visual styling alone does not establish accessibility.
        • Attributes belong in opening tags, with unique IDs when used for document identification.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB08 Lists, tables and navigation

      • Unordered <ul> and ordered <ol> contain <li> items.
        • Ordered lists can specify start and numbering type; use CSS list-style-type for presentation.
        • A definition list uses <dl>, <dt> terms and <dd> descriptions.
        • Navigation can be a semantic <nav> containing a list of links.
      • <table> contains rows <tr>, header cells <th> and data cells <td>; a td is not the table itself. colspan spans columns; rowspan spans rows.
        • Account for occupied cells before placing the next cell, and use header associations for accessible data.
        • CSS handles borders, background, cell padding and collapsed borders; legacy bgcolor/bordercolor are not preferred styling.
        • Resetting nav ul with list-style-type:none; margin:0; padding:0 removes bullets and default spacing only; it does not itself arrange links horizontally or create a dropdown.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB09 Form controls and successful submission

      • A form’s action identifies its processing URL, method its submission method, and enctype its encoding.
        • The default method is GET.
        • Named enabled successful controls contribute values: unchecked checkboxes/radios are usually absent.
        • A label’s for matches the control’s id; name identifies its submitted field.
        • Same-name radio buttons form a single-choice group; checkboxes permit independent selections. <select> contains <option>; textarea accepts multiple lines.
      • For a text input, size indicates approximate visible width, whereas maxlength limits entered text length.
        • Neither means a server security bound. type="password" masks display but does not encrypt. submit submits; button has no submission action by itself. type=email/required give browser validation feedback; arbitrary clients can bypass it.
        • No GET/POST method universally means “parse one element at a time.”
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-INPUT

    • WEB10 Frames, media and graphics

      • Legacy frameset/frame divides a window into separate documents; frameset replaced body in old frameset documents.
        • Named targets controlled which frame changed; independent scrolling could leave other frames stationary.
        • These elements are obsolete in modern HTML.
        • An iframe embeds a document within an ordinary page and needs appropriate permissions/sandboxing for untrusted content.
      • Modern audio/video elements embed supported media, often with controls and fallback content; embed/object can also embed supported resources.
        • Thus a generic video-embedding question may have several valid tags.
        • Old bgsound or Flash examples do not imply current browser support.
        • Canvas provides script-driven bitmap drawing via a context; SVG describes scalable shapes in the DOM.
        • For a simple canvas task, obtain getContext("2d"), then use fillRect(x,y,w,h); line/path methods require beginPath/moveTo/lineTo/stroke.
        • Preserve a text alternative where graphics convey information.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB11 CSS attachment and selector meaning

      • An external sheet uses <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in head; an internal sheet uses style; an inline declaration uses an element’s style attribute.
        • External CSS promotes reuse, consistent design and caching; it does not guarantee that every page becomes smaller or accessible.
        • A rule is selector { property: value; }.
        • Comments use /* ... */.
      • Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID, h1,h2 groups selectors, nav ul selects descendants and nav>ul direct children.
        • Attribute selectors match properties such as [type="email"], pseudo-classes states such as :hover/:focus, and pseudo-elements parts such as ::before.
        • A selector chooses where declarations apply; it is not itself the property that sets a color.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB12 Resolve cascade, specificity and inheritance

      • First compare applicable declarations in their cascade origin, importance and layer context; then compare specificity and order within the relevant context.
        • In an ordinary same-origin/same-layer author example, an ID outweighs class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, which outweigh type/pseudo-element selectors.
        • Compare counts lexicographically, not as an unlimited base-ten total.
        • Equally specific applicable rules use later source order.
        • An important declaration outranks a competing normal declaration in that context.
      • For <p id="intro" class="note">, #intro{color:blue} beats .note{color:red}.
        • A competing p{color:green!important} beats those normal declarations.
        • Inherited color/fonts apply when the element lacks a stronger specified value; margin/padding/borders do not normally inherit. :not() contributes the specificity of its argument rather than universally zero, correcting the module simplification.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-CSS

    • WEB13 Style properties and box calculations

      • color sets text color; background-color sets background; font-size size, font-family face, font-style italic, font-weight weight, text-align inline-content alignment, and text-decoration effects such as underline.
        • Margin lies outside the border; padding lies inside; border surrounds content/padding.
      • With content-box width200px, horizontal padding10px and borders2px, border-box width is224px, excluding margins.
        • With border-box width200px, content width is176px.
        • Shorthand values follow top/right/bottom/left: one applies everywhere, two vertical/horizontal, three top/horizontal/bottom, four each side.
        • Adjacent vertical block margins can collapse rather than add; padding does not collapse.
        • Non-replaced inline elements do not obey width/height like blocks.
        • A 1rem length uses root font size; font-size in em uses parent font size, whereas many other em lengths use the element’s computed font size.
      • In historical markup, the body text attribute controlled default text color, while bgcolor controlled background.
        • Current CSS uses color and background-color instead.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB14 Layout, alignment and responsive design

      • Normal flow lays out blocks/inlines.
        • Flexbox arranges direct children on a main axis; justify-content follows that axis, align-items the cross axis.
        • With row direction in ordinary horizontal writing, cross-axis alignment is vertical.
        • Grid organizes rows and columns with explicit tracks, such as grid-template-columns:1fr 2fr. vertical-align applies to inline/table-cell contexts and does not center every block. align-content distributes tracks/lines when there is applicable extra space, not arbitrary single-child centering.
      • Relative positioning offsets a box while retaining its flow space; absolute removes it and uses its containing block, often established by a positioned ancestor; fixed commonly uses the viewport.
        • Responsive design combines flexible layout, images, viewport metadata and media queries, for example @media(max-width:600px){.cards{grid-template-columns:1fr}}.
        • A min-width768px query targets wider viewports, not mobile alone.
        • Browser compatibility requires feature testing and fallbacks; responsive size handling is a different issue.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB15 JavaScript syntax, inclusion and declarations

      • Use <script src="app.js"></script> for an external .js file; script content has no HTML closing-tag syntax inside its JavaScript source.
        • A deferred script runs after parsing and before DOMContentLoaded.
        • JavaScript originated at Netscape; it is distinct from Java and supports sophisticated applications through prototype-based objects and first-class functions.
      • Identifiers are case-sensitive and may start with letters, underscore or $, not digits or spaces. var has function/global scope; let/const are block-scoped. const prevents rebinding but not mutation of an object’s contents. // comments end at line end; /* */ span a block.
        • Semicolons delimit statements, although automatic insertion exists.
        • Whitespace usually separates tokens but newlines can affect parsing, especially after return. “use strict” is a directive string, not a reserved statement keyword.
        • Parse syntax before computing outputs.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB16 Types, conversions and missing values

      • JavaScript primitives are undefined, null, Boolean, Number, BigInt, String and Symbol; objects include arrays, functions and dates.
        • Float is not a separate Number primitive type.
        • Arrays are objects, even though informal texts call them an array data type. typeof new Date() is "object"; typeof null is historically "object".
      • An unassigned declared variable or missing ordinary object property evaluates to undefined; directly reading an undeclared variable usually throws ReferenceError.
        • Strings use either quote style, with appropriate escaping. + can concatenate when a string is involved; arithmetic / converts ordinary numeric strings. "abc"/"def" produces NaN; nonzero Number divided by zero produces signed Infinity, while 0/0 produces NaN. parseInt("12.8",10) reads12, stopping at the dot; this is parsing, not rounding.
        • Global isNaN converts first; Number.isNaN does not.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-TYPES

    • WEB17 Trace assignments, comparisons and postfix updates

      • Evaluate operators in their specified order and write down both value and type.
        • JavaScript has ==/!= with coercion and ===/!== without coercion; strict operators do not replace or remove the loose ones.
        • A condition ? x : y chooses one branch.
      • var a="20"; var b=a=30; assigns Number30 to both, so a+b is60; a source key of50 is wrong. "1 plus 1 is "+1+1 concatenates left to right to "1 plus 1 is 11".
        • Postfix a++ yields the old value and then increments a. If a=10, a==a++ compares10 with10, then the body sees11.
        • With a=1, printing a-- then a prints10.
        • These JS evaluation rules are not portable to C/C++ expressions with unsequenced modifications.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-EQ, WEB-INC

    • WEB18 Math, string and array API microtraces

      • Math.abs(-9)=9, Math.floor(5.9)=5, and Math.sqrt(36)=6.
        • A JS string’s substring(start,end) includes start and excludes end: "exitexam".substring(2,6) is "itex".
        • Indexes start at zero.
      • Array push/pop add/remove at the end; unshift/shift act at the beginning. slice returns a selected shallow copy; splice(start,deleteCount,...items) mutates by removal/insertion. reverse reverses in place. reduce combines sequentially from left to right; reduceRight combines sequentially from right to left with an accumulator, not simultaneous parallel execution.
        • For [1,2,3].reduceRight((a,v)=>a-v,0), accumulator values are -3,-5,-6.
        • An absent initial value uses the last present item first; an empty array without one throws.
        • Method spelling and case matter.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-ARR, WEB-MATH, WEB-SUBSTR

    • WEB19 Control flow, functions and errors

      • for(initialization;test;update) initializes once, checks before each iteration, then updates after each body. while checks before its body; do...while executes at least once. break exits and continue advances to the next iteration.
        • A loop from n=1 while n<7 prints a message only at n=5 when testing n%5==0.
      • function f(x){return x*2;} has a parameter and returns a value; functions can be passed/stored like other values.
        • Arrow syntax is compact but differs in this/constructor behavior.
        • Runtime argument limits mean “no limit whatsoever” is too absolute. try/catch handles thrown errors during execution; throw signals one; finally runs cleanup.
        • Parse-time syntax errors and logical errors are different. bool ans=true is not JavaScript declaration syntax; use let ans=true.
        • A literal type of expression is not the typeof operator.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB20 DOM selection, creation and safe updates

      • The DOM is a hierarchy of nodes representing the document. document.getElementById("x") returns the matching element or null; querySelector(".item") returns the first match, and querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList.
        • Other plural lookup methods can return live collections.
        • Guard missing elements and run code after the relevant markup exists.
      • To add a div: const el=document.createElement("div"); el.textContent="Hello"; document.body.appendChild(el);.
        • Creation alone does not insert it. createTextNode makes text; appendChild attaches an existing node. innerHTML parses/replaces descendants, so += reparses/replaces the prior descendant content too and can destroy listeners/state.
        • Use textContent for untrusted plain text. element.style.backgroundColor sets a style property; classList.add changes a class. getElementByld with a lowercase l replacing I is a different, nonexistent method.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB21 Events and validated submission

      • An event handler runs when an event occurs: click, input, keydown, mouseover, submit and load are examples. addEventListener("click",handler) registers a function without calling it immediately.
        • Multiple listeners may coexist; once removes one after use, capture selects an earlier propagation phase and passive promises no default cancellation.
        • Event bubbling is distinct from the browser’s default action.
      • For submission, form.addEventListener("submit",e=>{if(!valid()){e.preventDefault();}}) stops the default only on failure.
        • Returning false from an addEventListener callback does not cancel it; return false works in an appropriate inline/onsubmit property handler whose caller uses that return.
        • For cancelable keyboard defaults, call preventDefault rather than assuming a different key event itself disappears.
        • Browser checks improve feedback; repeat validation and authorization on the server.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-EVENT

    • WEB22 Window, dialogs and browser properties

      • In a normal browser page, window exposes the browsing context and document is its document property. alert displays information, confirm returns a Boolean, and prompt requests text or returns null on cancellation. console.log logs diagnostics. location.reload() reloads the current page. screen.availHeight, screen.availWidth and screen.colorDepth have exact camelCase spelling; ColorsDepth is not the property.
      • window.onload is a handler property for the load event, typically after dependent resources finish.
        • Global let/const are not window properties like classic top-level var bindings. document.write is a method/function property; writing after document load can replace the document. document.bgColor is a legacy property; Document.bgcolor has wrong object/case.
        • Use document.body.style.backgroundColor for current styling.
        • Browser workers support concurrent computation, but DOM access normally remains on the page’s main thread.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-SCREEN

    • WEB23 PHP syntax, names and types

      • PHP means PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
        • Use <?php ... ?> in a .php file; a closing tag can be omitted at file end.
        • It can emit ordinary text and HTML.
        • PHP8 no longer accepts historical <script language="PHP"> delimiters; short <? depends on configuration, so use the full form.
        • A stray >> is not a closing PHP tag.
      • Variables begin with $, then a letter/underscore and subsequent letters/digits/underscores; $AGE18 works but $18AGE does not.
        • Names are case-sensitive.
        • Dynamic typing permits values of different types without a preceding type declaration, though optional declarations can constrain them.
        • Scalars include int,float,string,bool; arrays/objects are structured values and null means no value. var_dump displays type and value.
        • Constants cannot normally be redefined during execution.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB24 PHP output, strings and comparisons

      • echo is a language construct with no return value and can emit comma-separated expressions. print takes one expression and returns1.
        • They are two basic output constructs, not the only output mechanisms; printf, print_r and others exist.
        • Neither automatically inserts spaces/newlines.
        • Two prints of5 emit55; "I"."am" emitsIam.
        • Dot concatenates; + is arithmetic.
      • Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and escapes such as \n; single quotes normally preserve dollar names literally.
        • To emit literal $lfc use echo '$lfc'; or escape the dollar in double quotes.
        • String offsets start at zero: "maroon"[2] is r when the surrounding PHP is valid. strlen counts bytes; strpos can return integer0 or false, requiring ===false for failure. strrev reverses bytes and str_replace replaces matching content.
        • PHP 8==8.0 is true, but 8===8.0 is false because types differ; echo false emits an empty string, echo true emits1.
      • PHP sends markup as response characters; a browser then interprets it. echo "A<br>B" emits a tag in raw output but normally displays two text lines.
        • The malformed </br> found in a bank trace depends on HTML error recovery, so specify raw versus rendered output.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-PHPS, WEB-PHPO

    • WEB25 PHP scope, parameters and persistent locals

      • A variable outside a function has global scope.
        • A function’s locals and by-value parameters are separate bindings; use global $x or $GLOBALS["x"] to refer to a global explicitly.
        • Superglobals are available across scopes.
        • A static local retains its value across calls during the execution lifecycle; static storage is not simply another visibility scope.
        • An uninitialized static local begins as null, so echo emits no characters.
      • If global $i=10 and sample($i) increments/prints its by-value parameter, the caller’s $i stays10.
        • Printing before, during and after gives10,11,10 when commas are written by the source.
        • A global statement outside the function does not turn its value parameter into a reference.
        • Common “three scopes” teaching counts local, global and static, but state the taxonomy.
        • A static counter initialized0 then incremented on each call emits1 then2.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-PHPSC

    • WEB26 PHP arrays, loops and callable behavior

      • PHP arrays map integer/string keys to values.
        • Numeric arrays start at index0 unless keys are supplied: [20,12,23,19,18] has19 at index3.
        • Associative syntax uses a contiguous => operator: ["top"=>"black"] stores black under key"top".
        • Splitting it as = > is a parse error, not valid array syntax.
      • foreach($items as $key=>$value) iterates entries; for and while use tests/updates much like the corresponding JS forms. $sub-=$sub is $sub=$sub-$sub, not decrement.
        • For $sum=0; foreach([2,4] as $v){$sum+=$v;} the result is6.
        • A function can receive arguments, return a value, or produce output; classes/objects/variables also support server processing, so no single one of these mechanisms alone defines “dynamic PHP.” Use braces to make nesting explicit.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB27 Request data, server validation and injection

      • $_GET contains query parameters; $_POST contains supported form POST data; $_FILES upload metadata; $_SERVER request/environment details; $_COOKIE cookie values; $_SESSION session data after startup. $GLOBALS is the actual global-symbol array; $_GLOBAL is not the built-in name. $_REQUEST may combine GET/POST/cookie data according to configuration; it is not a database interface and has ambiguous precedence, so prefer the intended source. isset tests existence and non-null, not truth or valid syntax.
      • Read input, check required fields/type/length/range, authenticate and authorize, then process.
        • Bind SQL parameters to keep values separate from commands.
        • Encode output for HTML/attribute/JS context; textContent handles plain browser text.
        • A security test can detect SQL injection or XSS but does not itself fix either.
        • Client validation, encryption and a database connection do not replace these controls.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB28 Cookies and browser storage

      • Cookies are browser-held name/value data automatically attached to matching requests subject to domain, path, expiry, Secure and SameSite rules.
        • HttpOnly restricts script access; Secure requires secure transport.
        • They are not attached to every site indiscriminately.
        • PHP setcookie sends a response header, so set it before output unless buffering correctly defers output; $_COOKIE reflects received cookies.
      • localStorage persists origin-specific string values across sessions until removed/cleared; sessionStorage is scoped to a page session/tab.
        • Neither is automatically transmitted like matching cookies, but JavaScript can send stored data explicitly.
        • IndexedDB supplies structured local storage.
        • Thus all four are client storage techniques, and localStorage can participate in token-based session designs, with script-access risks.
        • Storage size limits vary.
        • Being logged in after reopening may use a persistent session/remember token or browser restoration; storage alone does not prove server acceptance.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-STORE

    • WEB29 Server sessions and the authorization trust path

      • session_start() starts/resumes PHP session handling and makes $_SESSION available.
        • Normally the browser holds an opaque session identifier while data resides in server-controlled storage.
        • A counter initializes missing $_SESSION["views"] to1 and increments on later requests. unset removes one entry; destroying stored session data is distinct from clearing the browser cookie/current variables, so logout must handle the full lifecycle.
      • A client cookie logged_in=1 is attacker-controlled.
        • If the server trusts it alone, authorization can be bypassed.
        • If the server checks a valid session ID and its server-side user/role on every protected action, editing that unrelated flag does not grant rights.
        • HTTPS does not make client-generated claims trustworthy.
        • The bank scenario omits which check the server uses, so it cannot establish uniquely secure versus vulnerable behavior.
        • Protect session IDs, regenerate after login, expire appropriately and avoid putting sensitive tokens in URLs.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB30 Uploads, files and storage safety

      • Uploads ordinarily use method="post", enctype="multipart/form-data" and a named file input. accept hints to the browser which file types to offer; it does not enforce the server’s policy.
        • Validate server-side size/content, inspect upload errors, use the temporary upload path, choose a safe generated destination and use move_uploaded_file.
        • Avoid executable storage and trusting a client filename/extension.
      • file_exists tests files or directories; is_file narrows to regular files. fopen returns a stream or false: r reads an existing file, r+ reads/writes without truncation, w truncates/creates for writing, w+ adds reading, a appends/creates, and x exclusively creates. fclose releases it. readfile emits content and returns a byte count, so echo readfile(...) also prints that count.
        • Check failures before reading/writing and constrain paths to permitted locations.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-INPUT

    • WEB31 Database connections, TLS and actual APIs

      • MySQL is a relational DBMS; a database persists structured application data and supports concurrent clients.
        • PHP8 uses MySQLi or PDO; the old mysql_* extension was removed and module snippets need migration. mysqli_connect(host,user,password,database,port,socket) opens a connection; selecting a database can be deferred, and defaults make several arguments technically optional.
        • Do not reduce the full signature to exactly one optional field.
      • Configure MySQLi TLS options through mysqli_init(), mysqli_ssl_set(...) and mysqli_real_connect(...) with the required verification configuration.
        • None of mysqli_ssl_connect(), pdo_connect_ssl(), mysql_ssl_connect() or secure_connect() is the standard offered function.
        • PDO uses an appropriate driver DSN/options instead.
        • MySQLi procedural functions, object methods and PDO methods have distinct signatures; affected_rows() alone is not a generic PHP function.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-SSL, WEB-AFFECT

    • WEB32 SQL operations, result rows and safe rendering

      • SELECT retrieves rows; INSERT adds; UPDATE ... SET changes values; DELETE removes rows.
        • WHERE limits affected/matching records; omitting it from DELETE ordinarily targets every row, subject to constraints, permissions and errors.
        • CREATE DATABASE/TABLE defines storage; a primary key identifies rows.
        • AUTO_INCREMENT generates numeric values but gaps and explicit values are possible; do not promise gapless consecutive business numbering.
      • mysqli_query returns a result object for successful result-producing queries, true for other successful statements, or failure/exception depending on settings.
        • Fetch associative rows with mysqli_fetch_assoc, positional rows with mysqli_fetch_row, or objects with mysqli_fetch_object. mysqli_num_rows counts a result’s rows; mysqli_affected_rows($conn) counts changed/inserted/deleted rows under its options; mysqli_insert_id($conn) reports a generated AUTO_INCREMENT value from the connection.
        • Escape rendered cell text; use prepared statements for submitted values; mysqli_close closes the connection.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-AFFECT

    • WEB33 PHP includes, objects and dates

      • include evaluates another file in the current scope and warns on failure; require fails critically.
        • In PHP8 a failed require raises Error, which can be caught; uncaught it stops normal execution.
        • The source’s E_COMPILE_ERROR description belongs to older PHP. include_once/require_once avoid repeated inclusion.
        • Do not include a user-selected arbitrary path.
      • A class defines properties/methods; new creates an object, $obj->field accesses a property, and $obj->method() calls a method. public is externally accessible, private is class-restricted, and a constructor initializes an instance.
        • Use $this inside instance methods.
        • DateTime/DateTimeZone represent time and zone; diff returns a DateInterval and DatePeriod iterates intervals.
        • Time calculations require explicit zones and calendar assumptions, not an assumed server-local timezone.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-PHPR

    • WEB34 AJAX and response handling

      • AJAX means Asynchronous JavaScript and XML, but responses can be JSON, text, HTML or XML.
        • It is a technique, not a language, standalone framework or mandatory XML protocol.
        • Configure an XHR with open("GET",url,true), register response/error handlers and call send(). onreadystatechange may run several times; readyState4 means completion, after which status and data must be checked.
      • A callback is a function invoked later by the runtime/API.
        • The browser invokes its response handler when the response is available; the remote server does not directly execute browser code.
        • With fetch, await fetch(url) obtains a response, then check response.ok and parse await response.json().
        • Handle network/parse errors.
        • Starting an asynchronous operation does not make its result synchronously available to the next statement.
        • Avoid overwriting a newer search result with an older response that arrives late.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB35 Polling, WebSockets and data formats

      • Short polling repeatedly requests updates.
        • Long polling holds one client request until an event or timeout, returns a response, then the client reconnects; it is not continuous unsolicited streaming on that same finished response.
        • WebSocket establishes a persistent bidirectional message channel after its handshake.
        • Either HTTP-based AJAX or WebSockets can support nonblocking user interaction and carry JSON, so generic questions may be nonexclusive.
      • JSON represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, Booleans and null; keys/strings use double quotes, and functions/undefined are not JSON values.
        • XML is another valid interchange format.
        • A REST API can return either.
        • Select transport by latency, direction, connection cost and recovery requirements, not merely the occurrence of “asynchronous.” Validate incoming messages and enforce authorization per operation.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB36 Node server, event loop and scaling

      • A minimal CommonJS Node server can use const http=require("node:http"); http.createServer((req,res)=>{res.writeHead(200,{"Content-Type":"text/plain"});res.end("Hello");}).listen(8000);.
        • The request listener runs for incoming requests; end completes the response.
        • Define every variable used in startup logging: the module example’s hostname is otherwise undefined.
      • Node schedules JavaScript callbacks through an event loop and uses OS/worker facilities for asynchronous work.
        • Concurrency means overlapping progress; parallelism means execution at the same instant.
        • One event-loop thread can handle many waiting requests, but long CPU loops or synchronous I/O block its callbacks.
        • Workers/processes and a load balancer distribute work across server instances; they do not automatically coordinate shared data or session state.
        • Multiple clients, or one client with overlapping requests, can both create concurrency.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-NODE

    • WEB37 Races, locks and transaction invariants

      • Suppose two requests read a stock count1, both decide it is available and both write0: two sales consumed one item.
        • Correctness depends on interleaving, even if each callback has only a short synchronous body.
        • A mutex protects one critical section; semaphores can coordinate bounded access; spinlocks busy-wait and are unsuitable for blocking a browser/event-loop thread.
        • Several listed mechanisms can synchronize, so mutex is not the only possible answer.
      • In a relational database use an atomic conditional UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE id=?
        • AND qty>0, check affected rows, and combine related writes in an appropriate transaction.
        • A row lock or serializable transaction can protect multi-step logic; handle rollback/retry on conflicts.
        • A process-local lock does not cover all load-balanced servers.
        • Idempotency tokens with unique storage constraints prevent a retried payment from becoming a duplicate transaction.
      • References: WEB-N, WEB-ISO

    • WEB38 Frameworks and version-aware setup

      • A framework supplies conventions and reusable structure; a library supplies callable capabilities. jQuery simplifies DOM operations; React builds component interfaces; Angular is a component platform, distinct from older AngularJS; Vue also builds interactive interfaces.
        • Each can contribute to a responsive interface, so those generic descriptions do not identify one unique framework.
        • React props pass inputs; state records changing component data; JSX needs transformation rather than being ordinary browser JavaScript syntax.
      • Bootstrap supplies layout/components.
        • The module’s jQuery→Popper→Bootstrap dependency order is version4-era guidance; Bootstrap5 drops required jQuery.
        • Angular CLI commands include ng new, ng serve, ng build, ng generate and ng test, with e2e support depending on configuration. ng server is a source typo.
        • Create React App is deprecated; recognize it as historical module tooling rather than a universal current recommendation.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-BOOT, WEB-REACT, WEB-PROPS

    • WEB39 Manage content, performance and revisions

      • A CMS gives editors content creation, publishing, roles and media management without editing every source file.
        • A database stores persistent facts; it is not itself the whole server application.
        • A VCS records source history, branches and merges to support review/collaboration; deployment publishes a chosen build and is a separate operation.
      • SEO improves discoverability through meaningful content, headings, metadata, accessible links and crawlable structure; keyword metadata alone does not guarantee ranking.
        • Caching reuses a representation/result and requires validity/invalidation rules.
        • Server caching can hold rendered pages or expensive query results; never share private user content under an unsafe common key.
        • Minification removes unnecessary source characters; bundling combines files; compression changes transfer encoding; preloading fetches anticipated resources early.
        • Measure performance because excess preloading/bundling may compete with critical work.
        • Responsive design and cross-browser compatibility need separate testing.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N, WEB-CMS, WEB-SEO, WEB-VCS

    • WEB40 Assemble and evaluate an end-to-end feature

      • For a course-search page, write semantic headings/navigation and a labeled search form.
        • Use a responsive grid with a single-column fallback, then register a submit handler after parsing.
        • Prevent default only when implementing asynchronous submission; encode search values in the query and send GET /courses?q=.... Show loading and useful error feedback without inserting untrusted HTML.
      • The server validates query length/type, authenticates where required, runs a parameterized SELECT with a bounded result size, and returns JSON with an appropriate status/content type.
        • The client checks status, parses data and builds nodes with textContent.
        • For an enrollment action use POST with CSRF controls, server authorization, capacity checks and a transaction; show success only after commit.
        • Evaluate empty/bad input, access denied, network failure, delayed responses, repeated clicks, simultaneous enrollments, narrow screens and keyboard use.
        • This integrates all four blueprint outcomes beyond tag recall.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

    • WEB41 Literal code defects and answerability limits

      • A trace requires syntactically valid source, known initial values, execution context and output representation. x=4+"4"5 is a syntax error because an operator is missing; bool ans=true and type of new Date() are syntax errors too.
        • PHP with >> instead of ?> may fail parsing; do not silently replace it and report the repaired output.
        • A split = > array operator is invalid unless the task explicitly authorizes typographic repair.
      • Distinguish response text from browser rendering: PHP may emit markup that the browser interprets, and visual line breaks need not appear in a plain-text choice.
        • If the correct output60 is absent, none of the options becomes correct.
        • Multiple storage techniques, interface libraries, script-capable languages and cryptographic channels often satisfy broad descriptions.
