        • Record the minimal missing distinction, preserve the original question ID and leave the item ambiguous until repaired.
      • Retained source images resolve two OCR conflicts: Q00160 originally shows x=4+"4"; and therefore prints44 (A); the extracted extra5 makes a different, invalid program.
        • Q00161 originally closes with ?> and prints r (D); extracted >> falsely introduces a syntax error.
        • Both original images were inspected.
        • Use those original outcomes for restored source, and identify the extraction conflict when answering the current text.
      • References: WEB-M, WEB-N

  • Operating System

    • An OS controls resource sharing, protects programs and provides convenient services.
      • Learn the state changes and algorithms behind each term.
      • Scheduling and deadlock questions require explicit assumptions; a policy name alone does not establish a universal performance ranking.
    • Draw process-state transitions and a Gantt chart before calculating scheduling metrics.
      • Record arrivals, burst lengths, priority convention, quantum and switch cost.
    • For deadlock, identify held resources and directed waits; distinguish prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery.
      • CPU preemption is not the same as resource preemption.
    • Trace address translation, page replacement and file-block lookup with small numbers.
      • Compare convenience, efficiency and ability to evolve using concrete mechanisms.
    • Sections in this course
      Objectives, resource management and evolutionBatch, multiprogramming, time-sharing and real timeKernel, shell, privilege and bootAPIs, system calls and virtualizationPrograms, processes and PCB contentsProcess states, queues and schedulersCreation, fork/exec and terminationThreads and mapping modelsIPC and blocking semanticsRaces, critical sections and correctnessSemaphores and resource-count tracesTurn variables and atomic primitivesScheduling metrics and calculation methodPreemptive versus non-preemptive decisionsFCFS and the convoy effectSJF/SJN and shortest remaining timePriority, starvation and agingRound Robin, quantum and bounded turnsMultilevel queues and feedbackFair-share, proportional shares and guaranteesHow to evaluate scheduling claimsDeadlock and its four necessary conditionsResource graphs and missing-diagram limitsPrevention: identify the condition removedAvoidance and the Banker safety testDetection, recovery and intentional ignoringAddress binding, dynamic loading and linkingContiguous allocation and fit policiesInternal and external fragmentationPaging, page tables and TLBSegmentation and contrasts with pagingVirtual memory and page-fault handlingReplacement-policy tracesDevice controllers, drivers and I/O servicesBuffering, caching, spooling and clocksFiles, descriptors and ordinary operationsDirectories, mounting and linksContiguous, linked and indexed file allocationProtection, authentication and threatsLinux, Android and product-history limitsBank ambiguities: identify the missing condition

    • OS01 Objectives, resource management and evolution

      • An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.
        • Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions.
        • Efficiency means using resources effectively; it is not synonymous with the fastest response for every process.
        • Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.
      • Ability to evolve means adding hardware support, features and repairs through maintainable interfaces/modules.
        • Backward compatibility preserves supported older application behavior; it is not a promise that every old binary works.
        • Scalability means handling greater workload/resources; portability means adapting to other platforms.
        • Fault tolerance continues correct service despite specified failures; recovery restores service afterward.
        • Updates and monitoring help administration, but automatic updates are not a defining property of every OS.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N, OS-SOLARIS

    • OS02 Batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing and real time

      • Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission.
        • Multiprogramming keeps several jobs available so another can use the CPU while one waits; it does not require fixed time slices.
        • Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users.
        • A single CPU interleaves execution; multiple CPUs can execute work truly in parallel.
        • Shared-memory multiprocessors do not require each CPU to have private main memory.
      • Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications.
        • Network systems expose remote services; distributed systems coordinate work across machines, sometimes hiding location.
        • Real-time correctness includes timing: hard deadlines must be met, while soft deadline misses degrade service. “Real time” does not simply mean fast.
        • Spooling and multitasking are mechanisms, not proof of a particular OS generation.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS03 Kernel, shell, privilege and boot

      • The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling.
        • A shell reads/interprets user commands; a GUI is another interface.
        • Browsers, office tools and editors are applications.
        • Device drivers are commonly kernel components, although user-space drivers also exist.
        • Kernel mode has privileged operations; supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode, so offering both as exclusive answers is ambiguous.
      • Firmware/bootloader stages execute before transferring control to a kernel loaded into RAM.
        • The kernel is the first core OS component, not the first program ever executed at power-on.
        • Loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel; “kernel modules cannot be loaded while running” is false in modular systems.
        • A resident kernel remains active through the session.
        • Utilities such as antivirus and disk tools can combine user processes with privileged components.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS04 APIs, system calls and virtualization

      • A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket.
        • A user-facing API/library may wrap that request; not every library function enters the kernel.
        • Therefore a stem asking merely for the interface to OS services must distinguish the application API from the direct user/kernel boundary.
      • Process control, file/device management, information retrieval and communication are service categories.
        • Video editing and a database-specific write_database() are application operations, not standard generic syscall categories/names.
        • Virtualization presents a virtual machine environment, often allowing guest operating systems on one host through a hypervisor.
        • It differs from virtual memory, which translates a process’s addresses.
        • Kernel, shell, API and VM are not interchangeable labels.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS05 Programs, processes and PCB contents

      • A program is stored instructions; a process is an executing instance with address space and resources.
        • A process does not universally “manage applications” or “provide a user interface.” The PCB records identity, state, PC/registers, scheduling information, memory/accounting details and I/O/open-resource state.
        • A saved PC identifies where execution resumes.
      • A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead.
        • An interrupt or system call can switch privilege without switching process.
        • Task is OS-specific terminology: it may mean process, thread or schedulable entity.
        • No universal process-versus-task distinction follows from the word alone.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS06 Process states, queues and schedulers

      • New processes are created/admitted; ready means eligible for CPU but not currently running.
        • Running uses a CPU.
        • Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended.
        • Running→ready follows time-slice expiry or another preemption.
        • Running→waiting follows blocking I/O. I/O completion normally gives waiting→ready, not a guaranteed immediate running state.
      • The ready queue contains eligible work; device queues hold blocked requests.
        • The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission.
        • Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.
        • The dispatcher performs the handoff/context restore after selection.
        • A bare “priority” causes running→ready only if a preemptive policy chooses another process.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N, OS-SCHED

    • OS07 Creation, fork/exec and termination

      • Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call.
        • In POSIX-style systems fork() creates a child: zero is returned in the child and the child PID in the parent on success.
        • The two have distinct address spaces, although resources may be shared through explicit mechanisms. exec replaces the current process image; it does not itself create another process.
      • Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary. exit() terminates normally through the runtime; abort() requests abnormal termination.
        • A reference to nonexistent/protected memory is a fatal fault, unlike an application deciding to exit after bad input. “Terminate exit” is not a precise standard category.
        • Parent termination does not universally kill all descendants.
      • References: OS-N, OS-FORK, OS-EXEC

    • OS08 Threads and mapping models

      • A thread has its own PC, registers and stack.
        • Threads in a process share code, address space and usually open-file resources.
        • A process can contain many threads; a thread belongs to one process at a time.
        • Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially.
        • Independent processes can exist; cooperating ones communicate/share data.
      • User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS.
        • In many-to-one mapping, a blocking kernel call can block all user threads and one kernel execution context cannot use multiple CPUs simultaneously.
        • One-to-one permits another kernel thread to run when one blocks.
        • Many-to-many multiplexes user threads over several kernel threads.
        • Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither.
        • Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS09 IPC and blocking semantics

      • Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates.
        • Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations.
        • Pipes provide streams; message queues preserve messages; sockets connect endpoints; RPC requests a remote operation.
        • HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.”
      • Blocking send waits for the required handoff/buffering/receipt condition defined by its API.
        • Blocking receive waits for a message.
        • Nonblocking operations return promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. “Sender blocked until received” identifies blocking send under rendezvous semantics.
        • File locks coordinate access rather than transfer arbitrary payloads, though locking is synchronization within IPC.
        • Do not equate asynchronous messaging with no synchronization ever.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS10 Races, critical sections and correctness

      • A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.
        • A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself.
        • A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions.
        • Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.
      • Keep critical regions small and ensure every conflicting access uses the same protection.
        • A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization.
        • Locking can itself introduce deadlock if acquisition order is inconsistent.
      • Worked microexample
        • Two threads read counter=0, each computes 1 and each stores 1. Two increments produce 1 instead of 2. Protecting the entire read-modify-write with one lock prevents that lost update.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS11 Semaphores and resource-count traces

      • A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations.
        • Under the nonnegative-token model, wait consumes one available token or blocks when none is available; signal supplies a token and may wake a waiter.
        • Implementations using negative internal counts encode waiters differently, so state the model.
        • A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several.
        • A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.
      • Worked microexample
        • Initialize a mutex semaphore to 1. Each thread does wait(m); critical work; signal(m). For a buffer of N slots use empty=N, full=0 and mutex=1: producer waits empty then mutex, inserts, unlocks then signals full. Waiting for empty while already holding mutex can prevent the consumer from freeing a slot.
      • References: OS-N, OS-SEM

    • OS12 Turn variables and atomic primitives

      • Strict alternation uses turn=0/1: process i waits while turn≠i, then enters and sets turn to the other process on leaving.
        • It enforces turns but can violate progress if the other process stays outside its critical region.
        • A naive lock-variable test followed by a separate set races because both processes can observe free before either sets it.
      • Test-and-set and compare-and-swap combine checking/updating atomically; ordinary check-then-write does not.
        • Peterson’s classic algorithm uses flags plus turn for two processes under its memory-model assumptions; a semaphore can coordinate more than two.
        • Disabling local interrupts does not exclude other CPUs and is not a general user-space locking solution.
        • Interrupts can notify/synchronize events, so they cannot be universally excluded from every synchronization-related classification.
      • References: OS-SYNC, OS-N

    • OS13 Scheduling metrics and calculation method

      • For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B. With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting.
        • Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time.
        • Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.
      • First construct a time line with arrivals, idle gaps, preemptions and overhead, then calculate per-process values before averages.
        • Do not confuse first response with final completion.
      • Worked microexample
        • A job arrives at 2, starts at 5, uses 4 CPU units without interruption and finishes at 9: response=3, turnaround=7, waiting=3. Six completions in two hours means throughput=3 jobs/hour.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS14 Preemptive versus non-preemptive decisions

      • Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding.
        • Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival.
        • FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive.
        • Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide.
        • Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
      • CPU preemption saves a context and reallocates processing time; taking an occupied printer or lock may be unsafe.
        • This is why time-slicing does not automatically remove the no-resource-preemption condition for deadlock.
        • Frequent switches have cost; non-preemptive policies can delay interactive work behind long bursts.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N, OS-SCHED

    • OS15 FCFS and the convoy effect

      • FCFS runs ready bursts in arrival order and ordinarily does not preempt.
        • If the CPU is idle, jump to the next arrival.
        • Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect.
        • A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
        • FCFS does not universally have the worst turnaround for every possible workload.
      • Worked microexample
        • All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3. Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17. Turnarounds 24,27,30 average to 27. If arrivals are not simultaneous, recompute using their actual times.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS16 SJF/SJN and shortest remaining time

      • Non-preemptive SJF/SJN chooses the shortest next burst among currently ready jobs.
        • SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.
        • Future burst lengths normally need estimates.
        • SJF minimizes average waiting for the usual fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no preemption/switch cost; that theorem is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy.
      • Repeated short arrivals can starve a long job.
        • The shortest total original burst is not necessarily the shortest remaining burst after execution has begun.
      • Worked microexample
        • P1 arrives 0 with burst 8; P2 arrives 1 with burst 2. SRTF runs P1 0–1, P2 1–3, P1 3–10. P1 waiting=2 and P2 waiting=0. Non-preemptive SJF cannot interrupt P1 once it has started.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS17 Priority, starvation and aging

      • Priority scheduling chooses the highest-priority ready job.
        • Check whether a smaller or larger numeric value means higher priority.
        • State whether a high-priority arrival preempts.
        • Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load.
        • SJF can also starve long jobs, so a single-choice question offering both as starvation-prone has multiple answers.
      • Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.
        • It is not a deadlock cure.
        • Priority inversion occurs when urgent work waits on a resource held by lower-priority work; priority inheritance can temporarily raise the holder’s priority.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS18 Round Robin, quantum and bounded turns

      • RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn.
        • Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.
        • Specify how arrivals at a quantum boundary enter the queue.
        • A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead.
        • RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths.
      • With n continuously ready jobs, no priority bypass and zero overhead, a just-requeued job waits at most (n−1)q for its next turn.
        • This bounds one interval, not total lifetime waiting when arrivals or blocking are unrestricted.
        • Include context-switch costs if given.
      • Worked microexample
        • P1=5,P2=3, both arrive 0, q=2: P1 0–2,P2 2–4,P1 4–6,P2 6–7,P1 7–8. Completions 8,7; waiting=8−5=3 and 7−3=4; average 3.5.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS19 Multilevel queues and feedback

      • A multilevel queue separates classes, such as foreground interactive and background batch, and chooses both between queues and within them.
        • Fixed interqueue priority may starve lower queues; allocating time shares between classes can avoid this.
        • A multilevel feedback queue allows movement according to observed behavior, commonly demoting CPU-intensive jobs and periodically boosting priority.
      • Do not infer movement from a simple multilevel-queue label.
        • State initial class, quantum per level, promotion/demotion rules and interqueue policy before tracing.
        • A binary search tree is a data structure that might implement a queue; it is not itself a CPU selection policy. “Infinite” is not a standard scheduling-policy category.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS20 Fair-share, proportional shares and guarantees

      • Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process.
        • Equal per-process RR can let a user obtain more aggregate CPU by launching more processes.
        • Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
      • Lottery scheduling assigns tickets and selects a winning ticket each turn.
        • With weights 3:1, expected shares are 75% and 25%; short-run results vary and this is not a deterministic no-starvation deadline.
        • Stride-style scheduling tracks progress toward shares deterministically.
        • Any “guaranteed scheduling” answer needs the actual guarantee and assumptions; finite FCFS and RR can also avoid indefinite postponement.
      • Worked microexample
        • If user A runs four ready tasks and B runs one, plain RR gives A about 80% overall. A policy granting each user half the CPU instead gives A’s tasks about 12.5% each and B’s task 50%.
      • References: OS-FAIR, OS-M

    • OS21 How to evaluate scheduling claims

      • There is no universally best policy for response, waiting, fairness and throughput simultaneously.
        • State the workload and objective, apply the algorithm and compare measured results.
        • Maximum waiting at submission is not determined from burst times alone if future arrivals, priorities or overhead are unconstrained.
        • Known finite workloads are different from an open stream with potential starvation.
      • An item asking for one non-preemptive algorithm while offering FCFS and SJN has multiple answers.
        • Equal share needs a process/user/group definition. “Highest average turnaround” requires a concrete workload; do not memorize FCFS as an absolute.
        • RR is a conventional interactive choice because turns improve responsiveness, subject to quantum and overhead.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS22 Deadlock and its four necessary conditions

      • A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide.
        • Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.
        • Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource.
        • Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another.
        • No resource preemption means release must be voluntary.
        • Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.
      • All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.
        • Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.
        • Preventing any one condition prevents that class of deadlock.
        • A preemptive CPU scheduler can coexist with deadlocked locks.
      • Worked microexample
        • P1 holds lock A and requests B; P2 holds B and requests A. Neither releases before acquiring the other: nonshareable locks, retained holdings, no forced release and a cycle all occur.
      • References: OS-N

    • OS23 Resource graphs and missing-diagram limits

      • In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment.
        • Follow these directions to form waits.
        • No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock.
        • With multiple instances a cycle alone is insufficient: another instance may permit completion.
        • A wait-for graph replaces single-instance resource nodes with P→Q when P waits for Q.
      • For a complete single-instance example, suppose P0 holds R0 and requests R1, while P1 holds R1 and requests R0.
        • The wait-for edges P0→P1 and P1→P0 form a cycle, so neither can proceed.
        • With multiple resource instances, inspect all assignments and available instances before concluding that a cycle is a deadlock.
      • References: OS-N

    • OS24 Prevention: identify the condition removed

      • Prevention constrains how requests are made.
        • Share a resource where safe to remove mutual exclusion; request all needed resources before holding any to remove hold-and-wait; permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption; impose a global acquisition order to remove circular wait.
        • Not every physical resource is shareable or safely preemptable.
      • “If waiting, release all held resources and try again” removes simultaneous holding while waiting.
        • It may also be described as reclaiming resources, so the question must distinguish voluntary release from forced preemption.
        • Prevention can waste utilization or cause starvation; avoiding deadlock is not the same as treating every process fairly.
      • References: OS-N

    • OS25 Avoidance and the Banker safety test

      • Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe.
        • Banker requires maximum claims.
        • Compute Need=Max−Allocation.
        • Set Work=Available and repeatedly find an unfinished process with Need≤Work componentwise; simulate completion by adding its Allocation to Work.
        • Finishing all gives a safe sequence.
        • Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds.
        • Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked.
        • Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.
      • Worked microexample
        • One resource type: Available=1; P1 holds 1 and needs 1 more; P2 holds 2 and needs 2 more. P1 can finish, returning its allocation so Work becomes 2; P2 can then finish. Safe order P1,P2. A maximum claim must be known before testing.
      • References: OS-DEAD

    • OS26 Detection, recovery and intentional ignoring

      • Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked.
        • Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.
        • Termination and rollback are both possible tools, so a question offering both as recovery methods needs a criterion.
        • Repeatedly sacrificing the same victim can cause starvation.
      • Checking on every request versus periodically trades overhead against detection delay; no universal best interval exists.
        • Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks. “Deadlock acceptance” can mean intentional ignoring, not necessarily an invalid approach.
        • A detection graph, avoidance safety graph and ordinary scheduling queue solve different problems.
      • References: OS-N, OS-DEAD

    • OS27 Address binding, dynamic loading and linking

      • Compile-time binding uses absolute addresses if placement is known.
        • Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory.
        • Execution-time binding translates while running and permits movement with hardware support.
        • Logical/virtual addresses are generated for a process; physical addresses select RAM.
        • An MMU translates logical to physical, not the reverse as one malformed bank stem says.
      • Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed.
        • Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable.
        • Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.
        • These differ from a context switch, which primarily changes execution state.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS28 Contiguous allocation and fit policies

      • A contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region.
        • In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length.
        • Check 0≤logical_offset<limit, then physical=base+offset.
        • The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base.
        • If limit instead means last valid offset, the inequality changes; specify the convention.
      • First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.
        • No policy universally optimizes both search time and future storage utilization.
        • Binary-fit is not one of these standard names.
      • Worked microexample
        • Holes 100,500,200,300 and request 180: first-fit selects 500, best-fit 200, worst-fit 500. For base=4000,length=100, logical offset 99 maps to 4099; offset 100 traps.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS29 Internal and external fragmentation

      • Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit.
        • External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.
        • Coalescing joins adjacent free holes; compaction moves allocated regions to consolidate free space and requires relocation support.
      • Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally.
        • Variable-length segmentation/contiguous partitions can fragment externally.
        • This is not a statement that every allocator inside a paging OS is fragmentation-free.
        • Track units and round allocations up rather than assuming all requests exactly fill blocks.
      • Worked microexample
        • A 10 KiB object in 4 KiB pages needs ceil(10/4)=3 pages: 12 KiB allocated and 2 KiB unused. Two 3 KiB free holes cannot serve one contiguous 5 KiB request although 6 KiB is free.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS30 Paging, page tables and TLB

      • Pages and physical frames have equal fixed size P. Divide virtual address v into page=floor(v/P) and offset=v mod P. The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.
        • Physical address=frame×P+offset.
        • A TLB caches translations; a TLB miss may require a table walk while the page is already resident.
      • Table size depends on the number of virtual pages and entry size, not just physical RAM.
        • Protection and present bits must be checked before access.
        • A page-table lookup is not a CPU scheduling operation.
      • Worked microexample
        • Page size 1024, v=2053: page 2, offset 5. If page 2 maps to frame 7, physical address=7173. With 16-bit virtual addresses and 1 KiB pages, there are 64 virtual pages and a 6-bit page number.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS31 Segmentation and contrasts with paging

      • Segmentation uses logical variable-length units such as code, stack and arrays.
        • A segment-table entry provides base, limit and permissions.
        • For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset.
        • An out-of-range offset traps; it must not spill into the next segment.
      • Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally.
        • Segments reflect program structure whereas ordinary pages are largely transparent to applications.
        • Consequently an old item offering all three true contrasts A/B/C cannot have a unique correct choice.
      • Worked microexample
        • Segment 1 has base 8000 and length 500. Offset 120 maps to 8120; offset 500 is invalid under the length convention.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS32 Virtual memory and page-fault handling

      • Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage.
        • It does not add physical RAM or remove all capacity constraints.
        • Demand paging brings a page in when accessed.
        • On a nonresident access: trap, validate mapping/permissions, find a frame or choose a victim, save a dirty victim if needed, obtain contents, update mapping and restart.
      • Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings.
        • An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded.
        • Excessive active-page demand can cause thrashing: repeated faults dominate useful computation.
        • Reducing active load or adding suitable memory can help.
      • Worked microexample
        • If access costs 100 ns and an additional page-in costs 5 ms, a fault probability of 10^−4 adds roughly 500 ns per access; rare long delays still matter.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS33 Replacement-policy traces

      • Replacement chooses a victim when no suitable free frame is available.
        • FIFO evicts the earliest loaded page; a hit does not refresh insertion time.
        • LRU evicts the least recently accessed and updates recency on every access.
        • Optimal evicts the page used farthest in the future, serving as an offline lower bound.
        • LFU uses reference counts and needs tie/aging rules.
      • Write a row per reference, identify hits before evicting, and count initial loads as faults.
        • FIFO may exhibit Belady’s anomaly when more frames cause more faults; LRU and optimal have the stack property.
        • Page buffering retains useful free/modified pages to reduce effective fault cost.
      • Worked microexample
        • Three empty frames, references 1,2,3,1,4,1: FIFO faults at 1,2,3,4 and the last 1: five faults. LRU updates page 1 on its hit, evicts 2 for 4, and ends with a hit on 1: four faults.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS34 Device controllers, drivers and I/O services

      • A controller is device hardware exposing status, control and data registers.
        • A driver converts OS requests into device-specific operations.
        • Device independence and uniform naming hide brand-specific details; error handling reports/retries supported failures.
        • Polling checks readiness repeatedly; interrupts request CPU attention; DMA transfers blocks after setup without CPU work for every byte.
      • A broad question can name both the kernel and drivers as responsible for I/O; specify the abstraction level.
        • Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver.
        • Input/output/storage/NIC devices are OS-managed hardware; user accounts are identities.
        • Printer-paper and network errors can be handled/reported, but continued operation during total power loss requires hardware support, not OS software alone.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS35 Buffering, caching, spooling and clocks

      • Buffering temporarily holds data in transit to absorb speed/transfer-size differences.
        • Caching retains copies to accelerate reuse.
        • Spooling queues jobs for a device such as a printer, usually on disk, so producers need not own it throughout job creation.
        • These have different purposes even if one implementation combines them.
      • The clock/timer supports timekeeping, timeouts, accounting and preemptive scheduling.
        • A system monitor reports CPU, memory, storage and network usage; it measures rather than directly creating more resources.
        • Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors.
        • A broad “OS does all disk functions” claim needs these responsibility boundaries.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS36 Files, descriptors and ordinary operations

      • A file has content and metadata such as name, size, owner, permissions and timestamps. open obtains an open-file reference, read/write transfer bytes, seek changes an offset, close releases a reference, truncate changes size and unlink removes a name.
        • A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode.
        • Descriptor and offset are not synonyms.
      • Read advances the offset on seekable files and may return fewer bytes than requested; zero normally indicates end-of-file.
        • Sockets also support ordinary read/write, alongside socket/connect/send operations, so read is not uniquely “not a network call.” FAT32, NTFS and ext4 are filesystem formats; HTTP is an application communication protocol.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N, OS-READ

    • OS37 Directories, mounting and links

      • A single-level directory requires unique names in one namespace.
        • Two-level directories separate users.
        • A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs.
        • Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.
      • A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling.
        • Removing one hard link does not erase content while other names/open references retain it.
        • Mounting attaches a filesystem at a mount point; it does not format the device.
        • NFS provides remote filesystem access; FTP transfers files rather than itself mounting a local filesystem.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS38 Contiguous, linked and indexed file allocation

      • Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems.
        • Extents allow several contiguous runs.
        • Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links.
        • FAT stores chains in a table; caching that table does not change the chain into a direct arithmetic mapping.
      • Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.
        • A Unix inode can combine direct pointers with indirect levels.
        • Check pointer size, block size, index capacity and whether metadata reads are cached.
      • Worked microexample
        • A 1024-byte index block with 4-byte pointers holds 256 block addresses. With 1024-byte data blocks, one such index level addresses 256 KiB of file data, excluding metadata and any reserved entries.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS39 Protection, authentication and threats

      • Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks permitted operations.
        • An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model, not universal defaults granting all owners full access or everyone read.
        • Read, write, execute, append and delete are different rights, with filesystem-specific rules.
      • Least privilege limits damage.
        • Password hashing verifies secrets without storing plaintext; one-time passwords expire after use.
        • Encryption protects confidentiality under correct key use but does not automatically provide integrity.
        • Trojans masquerade as useful software, worms propagate independently and viruses attach to hosts; denial of service harms availability.
        • Modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, but support/configuration depends on product.
        • CLI, GUI, speech/natural language and VR are possible interfaces, not a closed list excluding the last two.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

    • OS40 Linux, Android and product-history limits

      • Linux is a Unix-compatible kernel written from scratch by Linus Torvalds; a distribution combines it with userland, libraries and tools.
        • Android’s base kernel layer is Linux; its framework and applications are higher layers.
        • AOSP is open source, while a shipped device can include proprietary applications/services.
        • Windows and macOS are both proprietary products, although macOS contains open-source components, so “which is not open source?” offering both is ambiguous.
        • Microsoft Office is an application suite.
      • Windows is the Microsoft family commonly described as succeeding the MS-DOS desktop era; Solaris originated at Sun. “First widely used OS,” “first multitasking OS,” and generation/function pairings require a definition and historical evidence; UNIX was not the first system ever to multitask. “Most mobile devices” needs a population and date; architecture facts do not prove market share.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N, OS-AOSP, OS-LINUX, OS-SOLARIS

    • OS41 Bank ambiguities: identify the missing condition

      • Reject a unique answer when the choices omit the requested concept or contain several valid examples.
        • A general system-call purpose should say requesting a kernel service; a process purpose should say executing a program.
        • CPU/memory/I/O management spans multiple managers, so a question listing only device/process/file/security management lacks an umbrella answer.
        • Virtual memory provides isolation and translated space; it does not remove every memory constraint.
      • For flawed wording, state the minimum repair: specify OS/API, scheduling variant, arrivals/quantum, exact graph, base-limit convention or scope of comparison.
        • A marked answer is not evidence.
        • Keep missing diagrams distinct from concepts that have now been taught: additional theory cannot reconstruct absent process/resource edges.
      • References: OS-M, OS-N

  • Software Engineering

    • Apply requirements, models, design and testing as one connected engineering workflow.
      • The official blueprint allocates six items; this chapter also teaches the management, architecture and testing concepts appearing outside the original module.
    • Classify the actual scenario before choosing a process, requirement type, model or test level.
      • Broad labels often overlap.
    • Write one use case with an exception flow, derive boundary/control/entity objects and a service contract, then derive tests from those obligations.
    • Draw dependency networks and calculate times before inspecting choices; qualify missing context instead of trusting a weak key.

    • SE01 Software engineering, processes and work products

      • Software engineering applies systematic methods to development, operation and maintenance.
        • A software product includes executable code and relevant requirements, designs, test assets, configuration and user documentation.
        • A process defines activities, ordering, roles, products and entry/exit conditions.
        • Its four broad activities are specification, design/implementation, validation and evolution.
      • Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior.
        • Either can use iterative or sequential development.
        • OOP does not automatically shorten every project.
        • Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex.
        • Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE02 Lifecycle phases and model selection

      • A common lifecycle names requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
        • Analysis clarifies the problem; system design chooses architecture; object/detail design specifies interfaces and algorithms; implementation writes code; testing evaluates behavior; deployment puts it into service.
        • These activities may overlap and repeat.
      • Select a process using requirement stability, technical risk, delivery urgency, stakeholder availability, team skills and assurance needs. “Team has little experience” alone does not uniquely identify a process.
        • A risk-driven cycle, prototype or carefully planned staged process may each help, depending on the actual uncertainty.
        • No process eliminates the need for testing or documentation.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE03 Waterfall and the V-model

      • Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables.
        • It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly.
        • It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback.
        • Rigidity offers milestone visibility but can freeze incorrect assumptions.
      • The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels.
        • Requirements inform acceptance tests; system design informs system tests; component/detail design informs integration/unit tests.
        • Coding lies at the bottom.
        • Test planning starts early.
        • Stable requirements and strong assurance may favor this organization, but neither a V shape nor waterfall guarantees safety or correctness.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE04 Iteration, increments and early delivery

      • Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality.
        • A process may do both.
        • Delivering registration first, then payments, then reporting is incremental; revising a registration prototype after feedback is iterative.
        • Each increment still needs design, implementation and testing.
      • Choose incremental delivery when prioritized partial capability must reach users early.
        • Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning.
        • Iteration need not rebuild the whole system every time, and increments need not be perfectly independent modules.
        • Broad descriptions of early working software can fit prototypes, iterative or Agile processes; identify the purpose of that early version.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE05 Agile values, stories and Scrum

      • Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans.
        • The latter still have value.
        • Agile does not mean no planning or no documentation.
        • A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.
      • Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month, with a Sprint Goal, selected work and a usable Increment meeting a Definition of Done.
        • Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope.
        • Timeboxes tend to stay fixed while content is adapted without endangering the goal.
        • Agile can be combined with required assurance/documentation; safety-critical context alone cannot prove it is unsuitable.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-AG, SE-SC

    • SE06 Spiral development and risk

      • Spiral development is risk driven.
        • Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks, develops/verifies an appropriate next result, and plans further commitment.
        • A prototype may test a risky technology before a large investment.
        • The amount and type of work depend on the risks.
      • Use risk emphasis to distinguish spiral from a generic changing-requirements scenario.
        • Spiral can incorporate incremental, prototyping or sequential activities, but calling it the uniquely “most general” process is a textbook convention rather than a universal theorem.
        • Risk analysis requires skill and may impose excessive overhead on a small low-risk project.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE07 Prototypes, RAD and reuse-oriented development

      • A prototype explores requirements, usability or technical feasibility.
        • A throwaway prototype is discarded after learning; an evolutionary prototype is deliberately refined toward production.
        • A quick prototype may omit robustness, security or architecture, so do not deploy it unchanged without evaluation.
        • Coding may occur during prototyping even if a diagram labels that activity construction rather than coding.
      • RAD uses rapid construction, timeboxing, user participation and often reusable components; it requires available users and skilled designers/developers.
        • Reuse-oriented development searches components, evaluates fit, may adjust requirements, designs around interfaces and builds missing parts.
        • Product-line assets may include requirements, architecture, components and tests; all are potentially reusable.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE08 Feasibility and levels of requirements

      • Feasibility asks whether a proposal is worth doing and can be delivered within technical, economic, operational and schedule constraints.
        • Examine existing limitations, organizational impacts, benefits, cost, available skills and integration risk.
        • System analysis studies the problem and needed behavior in more detail; the activities inform each other.
      • Business requirements explain why the project exists and its goals.
        • User requirements describe stakeholder needs at a useful high level; system requirements specify detailed services and constraints.
        • The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements.
        • In the module, a natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE09 Functional requirements include prohibited behavior

      • A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions. “When the sensor detects intrusion, send an alert” is functional. “Only a manager may approve refunds” also specifies permitted/prohibited behavior.
        • A negative statement is not automatically nonfunctional.
      • Write one clear obligation with an actor/trigger, action and observable result. “The system shall generate a PDF report” is functional. “The system shall not reveal another customer’s balance” can be a security-related functional rule.
        • Security as a broad quality goal and the functions implementing it must be distinguished.
        • The bank’s must/should/not-work wording often fails to establish a unique classification.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE10 Nonfunctional qualities and measurable constraints

      • Nonfunctional requirements include quality attributes and constraints.
        • Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use; reliability concerns failure-free service; availability concerns being ready for use; usability concerns task success and ease of learning.
        • Security concerns protection; compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments; maintainability/supportability concern change, diagnosis and evolution.
      • “Search responds within two seconds under 100 concurrent users” is measurable performance. “New users finish checkout within one minute without help” is usability. “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint.
        • Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category.
        • Performance degradation at peak load primarily concerns performance, not automatically reliability.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE11 Validate requirements and maintain traceability

      • Correct requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs.
        • Complete requirements address the agreed scope, normal and exceptional behavior.
        • Consistency excludes contradictions.
        • Clarity/unambiguity gives one intended interpretation; feasibility/realism means achievable within constraints.
        • Verifiability means objective evidence can check fulfillment.
        • Replace “fast for most users” with a defined metric, workload and threshold.
      • Trace each requirement backward to its source/rationale and forward to design, code and tests.
        • Record dependencies among requirements.
        • A traceability matrix links these artifacts and helps impact analysis; it is not just a cost/schedule ledger.
        • Stakeholders must negotiate conflicting requirements rather than independently approving incompatible demands.
        • Scope, understanding and volatility are distinct elicitation difficulties.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE12 Elicitation techniques, FAST and QFD

      • Interviews ask stakeholders about needs; document analysis examines manuals, contracts and current records; observation/ethnography studies actual daily work.
        • Prototypes reveal tacit expectations.
        • Workshops/JAD bring users, managers and developers together with a facilitator and recorder to build consensus.
        • Use several sources and check assumptions against observed work.
      • In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs, consolidate lists and develop smaller specifications.
        • QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit.
        • Brainstorm first to generate ideas, then evaluate and prioritize; do not confuse that with letting every idea become a committed requirement.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE13 From scenarios to analysis objects

      • A scenario is one concrete execution; a use case abstracts the related successful and alternative scenarios.
        • Analysis integrates functional (use cases/scenarios), structural/object (classes) and dynamic (states/interactions) models.
        • Entity objects represent domain information such as Incident; boundary objects mediate interaction, such as ReportForm; control objects coordinate a use case.
        • A UI form is normally boundary, not entity.
      • Use nouns as candidate objects, possessive descriptions as candidate attributes, and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations.
        • These are heuristics, not automatic parsing rules.
        • CRC means Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators.
        • A control per use case or participating actor can be a useful starting point, not a mandatory UML rule or fixed object lifetime.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE14 Actors, use cases and scope

      • An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system.
        • A person may play several roles, and several people may play one role.
        • A primary actor seeks a goal; a supporting actor provides a service.
        • Ask which user groups perform main functions, administer or maintain the system, and which external systems exchange information.
      • Draw actors outside the system boundary rectangle and use-case ovals inside.
        • Name a goal with a verb and noun.
        • The diagram shows roles, goals and relationships, not the full detailed algorithm or UI layout.
        • Being an internal component is different from being an external actor; the chosen boundary determines which role applies.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE15 Write a complete use case with alternatives

      • Record name/goal, actors, trigger, preconditions, main success flow, alternatives/exceptions and postconditions.
        • Use active subject–verb steps at one abstraction level; separate errors from the normal flow.
      • Example: Submit Incident.
        • Precondition: officer authenticated. 1 Officer supplies location and description. 2 System validates details. 3 System records the incident. 4 System returns its ID.
        • Alternative 2a: location missing → report the problem and request correction; save nothing.
        • Success postcondition: incident and ID persist; failure guarantee: no partial record.
        • An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure.
        • Preconditions hold before entry, while a trigger starts the use case.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE16 Include, extend, generalization and abstract use cases

      • Include factors required reused behavior: Submit Order includes Validate Order, with the dashed arrow from the including/base use case to the included one.
        • Extend adds conditional behavior at extension points: Apply Discount extends Checkout, with the arrow from the extension to the base.
        • The base is meaningful independently.
        • The short note’s receipt example reverses this direction if it says Withdrawal extends Print Receipt.
      • Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element.
        • An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case.
        • It is not defined merely by reuse or lack of a direct actor line.
        • Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE17 Class diagrams, visibility and multiplicity

      • A class box lists name, attributes and operations; + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility.
        • A class diagram shows static types and relationships, while an object diagram shows particular instances/links.
        • UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process.
        • Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements.
      • Multiplicity at one end counts how many objects there may correspond to one object at the opposite end: 1 exactly one, 0..1 optional, 0..* any nonnegative number, 1..* at least one.
        • A one-to-many association does not automatically mean composition.
        • Read each end separately before choosing cardinality.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE18 Association, aggregation, composition and generalization

      • Association connects related instances.
        • A dashed dependency arrow means a client uses a supplier.
        • Generalization uses a solid line and hollow triangle pointing to the superclass/general element.
        • Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond at the whole end and weak whole-part meaning; it does not by itself define a detailed lifecycle policy.
      • Composition uses a filled diamond at the whole end and strong ownership: a part is in at most one composite at a time, and parts still owned are destroyed with that composite.
        • Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model.
        • Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification.
        • For Car composing Engine, the diamond belongs beside Car; saying it points to Engine is imprecise.
        • The intended bank relationship is composition.
      • References: SE-M, SE-G, SE-U

    • SE19 Sequence diagrams and the emergency-report example

      • Sequence diagrams show interactions across lifelines, with order/time generally downward.
        • Messages cross between participants; activation rectangles show execution.
        • A creation message starts a lifeline; an X marks modeled destruction, not a guarantee about when a garbage collector runs.
        • Synchronous calls wait for completion; asynchronous messages permit the sender to proceed.
      • The module’s layout heuristic puts initiating actor first, boundary second, control third, then entities.
        • This is not a required UML column order.
        • In ReportEmergency, FieldOfficer activates ReportEmergencyButton, enters details through EmergencyReportForm, and later sees AcknowledgmentNotice; DispatcherStation belongs to the dispatcher side.
        • Choose the button for initiating this particular scenario.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE20 Activity, state and data-flow models

      • An activity diagram models workflow: filled circle start, rounded actions, guarded decision diamond, thick fork/join bars and partitions/swimlanes for responsibility.
        • A diamond can also merge alternative flows; a join synchronizes concurrent flows.
        • A state machine models states and transitions triggered by events, often with guards/actions, for one object’s lifecycle.
      • Choose a sequence diagram for message order between participants, a state machine for event-dependent state changes, and activity for workflow.
        • Both sequence and state diagrams describe behavior over time.
        • State machines are useful for objects with significant states, whether entity or control.
        • A DFD shows data stores/flows and transformations from inputs to outputs; it is not a UML diagram.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE21 Design and subsystem decomposition

      • System design turns the analysis model into architecture: design goals, subsystem responsibilities, dependencies, hardware mapping, data management, access control, control flow and startup/shutdown/error policies.
        • Detail/object design refines APIs, parameter/return types, exceptions, component choices and algorithms.
        • A subsystem is a manageable logical collection with services and an interface; it need not be a physical replaceable artifact.
      • Group closely related objects and functionality, minimize associations crossing boundaries, and isolate communication infrastructure where useful.
        • User workflows inform decomposition but do not alone dictate the internal structure.
        • Analysis describes domain needs; subsystem decomposition is principally a design result.
        • Architecture documentation supports communication and records major decisions, not every source-level execution step.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE22 Cohesion, coupling, modularity and refactoring

      • Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules.
        • Seek high cohesion and low coupling.
        • Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling.
        • Information hiding exposes stable operations while concealing changeable decisions.
      • Logical cohesion groups similar-category operations, often selected by a flag; temporal cohesion groups operations done at the same time; functional cohesion focuses on one task.
        • Splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity.
        • If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers.
        • Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE23 Layers, tiers and architecture views

      • A layer is a logical abstraction level; a tier is a deployment separation.
        • A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping.
        • For top-to-bottom A,B,C,D, A→B obeys closed layering, A→C skips, and lower-to-upper calls violate the simple dependency rule unless explicitly mediated by a defined mechanism.
      • A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects.
        • Module structures show code organization, component-and-connector structures runtime interaction, and allocation structures map software to hardware, teams or environment.
        • Processes/threads belong in concurrency views.
        • Evaluate architectures against quality attributes and scenarios; processor allocation, decomposition and style selection can all be architectural concerns.
      • References: SE-M, SE-AR

    • SE24 Architecture styles and integration boundaries

      • Repository style shares central data, simplifying common access but creating bottleneck/schema dependencies.
        • MVC separates domain model, display view and interaction controller.
        • Client–server separates requesters from service providers; peer-to-peer permits both roles.
        • Pipe-and-filter applies successive transformations to data streams.
        • Three-tier separates presentation, application logic and storage; some four-tier variants split presentation client/server.
      • An API gateway presents one entry point and routes/combines calls to services, hiding service boundaries from clients.
        • It can centralize policies but also become a bottleneck.
        • A component diagram shows components/interfaces/dependencies; a deployment diagram places software artifacts on nodes.
        • Choose the style for the required interactions and qualities rather than selecting a universally best architecture.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE25 Design principles and operation contracts

      • Use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity; preserve consistency, traceability and clear responsibilities.
        • Top-down design refines high-level structure; bottom-up design assembles existing components.
        • A hybrid combines both.
        • SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion.
        • Depend on abstractions; add compatible extensions; avoid forcing unused operations.
        • DRY limits duplicated knowledge, KISS avoids unnecessary complexity, and YAGNI avoids speculative work.
      • A contract states preconditions, postconditions and invariants.
        • For withdraw(amount): require amount>0 and amount<=balance; ensure balance=oldBalance-amount; preserve balance>=0.
        • Validation checks inputs; implementation enforces the transition.
        • A complete feature needs both UI/API and persisted behavior, not only a diagram.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G, SE-SOLID

    • SE26 A small analysis-to-implementation example

      • For Submit Incident, let a boundary read input, a service validate and coordinate, and a repository save an Incident entity.
        • Pseudocode: submit(input){require authenticated; if missing(location) return validationError; incident=new Incident(input); repository.save(incident); return incident.id;}.
        • Save and ID assignment must succeed together, or roll back.
      • Derive tests from the model: missing location saves nothing; valid input returns a saved ID; a storage failure yields an error without a partial record; unauthorized input is rejected.
        • Trace requirement→use-case step→service operation→repository effect→test.
        • This closes the module’s implementation-practice gap and makes its analysis/design tools actionable.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE27 Patterns, variability and testability

      • Factory Method lets subclasses choose a concrete product through a creation operation, reducing coupling to concrete constructors.
        • A simple factory centralizes creation but is not identical to Factory Method.
        • Singleton controls access to one instance; Observer notifies subscribers; Memento stores/restores state while hiding representation; Iterator traverses; Decorator adds behavior through wrapping. “Momento” in the bank means Memento.
      • Variability can use selectable features, omission/inclusion and extension points; overloading supplies alternate signatures in code but is not every variability mechanism.
        • Testability improves with controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity.
        • A sandbox can isolate execution.
        • Self-referential combination choices such as “A and B” in option B cannot establish a unique correct answer.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G, SE-PAT

    • SE28 Planning, WBS, estimation and tools

      • Planning is continuous: identify scope/deliverables, decompose work, estimate effort/duration/cost, assign resources, sequence dependencies and revise as evidence changes.
        • A WBS is hierarchical and covers project scope without adding unrelated work.
        • Tools help coordinate ownership, dependencies and progress; they do not replace judgment or automatically fix bugs.
      • Function points estimate functional size using inputs, outputs, inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files, weighted under the chosen method.
        • They are not just lines of code and are not a direct exact measure of complexity.
        • Git tracks versions; issue trackers such as Jira track work/defects; CI tools such as Jenkins automate checks; Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE29 Critical path: forward and backward passes

      • In a dependency network, ES=max predecessor EF and EF=ES+duration; start tasks have ES=0 unless another constraint applies.
        • Project earliest finish is the maximum terminal EF.
        • Backward, LF=min successor LS and LS=LF-duration, starting from the required finish.
        • Total float/slack=LS-ES=LF-EF.
        • A critical path has the longest total duration and normally zero float in an unconstrained schedule.
      • If A takes 5 days and B=3,C=4 both follow A, project duration is 5+max(3,4)=9 days.
        • B finishes at 8, but the project waits for C at 9.
        • If paths B5+C6 and D8+E3 share a zero-duration start/end, both total 11; there are two critical paths, not one.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE30 Slack assumptions and PERT calculations

      • Early start/finish values alone do not determine slack without successor relationships and the project completion constraint.
        • If C3→D6 is a complete path parallel to A4→B5 and both finish at day9, C has zero float.
        • That network cannot be silently inferred from four unrelated ES/EF rows.
      • Traditional CPM uses point durations; PERT models uncertainty with optimistic a, most-likely m and pessimistic b. The classic estimate is TE=(a+4m+b)/6 and variance=((b-a)/6)^2.
        • For 3,6,15 days, TE=42/6=7 days and variance=4 days².
        • Do not replace the weighted estimate by a simple average.
        • These formulas are approximations, not guaranteed actual completion times.
      • References: SE-M, SE-PT

    • SE31 Business value, risks and resource optimization

      • With benefits and costs already discounted to a common date, ROI=(benefits-costs)/costs*100%.
        • Birr120000 benefits and Birr100000 costs give 20%, not 120%.
        • Identify project risks to resources/schedule, product risks to quality, and business risks to the organization.
        • Analyze likelihood and impact, plan responses and monitor.
      • Avoidance changes the plan to remove a risk, mitigation reduces likelihood/impact, transfer assigns consequences contractually, and retention/acceptance keeps the risk; passive acceptance may take no action.
        • Resource leveling adjusts dates to respect resource availability and can change project finish; smoothing uses available float within schedule constraints.
        • Neither magically creates extra staff.
      • References: SE-M, SE-RES

    • SE32 Team organization, development and maturity

      • Functional organizations group specialists by discipline; project organizations group people around projects.
        • Functional specialization helps staffing and knowledge continuity but may create handoff barriers.
        • Democratic teams share decisions; chief-programmer teams centralize technical coordination.
        • These are different classification dimensions.
        • Tuckman’s sequence is forming→storming→norming→performing→adjourning: orientation, conflict, norms, effective work and closure.
      • Historical Software CMM levels are 1 Initial, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed, 5 Optimizing.
        • Level2 establishes basic project discipline including requirements management, project planning, quality assurance and configuration management.
        • These historical labels must not be silently replaced by modern CMMI terminology.
        • A maturity model concerns process capability, not a guarantee that every product is defect free.
      • References: SE-M, SE-CMM, SE-TEAM

    • SE33 Configuration, change control and version control

      • Configuration management identifies controlled items, versions/baselines, change procedures, status and audits.
        • Items may include source code, requirements, manuals, test plans, environments and build configurations.
        • A team’s ordinary browser is usually a tool rather than product CI, but a controlled test-browser version may be an environment CI.
      • Change management handles request, impact assessment, decision/prioritization, implementation and validation; configuration management keeps all affected versions consistent.
        • Distributed Git gives each clone local history and supports independent branches followed by merging; it does not eliminate merge conflicts or approvals.
        • Plan test configuration management early and apply it throughout testing, not at just one exclusive phase.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE34 Quality assurance, verification and validation

      • Quality assurance establishes and checks processes/standards; quality control evaluates work products.
        • An SQA plan identifies standards, responsibilities, evaluations, reviews, audits and assurance records.
        • Quality of conformance means following the design/specification; a product can conform to a poor specification.
        • Verification asks whether specified obligations are implemented correctly; validation asks whether the product meets intended stakeholder needs.
        • Both can use reviews, analysis or execution, so “human-only versus computer-only” is false.
      • A fault/defect is an underlying problem; an error may be an incorrect internal state; a failure is an externally observed departure from required service.
        • Reliability is a product quality attribute; low cost or short development time are project outcomes.
        • Tests increase confidence and reveal defects but cannot generally guarantee correctness over every possible input.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE35 Testing levels and acceptance

      • Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks; a driver invokes the unit and a stub substitutes a called dependency.
        • Integration testing exercises interfaces and interactions among combined parts.
        • System testing checks the complete integrated system against functional and nonfunctional requirements in a representative environment.
      • Acceptance testing supports the customer/user’s acceptance decision against agreed needs and criteria.
        • Alpha typically happens in a controlled developer setting with selected users; beta uses external users in their environments.
        • None of these levels is universally the longest.
        • Unit is a level, while white-box is a technique; a unit can be tested using black-box cases too.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE36 Test types, regression and exploratory work

      • Functional tests check required behavior against the SRS and acceptance criteria.
        • Performance tests assess speed, throughput and resources under a specified workload; load uses expected demands and stress exceeds normal limits.
        • Usability, security, compatibility and reliability tests target their respective qualities. “Normal operating conditions” alone does not distinguish functional from performance testing.
      • Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge.
        • Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change; confirmation testing checks the particular defect repair.
        • Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution and is experience based.
        • Manual/automated describe execution support, not a compulsory black-/white-box classification.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE37 Equivalence, boundaries and decision tables

      • Equivalence partitioning groups inputs expected to behave alike, then samples valid and invalid groups.
        • For allowed age18..60, useful partitions are below18,18..60,above60.
        • Boundary tests target edges and neighbors, such as 17,18,19,59,60,61, with the exact set chosen under the stated coverage scheme.
      • A decision table lists condition combinations and resulting actions.
        • For validCard and enoughFunds, enumerate TT,TF,FT,FF; specify dispense only for TT and the proper rejection for others.
        • Cover feasible rules rather than blindly using every impossible combination.
        • These are specification-based techniques.
        • Test requirements can also define state-transition cases, such as rejecting dispatch from an already closed incident.
      • References: SE-M, SE-TEST

    • SE38 Statement, decision and branch coverage
