      • Statement coverage is the number of distinct executable statements exercised divided by the total executable statements in the declared test scope.
        • Unreachable statements can prevent100%; any justified exclusions must be documented with the adjusted scope.
        • Decision coverage counts decision outcomes; branch coverage counts control-flow edges, including unconditional edges under the stated convention.
        • Testing both true and false of each decision may need more than two overall test cases when branches nest.
        • Coverage is evidence of exercised structure, not proof of all behavior.
      • In the width/length/height bank program, the outer if has separate inner decisions in each branch.
        • Need outer true with inner true and false, and outer false with its inner true and false: four tests, for example (w,l,h)=(3,2,4),(3,2,1),(2,3,4),(2,3,1).
        • One run cannot exercise both outer branches.
        • All paths may be infeasible or infinite with loops; specify the chosen coverage target.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G, PRIMARY-ISTQB

    • SE39 Test process, plans and defect reports

      • Plan objectives, scope, resources, schedule, risks and entry/exit criteria.
        • Analyze the test basis for testable features and defects; design cases/expected results; implement data, scripts and environment; execute and compare; report defects; evaluate completion.
        • Analysis asks what to test and assesses testability; design asks how.
        • Monitoring/control run across these activities.
      • A test plan describes intended work; incident/defect reports are normally execution outputs.
        • A defect report should identify build/environment, steps, expected versus actual behavior, evidence and severity.
        • Anyone finding a fault should record it; testers often coordinate reporting, but it is not their exclusive permission.
        • Configuration control makes the tested version reproducible.
      • References: SE-M, SE-TEST

    • SE40 Maintenance and software evolution

      • Corrective maintenance fixes faults; adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes; perfective maintenance improves useful capability/performance; preventive maintenance reduces future risk, such as restructuring fragile code.
        • Motive determines category; refactoring can support preventive or perfective work.
        • Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.
      • A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release.
        • Among a list lacking the request step, impact analysis may be the earliest listed technical activity.
        • Major restructuring is reengineering; if the architecture itself changes, architectural transformation is the more specific description.
        • Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE41 Numerical and option defects in the bank

      • Q01600’s earliest finish is 9 days, absent from its choices.
        • Q01601 lacks latest times/full network, so zero slack follows only from an explicitly supplied completion-path assumption.
        • Q01644 has two equal 11-day paths, making both corresponding options true.
        • Use the network rules before consulting a supplied answer key.
      • Q00243 gives both a true description of structures and of views.
        • Q00240 contains a self-referential combined option.
        • Q01593 offers no genuine non-reusable exception because requirements, tests and architecture can all be product-line assets.
        • Such cases need corrected options or a multiple-answer instruction; they do not justify selecting a false rule.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE42 Context-dependent claims and model limitations

      • Several questions omit needed context: no test level is always most time consuming; no process is determined by team inexperience alone; no waterfall rule makes every later change impossible.
        • Requirements may describe required and prohibited behavior, including interface functions as well as usability qualities.
        • An interface question needs its exact obligation before functional/nonfunctional classification.
      • Sequence/state diagrams both show dynamic behavior.
        • Composition needs the diamond’s placement and ownership semantics. “Agile least suitable for safety-critical government work” assumes a particular lightweight process without required assurance; it is not universally true.
        • Treat the guide’s conventions as scenario hints and keep the stronger engineering rules explicit.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

    • SE43 Design choices, evidence and economical improvement

      • Choose designs by their effect on stated goals.
        • Fine-grained self-contained components, separation of producers/consumers and limited shared mutable data often improve maintainability.
        • Trade-offs remain: interfaces can add latency, isolation can complicate transactions, and global state can simplify one operation while coupling many others.
        • Prefer measurable quality scenarios to counting components alone.
      • Pareto’s 80/20 rule is a prioritization heuristic: a small subset of causes may account for much of the observed impact.
        • It does not guarantee 80% of defects can be fixed with exactly 20% effort.
        • Refactor to preserve behavior while improving structure; optimize only against measured needs; record rationale and update traceability and regression evidence after change.
      • References: SE-M, SE-N, SE-G

  • Design and Analysis of Algorithms

    • Design an algorithm by specifying its states, choices and correctness argument, then count its work and peak storage.
      • A familiar strategy name is not enough: independent subproblems, reuse, safe local choices, feasibility pruning and objective bounds lead to different methods.
    • For cost questions fix input size, case, primitive operation and arithmetic model.
      • Write the sum or recurrence before selecting an asymptotic bound.
    • For each design technique practice a small trace and explain why its discarded alternatives cannot improve the required answer.
    • Distinguish an exact algorithm from a heuristic, a decision problem from an optimization problem, and a tight bound from a merely valid upper bound.
    • Sections in this course
      Specify the problem and prove correctnessCost model, experiments and input sizeInput cases and bound notation are independentFormal asymptotic bounds and constantsGrowth ordering and loose boundsLoops, exact counts and additive costsConditional nested loops and malformed codePeak storage and recursion stacksRecurrences: substitution and expansionRecursion trees and the Master theoremComparison sorting lower boundsChoose a design from structural conditionsBinary search and simultaneous minimum/maximumMerge sort: invariant, trace and costsQuicksort: partition variants and worst casesSorting choices and comparison costsStrassen multiplication and divide/combine tradeoffsMaximum contiguous subarray: two valid strategiesGreedy correctness, limits and counterexamplesFractional knapsack versus indivisible itemsUnit-time job sequencing with deadlinesOptimal merge patterns and Huffman codingMSTs: Prim, Kruskal and the cut proofDijkstra: relaxation and the nonnegative conditionDP states, optimal substructure and proofMemoization, tabulation and FibonacciMultistage/DAG paths and Bellman–FordFloyd–Warshall, reachability and negative cycles0/1 knapsack DP and dominanceLCS: prefix states and reconstructionInterval DP: matrix chains and optimal BSTsReliability design under a budgetExact TSP with subset DPBFS, DFS and graph representationArticulation points and biconnected componentsBacktracking template and safe pruningN-queens: row, column and diagonal testsSubset sum: include/exclude and admissible boundsGraph coloring: feasibility versus minimum colorsHamiltonian cycles and permutation searchBranch and bound: node states and bound directionKnapsack branch and boundTSP branch and bound by matrix reductionP, NP, reductions and encoding sizeSpecific damaged items and minimum clarifications

    • DAA01 Specify the problem and prove correctness

      • State inputs, output, constraints and empty-solution policy.
        • Algorithms are finite, definite executable methods independent of source language; feasible satisfies constraints, optimal is best feasible.
        • Conditional branches are legitimate control flow.
      • Prove an invariant initially, after each step and at termination; for recursion prove base cases and the inductive reduction.
        • Testing finds failures but finite tests do not prove correctness for all inputs.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA02 Cost model, experiments and input size

      • Analysis counts operations and storage as functions of input size: array length n, graph vertices V/edges E, or the number of bits in integers.
        • A RAM model commonly gives constant cost to bounded-word arithmetic/access.
        • Arbitrarily large integer arithmetic and printing long outputs need their own costs.
        • Elapsed measurements also depend on hardware, compiler, cache, I/O and competing load.
      • Experimental/dynamic measurement observes actual runs; asymptotic analysis abstracts growth; probabilistic analysis studies expectations.
        • There is no universal taxonomy proving “graph analysis” or “dynamic analysis” is invalid.
        • Auxiliary space excludes input; I/O complexity counts transfers.
        • Representation affects costs; “data type complexity” is not a standard metric name.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA03 Input cases and bound notation are independent

      • At fixed size n, best case minimizes cost, worst case maximizes it, and average case takes an expectation under a specified input distribution.
        • Randomized expected cost may average internal choices for one fixed input.
        • Smallest input size is not best case.
      • O/Ω/Θ bound functions independently of case or resource.
        • A worst-case upper bound covers every size-n input, but O does not mean worst case.
        • Constant best case and quadratic worst case are not universal.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA04 Formal asymptotic bounds and constants

      • For eventually nonnegative f, g, f∈O(g) means f(n)≤c·g(n) for all n≥n 0, with fixed c>0. Ω reverses that inequality; Θ requires both bounds.
        • Little-o means f/g→0, and little-ω means f/g→∞ where the ratio exists. Θ specifies growth up to constant factors, not exact seconds or identical best/worst cases.
      • Prove the inequality for the whole tail, not selected values.
        • Transitivity allows chained upper bounds; sums are dominated by the largest nonnegative growth term.
      • Worked microexample
        • 10n+5≤15n for n≥1, so c=15,n 0=1 works. Also 3n²+4n+1≤8n² for n≥1. The notes’ claim 7n²+3n+5≤8n² at n=1 is false; c=15 works for all n≥1.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA05 Growth ordering and loose bounds

      • Representative growth is 1,log n,n,n log n,n²,n³,…,b^n,n! for fixed b>1.
        • Log bases differ by a constant.
        • Both n log n and n² are superlinear; log n is sublinear.
        • Polynomial growth has a fixed exponent in input size.
      • O(n²) also implies O(n³): upper bounds need not be tight.
        • Several offered bounds can be valid simultaneously.
        • Neither representative growth ordering nor Big-O labels alone determine finite-input speed.
      • Worked microexample
        • For f=4n² and g=8n, f/g=n/2→∞. Therefore f∈Ω(g) and evenω(g), while f is neither O(g) nor Θ(g).
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA06 Loops, exact counts and additive costs

      • Sequential costs add; independent nested loop counts multiply.
        • A dependent loop requires summation. n iterations of a constant body give Θ(n); ∑i=1.. n i=n(n+1)/2 gives Θ(n²).
        • Doubling i=1,2,4,… until i≥n takes ceil(log 2 n) iterations for n>1.
        • A 10n loop is linear under constant-cost output.
      • If m operations each have expected cost f(n) at the same fixed size, expected total is m f(n), by linearity of expectation; independence is unnecessary.
        • If sizes change, sum f(n_i).
        • Exact coefficients depend on whether tests, increments, arithmetic and assignments count separately.
      • Worked microexample
        • For sum=0; for(i=1;i<=n;i++) sum=sum+1; return sum: counting two initializations, n+1 tests, n increments,2n body operations and one return gives 4n+4. A different primitive-cost convention changes this exact expression, not Θ(n).
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA07 Conditional nested loops and malformed code

      • For the bank loop i=0.. n−1, j=i.. i²−1, and k=0.. j−1 only when j%i==0, i=0 and 1 have empty j ranges, so no remainder by zero is evaluated.
        • For i≥2, successful j values are i,2i,…,(i−1)i. The inner work is i∑m=1.. i−1 m=i²(i−1)/2=Θ(i³).
        • Summing over i gives Θ(n⁴); condition checks add only Θ(n³).
      • Neither offered n⁵ nor n⁷ is tight, though both are valid Big-O upper bounds.
        • This assumes mathematical integers and constant-cost output; literal signed C++ overflow in i*i is undefined, and mixed-language syntax must be repaired before claiming an executable runtime.
        • Redeclaring parameter n and return @;3 are syntax defects, not logarithmic algorithms.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA08 Peak storage and recursion stacks

      • Space complexity measures peak simultaneously live storage, not the sum of every allocation ever made.
        • Count input, auxiliary structures and stack according to the requested convention. n active recursion levels with constant-size frames need Θ(n) stack; depth log n with constant frames needs Θ(log n).
        • The number of total calls does not determine peak depth.
      • Slicing/copying arrays can add storage omitted by an index-based pseudocode analysis.
        • Tail-call elimination is language/runtime-dependent and cannot be assumed for ordinary C++/Java recursion.
        • Resource tradeoffs include caching subproblem results to save time while consuming memory.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA09 Recurrences: substitution and expansion

      • Include every recursive call, nonrecursive work and base case.
        • Expansion gives T(n)=T(n−1)+Θ(1)→Θ(n), and T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1)→Θ(log n).
        • For 2T(n/2)+Θ(n), logarithmically many levels each cost Θ(n), giving Θ(n log n).
      • Substitution guesses a bound and proves it inductively with constants/base cases; a lower-order correction may close the induction.
        • Unequal/decrementing recurrences need separate analysis.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA10 Recursion trees and the Master theorem

      • For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), a≥1, b>1, let p=log_b a. Level i has a^i nodes of size n/b^i. Compare f with n^p: a polynomial gap below gives Θ(n^p); f=Θ(n^p) gives Θ(n^p log n); a polynomial gap above gives Θ(f(n)) if a f(n/b)≤c f(n) for fixed c<1.
        • The third case needs this regularity condition.
      • A log-factor boundary may need an extended theorem or explicit summation.
        • State base work and include leaves.
        • This version does not apply to T(n)=T(n−1)+n or unequal-split quicksort.
      • Worked microexample
        • 4T(n/2)+n gives Θ(n²);2T(n/2)+n gives Θ(n log n); T(n/2)+n² gives Θ(n²). Each follows a different case. Also 4T(n/2)+n² gives Θ(n² log n), case 2.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S, DAA-MASTER

    • DAA11 Comparison sorting lower bounds

      • A comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves for distinct-key orderings.
        • Height h allows at most 2^h leaves, so h≥log 2(n!)=Ω(n log n); merge sort matches this worst-case bound.
        • Array indexing is not forbidden.
      • Counting/radix sorting exploits structured keys outside the comparison-only model.
        • Recurrences analyze particular algorithms; this decision tree bounds the entire comparison class.
        • None of the supplied “inappropriate technique because…” pairs is sound.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S, DAA-LOWER

    • DAA12 Choose a design from structural conditions

      • Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines results.
        • DP reuses a defined set of subproblem states.
        • Greedy commits to a feasible local choice only when a safety argument supports it.
        • Backtracking grows/retracts candidates when constraints fail; branch and bound also rejects candidates whose best possible objective cannot beat an incumbent.
      • “Breaks into subproblems,” “sequence of choices,” “incremental,” or “optimization” alone describes several strategies.
        • Exponential runtime is an outcome, not enough information to select a method.
        • Specify overlap, local-choice safety, revisability, exactness and usable bounds.
        • Selection sort’s appearance in the module’s divide-and-conquer list is an error; ordinary selection repeatedly selects one minimum.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA13 Binary search and simultaneous minimum/maximum

      • Binary search requires sorted random-access data.
        • Maintain inclusive low/high bounds, compute mid=low+(high−low)//2, and replace high with mid−1 or low with mid+1 according to the comparison.
        • Stop when found or low>high.
        • T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1): worst Θ(log n), best Θ(1); iterative auxiliary space Θ(1), recursive Θ(log n).
      • Finding both extrema by two unconditional comparisons per element costs 2n−2 comparisons, regardless of order.
        • Pair elements first, compare within each pair, then compare the smaller with minimum and larger with maximum: even n uses 3n/2−2 comparisons.
        • A balanced recursive version has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(1)=Θ(n).
        • The module’s unconditional two-if scan does not have an n−1-comparison best case.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA14 Merge sort: invariant, trace and costs

      • Split by indices, recursively sort each half, then repeatedly copy the smaller remaining front element into a temporary result.
        • The merge invariant says the output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest elements already consumed.
        • Append the unexhausted suffix.
        • Equal keys must be taken from the left half first to preserve stability.
      • Ordinary array merge sort has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n) across input orders, Θ(n) auxiliary buffer and Θ(log n) recursion depth.
        • A written +O(n) recurrence alone establishes an upper bound; the tight result also uses linear merge work.
        • Empty/singleton subarrays are base cases.
      • Worked microexample
        • [4,1,3,2] splits into[4,1] and[3,2], which sort to[1,4] and[2,3]. Merge selects 1,2,3 and appends 4. No assumption that the original array is already sorted is needed.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA15 Quicksort: partition variants and worst cases

      • Choose a pivot, partition, then sort the resulting smaller ranges.
        • In a two-pointer scheme, advance i while values are below pivot and j while above; when i≤j, swap and advance both.
        • Bound the scans and ensure progress on equal values.
        • Recurse on the resulting ranges.
        • Hoare-style partition boundaries need not put the pivot at its final position; Lomuto-style partition commonly does.
        • Do not mix their return conventions.
      • Balanced splits give Θ(n log n); repeatedly highly unbalanced splits give Θ(n²).
        • Random pivots give expected Θ(n log n), not a deterministic guarantee.
        • Median-of-three does not eliminate adversarial cases; three-way partitioning helps repeated keys.
        • Standard quicksort is unstable, uses expected Θ(log n) stack but worst Θ(n); recursing on the smaller side and iterating on the larger bounds stack by O(log n).
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA16 Sorting choices and comparison costs

      • Insertion shifts larger sorted-prefix keys: stable with strict comparisons, Θ(n) best and Θ(n²) worst.
        • Optimized bubble sort swaps adjacent inversions and stops after a no-swap pass: stable, Θ(n) best, Θ(n²) worst.
        • Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum: Θ(n²) comparisons in every order, normally unstable.
        • These use Θ(1) auxiliary array space.
      • Heap sort builds a max-heap in Θ(n), then extracts/restores in O(log n) per item: O(n log n) total, Θ(1) auxiliary space, ordinarily unstable.
        • It is not standard D&C. Merge sort offers stability/worst-case guarantees; quicksort’s practical advantage depends on implementation/workload.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA17 Strassen multiplication and divide/combine tradeoffs

      • Ordinary n×n multiplication computes n products/sums per output entry: Θ(n³).
        • Eight half-size block products still give 8T(n/2)+Θ(n²)=Θ(n³).
        • Strassen uses seven products plus block sums/differences:7T(n/2)+Θ(n²)=Θ(n^log 2 7)≈Θ(n^2.807).
      • Zero-padding preserves the required product.
        • The smaller exponent trades extra additions/temporary storage and possible numerical issues against multiplication work.
        • Use an ordinary base case for small matrices and specify exact versus floating-point arithmetic.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA18 Maximum contiguous subarray: two valid strategies

      • A maximum subarray is contiguous; it is not an arbitrary subsequence.
        • Divide-and-conquer compares the best left, best right and best crossing result.
        • The crossing result is the best suffix of the left half plus best prefix of the right, found in Θ(n).
        • This yields 2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n).
      • Kadane’s DP keeps the best sum ending at i: end[i]=max(A[i], end[i−1]+A[i]); keep the largest end seen.
        • This is Θ(n) time and Θ(1) extra space.
        • For a required nonempty subarray initialize from A[0], not zero; all-negative input then returns its largest element.
        • Empty-allowed variants may return zero.
        • Both D&C and DP therefore solve the bank’s unqualified strategy question.
      • Worked microexample
        • For[−2,3,−1,4,−5], ending sums are−2,3,2,6,1; optimum 6 comes from[3,−1,4]. For[−4,−2], a nonempty answer is−2.
      • References: DAA-S, DAA-MAX

    • DAA19 Greedy correctness, limits and counterexamples

      • A greedy algorithm repeatedly selects a locally attractive feasible option without later undoing it.
        • Optimal substructure alone does not prove this safe.
        • An exchange proof inserts the greedy choice into an optimum without worsening cost; recurse.
        • MST cut proofs use this exchange.
      • Advantages are often simple decisions and low overhead; limitations are irrevocable errors and problem-specific applicability.
        • A heuristic has no approximation guarantee merely because it is greedy.
        • For coins{1,3,4} and target 6, largest-first gives 4+1+1 while 3+3 uses fewer coins.
        • Activity selection instead has a safe earliest-finish rule for maximizing the number of nonoverlapping unweighted intervals; replacing the first chosen activity in an optimum with an earlier-finishing one leaves at least as much room.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA20 Fractional knapsack versus indivisible items

      • For positive weights/profits and divisible items, sort by decreasing value/weight, take complete items while they fit, then the fitting fraction of the next.
        • The exchange argument replaces lower-density selected weight by available higher-density weight; value cannot decrease.
        • Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by a linear scan.
        • Handle zero-weight beneficial items separately rather than divide by zero.
      • This proof depends on divisibility.
        • With capacity 10 and items(6,12),(5,8),(5,8), ratio-greedy chooses value 12; the two weight 5 items give 16 under 0/1 rules.
        • A generic “knapsack” question must specify fractional,0/1 or unbounded.
        • Feasibility alone does not guarantee optimality.
      • Worked microexample
        • Weights 15,10,18 and values 24,15,25 with capacity 20: take the weight 15 item and half the weight 10 item. Value 24+7.5=31.5; initial remaining capacity must be 20, not the number of items.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA21 Unit-time job sequencing with deadlines

      • Assume one machine, initially available jobs, unit durations, integer deadlines and profit only for on-time completion.
        • Process nonnegative-profit jobs by decreasing profit; place each in the latest free slot finishing by its deadline, or reject it.
        • Latest placement preserves earlier slots for tighter deadlines; feasible unit-job sets support profit-first exchange.
      • Sorting plus slot scans costs O(n log n+nD), with D capped at n. Equal-profit order is arbitrary; earlier deadline is optional.
        • Variable durations/release times invalidate this rule.
      • Worked microexample
        • Slots finishing 1…5 contain J 2,J 4,J 3,J 5,J 1. Profits 180+300+190+120+200=990; deadlines hold. J 6 cannot finish by 2. The five largest profits sum to 990, giving a matching upper bound.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA22 Optimal merge patterns and Huffman coding

      • Combine the two smallest weights, add their sum to total cost, and reinsert it.
        • A min-heap gives O(n log n) time/O(n) space.
        • Cost p+q counts moved records; worst-case comparisons are p+q−1 for nonempty lists, and actual comparisons may be fewer.
      • Huffman uses frequencies as weights and 0/1 branches to leaf symbols, making a prefix-free code.
        • Cost is∑frequency×depth.
        • An exchange makes the two least frequencies deepest siblings; contract them and induct.
        • Ties can change codes without changing optimal cost.
        • Header overhead can outweigh tiny-file savings.
      • Worked microexample
        • For weights 2,3,5,6: merge 2+3=5, then 5+5=10, then 10+6=16. Total weighted merge cost 31; the same tree construction minimizes weighted prefix-code length.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA23 MSTs: Prim, Kruskal and the cut proof

      • For a connected weighted undirected graph, an MST spans every vertex without cycles and minimizes total edge weight; it has V−1 edges.
        • Negative edges are allowed.
        • Equal weights may yield multiple MSTs; distinct weights suffice for uniqueness.
        • A tree is itself a graph.
      • Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex.
        • Kruskal sorts edges globally, accepting one only when union-find says its endpoints are in different components.
        • The cut proof exchanges a light crossing edge into some optimum without raising its weight.
        • Matrix Prim costs O(V²); binary-heap Prim O(E log V), and Kruskal O(E log E).
        • Dense-graph comparisons depend on these implementations.
        • Disconnected input gives a minimum spanning forest.
      • Worked microexample
        • Triangle AB=1,BC=2,AC=4: Kruskal accepts AB and BC for cost 3. If every edge is 1, any two edges give an MST, so uniqueness fails.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA24 Dijkstra: relaxation and the nonnegative condition

      • Initialize dist[source]=0, others∞ and predecessors unset.
        • Repeatedly extract the unsettled vertex u of minimum distance; relax each edge by dist[v]=min(dist[v], dist[u]+w(u, v)), updating predecessors when improved.
        • Once the minimum is∞, remaining vertices are unreachable.
        • A destination may be finalized before stopping, not merely discovered.
      • Nonnegative edges ensure a later path through unsettled vertices cannot improve a finalized distance.
        • With s→a=2, s→b=5, b→a=−4, finalizing a at 2 misses the later distance 1.
        • Binary-heap/list implementation costs O((V+E)log V), matrix scanning O(V²).
        • An MST minimizes total connection cost; Dijkstra minimizes each source-path distance, a different objective.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA25 DP states, optimal substructure and proof

      • Define state meaning, choices, recurrence, bases and dependency order.
        • Prove replacing a subsolution by a better one improves the full solution; otherwise state information may be missing.
        • Show the recurrence covers all legal final choices and generates feasible candidates, then induct in dependency order.
        • Store choices for reconstruction.
      • Overlapping states motivate reuse; optimal substructure supports optimization.
        • These are textbook signatures, not requirements that every DP problem optimize or every state have multiple users.
        • DP also counts/decides.
        • Cost=states×work per state and can remain exponential.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA26 Memoization, tabulation and Fibonacci

      • Memoization recursively checks a cache before solving a state and stores its result.
        • Tabulation orders dependencies explicitly; chosen domains may exclude irrelevant states.
        • Cache keys include all relevant parameters; recursion/locality/sparsity affect implementation cost.
      • Naive Fibonacci recomputes F(n−2) across branches: call count is Θ(φ^n), with O(2^n) a valid loose upper bound.
        • F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(i)=F(i−1)+F(i−2) yield Θ(n) unit-cost additions with memoization/tabulation.
        • Keeping only two recent values uses Θ(1) machine words; arbitrary-precision output needs growing bit storage.
        • This naive overlapping recursion is not the independent-subproblem ideal of D&C.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA27 Multistage/DAG paths and Bellman–Ford

      • For a DAG or multistage graph, compute cost-to-go in reverse topological order: F(t)=0 and F(u)=min over outgoing(u, v) of[w(u, v)+F(v)].
        • Missing routes have∞.
        • Record the minimizing next vertex.
        • Equivalently propagate source distances forward.
        • Complexity is Θ(V+E) with adjacency lists; negative edges are harmless without cycles.
        • Avoid relying on the module’s inconsistent forward/backward names; follow the recurrence’s dependencies.
      • For a general graph, Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges for up to V−1 passes and tests an additional pass for a reachable negative cycle: O(VE).
        • Thus “single-source shortest path” does not uniquely imply greedy; graph assumptions determine the algorithm.
      • Worked microexample
        • s→a=2,s→b=5,a→t=4,b→t=−1 gives F(a)=4,F(b)=−1 and F(s)=min(6,4)=4 via b.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA28 Floyd–Warshall, reachability and negative cycles

      • For all-pairs distances initialize D[i, i]=0, D[i, j] to the minimum direct edge weight, and missing edges to∞.
        • Preserve a negative self-loop by taking min(0, its weight).
        • For k outermost, update D[i, j]=min(D[i, j], D[i, k]+D[k, j]); before phase k, intermediates are restricted to earlier vertices.
        • Guard unreachable sums and numeric overflow.
      • Three loops give Θ(V³) time and Θ(V²) storage.
        • A negative diagonal afterward identifies a negative cycle; pairs able to traverse it have no finite minimum walk distance.
        • Warshall reachability replaces min/+ by OR/AND.
        • Floyd’s cost is not a universal best-achievable bound for all APSP settings; sparse nonnegative graphs permit repeated Dijkstra and other models permit other methods.
      • Worked microexample
        • If D[a,b]=4,D[b,c]=2,D[a,c]=11, phase b reduces D[a,c] to 6. Later phases must retain that improvement, unlike the module’s table that reprints 11.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA29 0/1 knapsack DP and dominance

      • For integer capacity W, K[i, w] is maximum value using the first i items within capacity w. Initialize K[0, w]=0.
        • If weight_i>w, use K[i−1, w]; otherwise take max(K[i−1, w], value_i+K[i−1, w−weight_i]).
        • The previous-row reference ensures each item is used at most once.
        • Backtrack changed values to recover chosen items.
      • Time O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial because W takes only O(log W) binary input bits.
        • Storage can be O(W); update capacities downward for 0/1 selection.
        • Upward iteration allows reuse and solves an unbounded variant.
        • In sparse(weight, profit) states, discard an option dominated by another with no greater weight and no smaller profit, provided both have the same remaining items.
      • Worked microexample
        • Weights 2,3,4, values 1,2,5 and W=6 yield value 6 by choosing weights 2+4. A state(weight 5,profit 3) is dominated by(weight 4,profit 5).
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA30 LCS: prefix states and reconstruction

      • A subsequence preserves order but need not be contiguous.
        • For prefixes of lengths i, j define L[i, j].
        • Empty-prefix rows/columns are 0.
        • If X[i−1]=Y[j−1], set L[i, j]=1+L[i−1, j−1]; otherwise use max(L[i−1, j], L[i, j−1]).
        • This corrects the short note’s mixed prefix lengths and zero-based character indexing.
      • Fill rows/columns in increasing order.
        • Reconstruct by taking matching characters diagonally or following a neighbor with the same optimal value; ties may produce different LCSs.
        • Time Θ(mn), table storage Θ(mn); two rows reduce value-only storage to O(min(m, n)), while ordinary reconstruction needs retained decisions or another technique.
      • Worked microexample
        • X=ABC,Y=AC: LCS is AC, length 2. Contiguous-substring matching would require a different recurrence, resetting a mismatch to zero.
      • References: DAA-S, DAA-LCS

    • DAA31 Interval DP: matrix chains and optimal BSTs

      • For matrix A_i of size p[i−1]×p[i], M[i, i]=0 and M[i, j]=min over i≤k<j of(M[i, k]+M[k+1, j]+p[i−1]p[k]p[j]).
        • Fill by increasing interval length and store the split.
        • Three matrices 10×30,30×5,5×60 cost 4500 under(AB)C versus 27000 under A(BC).
        • Time O(n³), space O(n²); multiplication order stays fixed while parentheses change.
      • For an OBST use sorted-key success weights p_i and gap failure weights q_i.
        • Let W(i, j)=∑p_i.. p_j+∑q_(i−1).. q_j.
        • Under the comparison-count convention, C(i, i−1)=0 and C(i, j)=W(i, j)+min_r(C(i, r−1)+C(r+1, j)); store r. CLRS-style dummy-node depths instead initialize empty cost to q_(i−1); final values differ by the fixed total gap weight.
        • Basic time O(n³), space O(n²).
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-INTERVAL

    • DAA32 Reliability design under a budget

      • Assume independent device failures.
        • With m_i parallel copies of stage i, each reliability r_i, stage reliability is φ_i(m_i)=1−(1−r_i)^m_i.
        • Series stages multiply: total∏φ_i.
        • Choose integers m_i≥1 with∑m_i c_i≤B; extra copies improve reliability but consume budget.
        • Correlated failures invalidate the simple independence formula.
      • Let R[i, b] be best reliability for the first i stages within budget b. Base R[0, b]=1; maximize R[i−1, b−m c_i]φ_i(m) over feasible m≥1.
        • Empty candidate sets give 0.
        • Time is O(stages×budget×maximum copies), with O(budget) value storage; reconstruct retained copy counts.
      • Worked microexample
        • For costs 30,15,20, reliabilities 0.9,0.8,0.5 and budget 105, copy counts(1,2,2) cost 100 and yield 0.9×0.96×0.75=0.648. Three copies of the weak last stage with the others single cost 105 but yield only 0.63.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA33 Exact TSP with subset DP

      • TSP asks for a minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex once and returning to its start; a shortest path need not visit all vertices or return.
        • Fix start s. Let F(S, j) be minimum cost from s through exactly S, ending at j∈S. Base F({s}, s)=0.
        • Transition F(S, j)=min_i∈S−{j}[F(S−{j}, i)+w(i, j)].
        • Finish with min_j≠s[F(V, j)+w(j, s)].
        • Missing edges cost∞.
      • Store predecessor choices to reconstruct a tour.
        • Held–Karp uses O(V²2^V) time and O(V 2^V) space, improving factorial enumeration but remaining exponential.
        • Greedy nearest-neighbor is a heuristic without a general exactness guarantee; backtracking and branch and bound can also solve exact TSP.
        • A generic method-selection question therefore needs more detail.
      • For Held–Karp, S contains the start s. Initialize F({s},s)=0 and impossible states to infinity; for larger sets, evaluate endpoints j other than s. These boundary cases prevent using a nonexistent predecessor state.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA34 BFS, DFS and graph representation

      • BFS marks a vertex when enqueued, explores neighbors with a FIFO queue and records predecessor/level.
        • Levels give shortest paths by edge count in unweighted/equal-weight graphs.
        • DFS marks on entry, recursively or iteratively explores an unvisited neighbor to completion, then resumes the parent.
      • Run from each unvisited vertex for a full disconnected traversal.
        • Adjacency lists give O(V+E) traversal time and O(V) auxiliary visited/queue/stack space; adjacency matrices give O(V²) scanning.
        • State neighbor order before requesting one exact traversal sequence.
        • Reverse DFS finish order gives a topological order only for DAGs.
        • BFS/DFS being printed under a DP unit does not make ordinary traversal a DP optimization algorithm.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA35 Articulation points and biconnected components

      • An articulation vertex increases the number of connected components when removed.
        • In an undirected DFS, disc[u] is discovery time and low[u] is the smallest discovery number reachable from u’s subtree using downward tree edges and at most one back edge.
        • Update low from children and nonparent back edges.
        • A root is articulation if it has at least two DFS children; a nonroot u is articulation if some child v has low[v]≥disc[u].
      • Such a child cannot reach an ancestor of u without u. A bridge has the stricter condition low[v]>disc[u].
        • An edge stack can output a vertex-biconnected block when low[v]≥disc[u], popping through edge(u, v).
        • With adjacency lists these checks cost O(V+E).
        • Distinguish vertex-biconnectivity from strong connectivity in directed graphs.
      • For a simple undirected graph initialize disc[u]=low[u]=++time on entry.
        • For an unvisited neighbor v, push tree edge(u,v), DFS(v), then low[u]=min(low[u],low[v]).
        • For a visited nonparent ancestor v, push the back edge once when disc[v]<disc[u] and use low[u]=min(low[u],disc[v]).
        • After a child returns with low[v]>=disc[u], pop through(u,v) to output one block.
        • Keep the separate root-child articulation rule and bridge test low[v]>disc[u].
        • Restart DFS at each unvisited vertex.
        • For multigraphs skip the parent edge by identity rather than skipping every edge to the parent.
      • A small procedure check
        • Two triangles A-B-C-A and C-D-E-C, DFS order A,B,C,D,E: disc=(1,2,3,4,5), low=(1,1,1,3,3). Only C is articulation; no edge is a bridge; stack yields blocks{A-B,B-C,C-A} and{C-D,D-E,E-C}. low[D]=disc[C] shows why articulation uses>= but bridge uses>.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-LOW, CMU-LOWLINK

    • DAA36 Backtracking template and safe pruning

      • Represent a partial assignment x[1.. k].
        • For each allowed next choice: assign it, test whether an extension remains possible, recurse if promising, and undo the assignment on return.
        • Report complete feasible candidates; stop after one only if the task requests existence/a single answer.
        • Explicit constraints restrict each variable’s domain; implicit constraints relate choices.
      • Correctness requires exhaustive consideration of every feasible extension and pruning only impossible branches.
        • Merely disliking a partial objective is not enough.
        • DFS recursion uses space proportional to search depth, while total search can remain exponential.
        • Memoizing equivalent states or stronger constraints can reduce work, but branch count depends on actual choices/tests.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA37 N-queens: row, column and diagonal tests

      • Use x[r]=column for one queen per row.
        • Reject against earlier row i when x[r]=x[i] or |x[r]−x[i]|=|r−i|; distinct rows are built into the representation.
        • Recurse after legal placement and remove it on return.
        • Column and r−column/r+column sets permit constant-time conflict tests.
      • Distinct columns leave at most n! complete permutations plus partial-node work; pruning does not guarantee polynomial time.
        • Placement/conflict storage is O(n).
        • Boards 2 and 3 have no solutions; state empty-board conventions.
      • Worked microexample
        • For n=4, column vector(2,4,1,3) is valid. Rows 1 and 2 with columns 2 and 3 would share a diagonal because both differences are 1, so that partial branch is rejected.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA38 Subset sum: include/exclude and admissible bounds

      • Include/exclude each item while tracking current sum s and remaining sum R. For nonnegative weights prune s>target or s+R<target.
        • On equality report the subset, considering zero-weight extensions if all subsets are needed.
        • Sorting positive weights can strengthen tests but cannot force inclusion of the next item.
      • With negative values, s>target may recover later; use valid attainable-range bounds.
        • There are up to 2^n subsets and O(n) recursion depth.
        • Define whether duplicate-valued items count by index.
      • Worked microexample
        • For{3,4,5,6}, target 13, subset{3,4,6} succeeds. At s=9 with remaining total 3, s+R=12<13 proves failure. At s=9 with remaining 4, equality can still be reached.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA39 Graph coloring: feasibility versus minimum colors

      • For a fixed m, assign colors 1…m to vertices, rejecting a color used by an already colored neighbor.
        • Backtrack when all colors fail.
        • At most m^V complete assignments exist, with additional checking cost; a simple O(V)-per-test implementation gives an exponential bound, not the module’s garbled polynomial-looking expression.
        • A self-loop makes proper coloring impossible.
      • The decision question asks whether m colors suffice; optimization asks for the chromatic number.
        • Trying increasing m with a complete decision search finds the minimum.
        • Greedy coloring chooses a color by vertex order and may use too many; it is not a general optimum proof.
        • An odd cycle needs 3 colors; an edge-containing bipartite graph needs 2, and an edgeless nonempty graph needs 1.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA40 Hamiltonian cycles and permutation search

      • Fix a start vertex to avoid rotational duplicates.
        • Extend a path with an unused vertex adjacent to its current end.
        • At V vertices require an edge back to the start; otherwise backtrack.
        • A Hamiltonian cycle visits vertices once, while an Euler cycle concerns visiting edges.
        • Fixing the start leaves up to(V−1)! candidate permutations, with polynomial checking overhead.
      • For a simple undirected graph with at least 3 vertices, a degree 1 vertex or articulation point rules out a Hamiltonian cycle, but their absence does not prove one exists.
        • TSP optimizes a weighted Hamiltonian tour; the decision existence search alone does not minimize its cost.
        • Reversed undirected tours may be equivalent if enumerating unique cycles.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA41 Branch and bound: node states and bound direction

      • A live node is generated and still eligible for expansion; the E-node is currently expanded; a dead node is finished or pruned.
        • FIFO selects live nodes by queue order, LIFO by stack order, and least-cost/best-bound uses a priority queue.
        • Selection changes work/storage; valid bounds preserve exactness.
      • For minimization, an incumbent feasible solution supplies an upper bound U; a partial node supplies a lower bound L on every completion.
        • Prune if L≥U when only one optimum/value is needed.
        • For maximization, feasible profit is a lower bound and an optimistic completion estimate is an upper bound; prune if upper≤incumbent.
        • Keep equality branches when all optimal solutions must be enumerated.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA42 Knapsack branch and bound

      • Sort positive-weight/value items by decreasing density and branch include/exclude.
        • Reject overweight nodes.
        • To bound a node’s possible profit, fill its remaining capacity fractionally from remaining items; this relaxation can only improve on 0/1 feasibility, so its value is an upper bound.
        • A whole-item feasible completion updates the incumbent; the fractional result itself is not a legal 0/1 answer.
      • With capacity 10 and items(6,12),(5,8),(5,8), the root fractional bound is 18.4: take the first and 4/5 of the second.
        • The first-item-in branch has whole-item value 12; excluding it permits the two other items, value 16.
        • Continue until every live upper bound is≤16 to certify optimality.
        • Avoid downward floating-point rounding that could invalidate the bound; worst-case search remains exponential.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

    • DAA43 TSP branch and bound by matrix reduction

      • For directed TSP, set diagonal/forbidden entries to∞.
        • Subtract each finite row minimum, then each finite column minimum, accumulating reductions.
        • Every tour uses one entry per row/column, so their sum is a lower bound; the relaxed assignment may contain disjoint subtours.
      • When including edge i→j, remove its used row/column, prevent premature subtours, reduce again and add the selected reduced-edge cost and new reductions to the parent bound.
        • Compare bounds with the best complete tour and expand a promising live node.
        • Never treat a reduced matrix’s zeros as proof of a complete valid tour.
      • Branch on an undecided edge i->j. The include child deletes row i/column j and adds its selected reduced cost plus new reductions to the parent bound.
        • The exclude child sets that entry to infinity and adds only new reductions.
        • Keep forced in/out-degree at most one.
        • Track each forced path from head h to tail t and forbid t->h until the path contains every vertex; this blocks premature cycles.
        • A required residual row/column with no finite choice is infeasible and pruned.
        • Accept only one complete cycle through every vertex, not a set of disjoint cycles.
      • A small procedure check
        • For four cities, cheap forced edges1->2,2->1 and3->4,4->3 satisfy one incoming/outgoing edge per city but are two disjoint2-cycles, not a tour. Once forced path1->2 is formed, forbid2->1 while fewer than4 vertices are in the path. Preserve the existing3-city reduction example: bound25 equals tour cost25.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S, BYU-TSP

    • DAA44 P, NP, reductions and encoding size

      • P contains decision problems solvable deterministically in polynomial input-bit time.
        • NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine.
        • NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP.
        • Whether P=NP remains open.
      • A polynomial many-one reduction A≤p B transforms each A-instance into a B-instance preserving yes/no. To prove B NP-hard, reduce a known hard A to B, not the reverse.
        • NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP; optimization TSP is normally called NP-hard, while its bounded-tour decision form is NP-complete.
        • A valid proposed tour and its cost are easy to check, but certifying global optimality is another task.
        • Pseudo-polynomial O(nW) knapsack is not polynomial in the bit length of W.
      • References: DAA-S, DAA-COMPLEXITY, DAA-REDUCTION

    • DAA45 Specific damaged items and minimum clarifications

      • For p=10,n=5, if(n>p) cout<<(n+p) skips output and terminates.
        • No offered violation of feasibility/finiteness/control flow follows.
        • Efficiency or a missing required output needs a specification.
      • The missing exponent in 3n?+7n+12 prevents a precise degree; fixed nonnegative integer exponents still give polynomials.
        • Stray ini/inl or redeclared n needs syntax repair; exact counts also need a primitive-cost model.
        • Do not substitute a marked key for these clarifications.
      • References: DAA-M, DAA-N, DAA-S

  • Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

    • Study intelligent agents, search and games, knowledge and reasoning, learning, and perception as connected ways to choose actions.
      • For each problem identify the available information, objective, assumptions, and evidence of success before choosing a technique.
    • Give this course its official six-item priority.
      • Learn the comparisons, then practise applying them rather than memorizing option letters.
    • Trace frontier order, path costs, quantifier scope, learning feedback, and evaluation splits on paper.
      • State the conditions behind completeness and optimality.
    • Use the question reference index to revisit weak concepts.
      • Some bank items have multiple valid choices or damaged source notation; the mapped clarification is part of the lesson.
    • Sections in this course
      AI capabilities and scopeFour approaches and the Turing testAgents, percepts and actionRationality and performanceSpecify the task with PEASSimple and model-based reflex agentsGoals, utility and model updatesLearning-agent componentsEnvironment dimensionsSingle-state, multiple-state and contingency problemsFormulate before searchingFrontiers and evaluation criteriaBreadth-first searchDepth-first searchUniform-cost search and DijkstraDepth limits, iterative deepening and two directionsHeuristics and greedy best-first searchAdmissibility, consistency and A*Work a heuristic-search exampleLocal optimization and evolutionary searchConstraint satisfactionGames and minimaxAlpha–beta and game evaluationRepresent knowledge for inferencePropositional logic and modelsFirst-order logic and quantifier scopeInference, unification and chainingDeduction, induction and abductionProbability and uncertain modelsFuzzy logic and vague categoriesSupervised learning and predictionUnsupervised, semi-supervised and active learningReinforcement learningNeural networks and deep learningGeneralization and validationMeasure the right errorsLanguage processing tasksMorphology, sounds and prosodyPerception, vision and roboticsExpert systems and choosing methodsClarify search and logic questionsClarify agent-category questionsClarify overlapping learning and AI labelsSource damage and assumptions that need repair

    • AI01 AI capabilities and scope

      • Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence: reasoning, learning, planning, perception and language.
        • Applied AI builds useful solutions; cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence.
        • A model should be compared with human behavior or experimental observations before claiming it explains human thought.
      • Narrow or weak AI addresses bounded tasks, such as face recognition, spam filtering or a voice assistant.
        • General AI denotes broad competence transferable across domains; strong AI also has a philosophical meaning involving actual understanding.
        • Do not equate a humanoid body, autonomous vehicle, or many features with general intelligence.
      • Exam trap
        • Data analysis overlaps AI when it uses learning or inference. It is not categorically excluded from AI.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI02 Four approaches and the Turing test

      • Thinking humanly models human mental processes; thinking rationally derives conclusions by valid logic.
        • Acting humanly seeks humanlike behavior; acting rationally selects actions expected to achieve objectives.
        • Thought processes and observed behavior are different evaluation targets.
      • The conversational Turing test asks whether a judge can reliably distinguish a machine from a human through their dialogue.
        • It requires language use, knowledge, reasoning and often learning.
        • It tests an operational behavior criterion, not proof of consciousness.
        • Cognitive models can be tested against response times, errors and psychological experiments.
      • Choose the approach
        • Finding a best action sequence to a goal fits acting rationally. Explaining human errors with a computational model fits thinking humanly.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI03 Agents, percepts and action

      • An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts through actuators or effectors.
        • Cameras sense; motors move.
        • Software sensors may be incoming messages and software actions may be API requests.
        • Humans are agents but are not artificial agents.
      • A percept is one observation; a percept sequence is the entire observation history.
        • An agent function maps percept sequences to actions: f:P*→A. An agent program implements that mapping on an architecture; agent = architecture + program.
        • Environment means the setting in which it senses and acts, not merely the search space.
        • Autonomy means relying substantially on experience rather than only a designer’s prior instructions.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI04 Rationality and performance

      • A performance measure defines success externally: safety, useful deliveries, elapsed time, or cost.
        • Rationality depends on that measure, prior knowledge, percept history, and available actions.
        • A rational agent selects the action with the best expected performance given its information.
      • Omniscience would mean knowing actual action outcomes in advance.
        • Rationality does not require omniscience or guaranteed success.
        • Even complete outcome knowledge cannot create a successful action when every available action fails.
        • Information gathering and exploration may therefore be rational actions.
      • Uncertain route
        • A route with expected travel time 20 minutes can be the rational choice even if an unforeseen closure makes it take 40 minutes.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI05 Specify the task with PEAS

      • PEAS means Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
        • Specify all four before designing an agent.
        • For a taxi: performance includes safety and travel time; environment includes roads, traffic and passengers; actuators include steering, brakes and displays; sensors include cameras, positioning and speed readings.
      • A sensor is not an actuator just because it influences a decision.
        • The performance measure is not the percept sequence: one defines success, the other supplies evidence.
        • Separate what the agent can observe from what a designer knows about the world.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI06 Simple and model-based reflex agents

      • A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean.
        • It has no persistent world-state memory.
        • This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions.
      • A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects.
        • It then applies rules to that state.
        • Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them.
      • Remember a hidden room
        • Remembering that a room was cleaned after it leaves sensor range requires internal state. Merely detecting current dirt does not.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI07 Goals, utility and model updates

      • A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state.
        • A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s).
        • Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes.
      • Updating an internal state after selecting an action predicts the action’s effect; it does not itself modify the external environment.
        • A stored variable named goal is insufficient to prove a goal-based policy if BEST_ACTION never uses it.
        • Model-based, goal-based, utility-based and learning capabilities can coexist.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI08 Learning-agent components

      • The performance element selects actions.
        • The learning element changes the agent to improve future performance.
        • The critic evaluates behavior against a performance standard and supplies feedback.
        • The problem generator suggests exploratory actions likely to yield useful experience.
      • Learning is improvement on task T, measured by P, through experience E. For spam filtering, T is classifying email, E is past labeled messages, and P might be recall at a required precision.
        • Exploration trades immediate reward for information; exploitation uses the best action currently known.
        • Learning can improve reflex, goal-based or utility-based agents.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI09 Environment dimensions

      • Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy.
        • Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness.
        • Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness.
      • Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations.
        • Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do.
        • A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic.
        • Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges.
        • Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability.
      • Classify examples
        • Chess is sequential, discrete and deterministic given both players’ chosen moves; untimed chess is static, timed chess semidynamic. A fixed crossword is static. Driving is partially observable, sequential, dynamic and partly continuous.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI10 Single-state, multiple-state and contingency problems

      • With a known deterministic model and full observation, a single current state can be used.
        • Without observation but with known deterministic transitions, a sensorless or multiple-state problem tracks a belief state: a set of possible states.
      • Nondeterminism or partial observation may require a contingency plan with branches based on later percepts.
        • Exploration or online search is required when the state space or transition model is unknown; observation alone does not identify this category.
        • These classifications can overlap.
        • A pairing based only on “partially observable, deterministic” cannot distinguish a known sensorless problem from an unknown exploration problem.
      • References: AI_AIMA

    • AI11 Formulate before searching

      • First formulate the goal; then formulate the problem by specifying initial state, legal actions, transition model, goal test, and action costs.
        • Search selects a sequence; execution applies it.
        • A state abstracts away irrelevant world details.
      • In route finding, states are cities, actions are roads, successors are neighboring cities, and path cost is accumulated distance or time.
        • A solution is a legal path ending at a goal; an optimal solution has minimum cost.
        • Automatic programming or program synthesis searches for a program satisfying a specification; conditional plans and loops require richer representations than a fixed action list.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI12 Frontiers and evaluation criteria

      • A search node records a state plus parent, action, depth and path cost.
        • Expanding a node generates its successors.
        • OPEN or frontier stores discovered candidates awaiting expansion; CLOSED records expanded states.
        • Reaching the same state through different paths does not imply the same node or cost.
      • Completeness means finding a solution if one exists under stated assumptions; optimality means returning the best solution.
        • Time counts work, often generated nodes; space counts simultaneous storage.
        • Let b be branching factor, d shallowest goal depth, m maximum search depth, and ℓ a depth limit.
        • Graph-search bounds in vertices V and edges E differ from implicit-tree bounds.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI13 Breadth-first search

      • BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue.
        • Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat.
        • It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal.
        • It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.
      • The tree contains 1+b+…+b^d nodes through depth d, giving O(b^d) under generation-time goal testing.
        • Expanding depth-d nodes before testing can generate depth d+1 and yields O(b^(d+1)); specify the convention.
        • Explicit finite graph traversal with visited-state tracking takes O(V+E) time and O(V) space.
      • Trace a queue
        • If S has children A,B and A has C,D, BFS removal order starts S,A,B,C,D, assuming that child order.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI14 Depth-first search

      • DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion.
        • FILO means the same order as LIFO.
        • With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.
      • Implicit-tree worst-case time is O(b^m), and space is O(bm) when pending siblings are stored, or O(m) for path-only recursive generation.
        • DFS is not generally optimal and can fail on infinite paths or cycles.
        • On a finite graph, visited-state tracking makes traversal complete but needs O(V) storage.
        • The bank’s O(b^m) space option confuses time with space.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI15 Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

      • UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n).
        • Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated.
        • Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent.
      • With finite branching and each step at least ε>0, UCS is complete and optimal.
        • Finite graphs permit nonnegative edges with proper duplicate handling.
        • Dijkstra uses the same minimum-distance principle, often computing all reachable distances; UCS commonly stops at a goal and generates states on demand.
        • Queue initialization is an implementation choice, not a fundamental distinction.
        • Negative edges invalidate the usual finalized-distance argument.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI16 Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

      • DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure.
        • It misses goals deeper than ℓ.
        • Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs.
        • Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.
      • Bidirectional search grows from start and goal until frontiers connect.
        • With suitable reverse actions, meeting tests and equal-cost BFS, time and space may fall to O(b^(d/2)).
        • Weighted variants require a sound stopping bound; the first intersection need not be cheapest.
        • IDA* deepens an f=g+h threshold rather than only a depth limit.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI17 Heuristics and greedy best-first search

      • A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge.
        • It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time.
        • Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.
      • Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function.
        • Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid.
        • It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch.
        • On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal.
        • Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI18 Admissibility, consistency and A*

      • A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n).
        • Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost.
        • Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths.
        • Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.
      • Admissibility suffices for optimal A* tree search; graph search that never reopens CLOSED states normally requires consistency.
        • With an admissible inconsistent heuristic, reopen states when g improves.
        • Test a goal when removed at minimum f. Completeness also needs finite branching and positive lower-bounded costs in infinite spaces.
        • Worst-case time and memory can be exponential; no heuristic universally guarantees speed.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SEARCH, AI_SHORT

    • AI19 Work a heuristic-search example

      • For S→A cost 2, S→B cost 1, A→G cost 2, B→G cost 10, set h(A)=2, h(B)=1, h(G)=0.
        • After expanding S, greedy chooses B because 1<2 and can then choose G, returning cost 11.
        • A* compares A:f=2+2=4 and B:f=1+1=2; after B, its G entry costs 11.
        • It next expands A and replaces G with cost 4, which is removed and accepted.
      • For a sliding puzzle with unit moves, misplaced-tile count and summed Manhattan distances excluding the blank are lower bounds.
        • Straight-line distance is a lower bound on road distance; it is not automatically a lower bound on travel time without conversion using a valid speed bound.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI20 Local optimization and evolutionary search

      • Local search keeps a complete candidate configuration and improves its objective; the path may be irrelevant.
        • Hill climbing chooses better neighbors.
        • First-improvement accepts the first improvement; steepest-ascent examines all neighbors; stochastic variants choose among improvements.
        • Local maxima, plateaus and ridges can stop progress.
        • Random restarts or limited sideways steps can help without guaranteeing success.
      • A genetic algorithm maintains a population, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and repeats replacement.
        • It searches without guaranteeing global optimality.
        • Means–ends analysis selects a difference between current and goal states, chooses an operator reducing it, and recursively solves its preconditions.
        • Neither method is simply A* running backward.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI21 Constraint satisfaction

      • A CSP specifies variables X, domains D, and constraints C. A solution assigns every variable a value and satisfies every constraint.
        • Complete means all variables assigned; consistent means no violated constraint.
        • A complete assignment can still be inconsistent.
      • Backtracking assigns a variable, tries a legal value, and undoes the choice on failure.
        • Choose the variable with fewest remaining values; break ties by degree; try values that rule out fewest neighbor choices.
        • Forward checking removes incompatible neighbor values.
        • Arc consistency removes a value when a binary constraint offers it no support in the other domain.
        • CSP is a problem framework using search and propagation, not a universal fourth uninformed traversal.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI22 Games and minimax

      • Adversarial search models agents with competing objectives.
        • A game specifies states, player to move, legal actions, successor function, terminal test and utility.
        • Perfect information means previous moves and current state are visible; it does not reveal future choices or imply absence of chance.
        • Zero-sum utility makes one player’s gain the other’s loss.
      • Minimax assigns terminal utilities, takes minima at MIN nodes and maxima at MAX nodes, then chooses a maximum-valued root action.
        • It gives the best guaranteed outcome against optimal opposition within the modeled tree.
        • For stochastic outcomes add chance nodes weighted by probabilities.
      • Back up leaves
        • If two MIN children have leaves [3,5] and [2,9], their values are 3 and 2. MAX chooses the first branch with value 3.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI23 Alpha–beta and game evaluation

      • Alpha is MAX’s best lower bound; beta is MIN’s best upper bound.
        • Pass bounds down, update alpha at MAX and beta at MIN, and prune when alpha≥beta.
        • Pruning preserves the minimax value for the same searched tree.
        • Good move ordering increases pruning: worst-case O(b^m), ideal ordering about O(b^(m/2)).
      • At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability.
        • Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss.
        • Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions.
        • These are different features, often combined.
        • Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI24 Represent knowledge for inference

      • Knowledge representation encodes facts, objects, relations, events and rules so a machine can use them.
        • Syntax defines legal expressions; semantics defines their meaning.
        • A knowledge base stores assertions; an inference system derives consequences.
        • Declarative knowledge says what is true; procedural knowledge specifies how to act.
      • A semantic network connects concept nodes by labeled relations such as is-a. Frames describe stereotyped entities through slots, values and defaults.
        • Production systems use IF conditions THEN conclusions or actions, matching rules against working memory and selecting among applicable rules.
        • A graph suits relationships such as frequently bought together; frames suit attributes.
        • No representation is always best for recommendation without task requirements.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI25 Propositional logic and models

      • Propositional atoms represent whole true-or-false claims. ¬P negates; P∧Q requires both; P∨Q requires at least one; P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; P↔Q requires matching truth values.
        • Thus P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q. De Morgan gives ¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q.
      • A model is an interpretation making a sentence true.
        • Valid means true in every interpretation; satisfiable means true in at least one; unsatisfiable means true in none.
        • Invalid means not valid, and may still be satisfiable.
        • P∨¬P is valid; P is satisfiable but not valid; P∧¬P is unsatisfiable.
        • Entailment KB⊨α means every model of KB also satisfies α.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI26 First-order logic and quantifier scope

      • First-order logic adds objects, predicates, functions and quantified object variables.
        • Human(a) is a property; Likes(a,b) a relation; father(a) a function term.
        • Propositional logic has no object quantifiers, but its truth still depends on the assigned atom values.
      • Use ∀x(Human(x)→Mortal(x)) for all humans, and ∃x(Student(x)∧Tall(x)) for at least one tall student.
        • These are useful translation patterns, not rules forbidding other connectives. ∀x∃y Likes(x,y) allows a different y for each x; ∃y∀x Likes(x,y) requires one shared y. Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x).
        • Only occurrences within the correct quantifier’s scope are bound.
      • Someone at the door
        • ∃x(StandingAt(x,door)∧Tall(x)) requires one individual satisfying both predicates. Using implication instead allows an unrelated individual to satisfy it vacuously.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI27 Inference, unification and chaining

      • Modus ponens derives Q from P and P→Q; modus tollens derives ¬P from P→Q and ¬Q. Affirming Q does not prove P. Universal instantiation substitutes an object for a universally quantified variable.
        • Unification finds a consistent substitution: Knows(x,Ada) and Knows(Ben,y) unify with x=Ben,y=Ada.
        • Distinct constants cannot be unified by renaming them.
      • Resolution combines clauses P∨Q and ¬P∨R into Q∨R. To prove α, add ¬α to KB in clause form and derive contradiction.
        • Forward chaining starts with facts and fires rules; backward chaining starts with a query and proves required premises.
        • Sound inference preserves truth; completeness means finding all entailed conclusions in its specified setting.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI28 Deduction, induction and abduction

      • Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal.
        • Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples.
        • Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it.
        • Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations.
      • Classical logical entailment is monotonic: adding premises preserves previous consequences.
        • Default reasoning can be nonmonotonic: infer a bird usually flies, then withdraw this when told it is a penguin.
        • Common-sense defaults are useful with incomplete knowledge, but are not guaranteed truths.
        • Blind search is a search strategy, not a definition of reasoning.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI29 Probability and uncertain models

      • Probability describes uncertainty about events.
        • P(¬A)=1−P(A); P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0.
        • Bayes gives P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E): posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence probability.
        • For mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses, P(E)=ΣiP(E|Hi)P(Hi).
      • A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with conditional probability tables; its joint distribution factors as the product of each node’s probability given its parents.
        • A Markov model assumes the next state depends on the current state rather than the entire past.
        • These represent uncertainty; fuzzy membership represents a different issue.
      • Update a hypothesis
        • If P(H)=0.1, P(E|H)=0.8 and P(E|¬H)=0.2, then P(E)=0.26 and P(H|E)=0.08/0.26≈0.308. Likelihood 0.8 is not the posterior.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI30 Fuzzy logic and vague categories

      • Fuzzy sets assign graded membership μ(x) between 0 and 1 to concepts such as warm or tall.
        • A temperature can belong to warm with degree 0.7.
        • This is not a 70% probability that an otherwise crisp warm proposition is true.
        • Boolean logic uses only true and false; probability describes uncertainty about events.
      • A fuzzy controller fuzzifies measurements, applies graded IF–THEN rules, combines outputs and often defuzzifies to a numerical action.
        • Fuzzy control suits linguistic rules about degrees; reinforcement learning suits reward-based adaptation.
        • Merely saying an environment is complex or uncertain does not uniquely select either method.
      • References: AI_FUZZY

    • AI31 Supervised learning and prediction

      • Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples.
        • Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices.
        • Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either.
        • Specify the target before choosing a method.
      • A decision tree tests an attribute at each internal node, follows the corresponding branch and predicts at a leaf.
        • ID3 chooses high information gain: H(S)=−Σpᵢlog₂pᵢ; gain is parent entropy minus weighted child entropy.
        • Gini impurity is 1−Σpᵢ², zero for a pure class.
        • Pruning limits overfitting.
        • Neural networks, support-vector machines and trees can all be supervised.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI32 Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

      • Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features.
        • Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance.
        • K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.
      • Semi-supervised learning combines some labels with additional unlabeled data.
