        • Active learning chooses informative cases for an oracle to label; it still uses labels. “Exploratory learning” is not an exclusive standard synonym: it can mean unsupervised exploration or active data acquisition, so define the feedback.
        • A task named summarization or time-series analysis is not automatically supervised; its training targets determine that.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_ACTIVE

    • AI33 Reinforcement learning

      • An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward.
        • Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label.
        • Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.
      • An illustrative discounted return is Gt=rt+1+γrt+2+γ²rt+3+…, with 0≤γ<1.
        • The policy maps states or histories to action choices.
        • Exploration gathers information; exploitation pursues currently estimated reward.
        • RL is part of machine learning, which is part of AI. “No labels” alone fits both unsupervised learning and RL; reward-driven interaction distinguishes RL.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI34 Neural networks and deep learning

      • A neuron computes z=Σiwixi+b and output a=φ(z).
        • For x=(2,1), w=(0.5,−1), b=0.2, z=0.2.
        • Linear activation returns z; sigmoid returns 1/(1+e^(−z)); tanh is bipolar; ReLU returns max(0,z).
        • Nonlinearities let multiple layers represent nonlinear relationships.
      • Feedforward networks pass signals toward outputs without recurrent state loops; recurrent networks carry state across sequence steps.
        • Training adjusts weights, often through gradients and backpropagation.
        • Backpropagation is not the same as a recurrent connection.
        • Deep learning uses multiple representation layers and can learn features from images, sound and text.
        • CNNs share filters across image locations.
        • ANN is a brain-inspired abstraction, not a literal brain simulation; DL⊂ML⊂AI.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI35 Generalization and validation

      • Overfitting means fitting training-specific details so performance drops on unseen data; underfitting means the model is too limited or poorly fitted even on training data.
        • A learning curve plots performance against training size or training progress.
        • Complexity control, regularization, pruning and more representative data can help.
      • Train data fits parameters; validation data selects models or settings; a held-out test set estimates final performance.
        • In k-fold validation, train k models, each on k−1 folds and evaluate on the remaining fold, then average scores.
        • Stratification approximately preserves label proportions.
        • Fit preprocessing within each training fold.
        • Time-ordered data needs splits respecting time; repeated tuning on the final test set leaks information.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_CV

    • AI36 Measure the right errors

      • With a fixed positive class, TP means true positives, FP false positive predictions, FN missed positives, TN true negatives.
        • Accuracy=(TP+TN)/N; precision=TP/(TP+FP); recall=TP/(TP+FN); F1=2PR/(P+R).
        • State the averaging and zero-denominator convention when relevant.
      • For TP=30, FP=10, FN=20, TN=40, accuracy=70%, precision=75%, recall=60%, and F1≈66.7%.
        • Accuracy can hide failure on a rare class.
        • Choose recall when missed positives matter; choose precision when false alarms are costly.
        • Regression errors include MAE=mean|y−ŷ| and MSE=mean(y−ŷ)²; squared error penalizes large misses more strongly.
      • References: AI_SHORT

    • AI37 Language processing tasks

      • NLP interprets and generates human language: translation, dialogue, summarization, question answering and text generation.
        • Speech recognition converts audio to text; speech synthesis generates speech.
        • They overlap language processing but solve different input/output tasks.
      • Tokenization divides text into processing units; tokens may be words, punctuation or subwords.
        • POS tagging assigns grammatical roles; named-entity recognition identifies people, organizations and locations.
        • Parsing identifies grammatical structure; semantics concerns meaning; discourse links sentences; pragmatics uses context and speaker intent.
        • Sentiment analysis predicts evaluative tone.
        • Ambiguity can occur at every level: “bank” has multiple senses, and “I saw the man with a telescope” has multiple attachments.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI38 Morphology, sounds and prosody

      • Morphology studies meaningful word parts: un-happi-ness contains a prefix, stem and suffix; cats contains cat and plural -s. It differs from tokenization, which identifies processing boundaries.
        • Phonetics studies physical speech sounds; phonology studies a language’s sound patterns and contrasts.
      • Prosody concerns stress, rhythm, timing, prominence and intonation across syllables and phrases.
        • A pitch rise can help signal a question; shifting stress can change emphasis.
        • These cues assist dialogue and speech processing.
        • Pragmatics concerns intended meaning in context, not the internal components of words.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_PROSODY

    • AI39 Perception, vision and robotics

      • Computer vision interprets images or video: classification names image content, detection locates objects, segmentation labels pixels, and recognition identifies objects or people.
        • Occlusion, lighting change, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context make open-world perception difficult even when a face detector works well.
      • Robotics combines mechanical, electrical, control and computing systems to sense, plan and act physically.
        • Components include sensors, controller, power supply, actuators and an end effector.
        • Locomotion may be legged, wheeled or tracked, with trade-offs in terrain, stability and efficiency.
        • Software can act autonomously without being a robot.
        • Humanoid shape is not evidence of general intelligence.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI40 Expert systems and choosing methods

      • An expert system applies specialized knowledge to a domain such as equipment diagnosis.
        • The domain expert supplies expertise; the knowledge engineer elicits and encodes it; the inference engine reasons over a knowledge base and working facts.
        • The user interface handles interaction; an explanation facility presents why or how a conclusion was reached.
      • Rules offer inspectable domain reasoning but can be brittle and costly to maintain.
        • Learned models handle data-rich patterns but depend on representative data and validation.
        • Search suits explicit action alternatives; probabilistic models suit uncertain evidence.
        • Bias in data or evaluation can create unfair outcomes.
        • Evaluate errors across relevant groups, robustness, privacy and human oversight rather than assuming automation is always beneficial.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI41 Clarify search and logic questions

      • A* is forward best-first search combining actual past cost with estimated future cost; it does not inherently run a backward frontier.
        • Both A* and IDA* can have exponential worst cases and optimality under their conditions. “Minimum heuristic” and “estimated closest” describe the same greedy choice.
        • LIFO and FILO are synonyms.
      • A stem saying only “uses information from the current state” does not establish a heuristic.
        • Ask whether remaining cost is estimated.
        • A request for a single false validity statement fails if both “invalid iff unsatisfiable” and “satisfiable implies valid” are offered.
        • Repair by asking for all false statements or specifying one claim.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SEARCH

    • AI42 Clarify agent-category questions

      • The common teaching list contains five agent classes when learning agents are included, or four decision architectures before learning is added.
        • A bare question asking how many types exist needs its convention. “Target-based” can mean goal-based; “unity-based” is not utility-based.
      • A generic rule does not distinguish simple from model-based reflex without specifying memory.
        • A goal declaration unused by the action policy does not establish goal-based behavior. “Sensors and effectors” describes interaction, not omniscience or intelligence by itself.
        • Where effectors and actuators are separate options, the requested acting component is not unique unless a mechanical distinction is defined.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI43 Clarify overlapping learning and AI labels

      • ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways.
        • Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives.
        • Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised.
        • To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure.
      • Face recognition is both an applied task and a narrow capability.
        • Broad machine-intelligence goals can include emulating human intelligence and building systems that learn.
        • Humanlike problem-solving alone does not uniquely select expert systems.
        • Python is widely used, but C++ and Java also implement AI; “commonly used” does not isolate one language.
        • McCarthy is associated with naming AI, not its sole invention.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_SHORT, AI_DEEP

    • AI44 Source damage and assumptions that need repair

      • The retained original image restores Q00183 as ∀x∃y∃t¬F(x,y,t): for each person there is a person and time at which fooling fails.
        • By quantifier negation this is ¬∃x∀y∀t F(x,y,t), so nobody fools everybody all the time (D).
        • The bold C key is wrong: forbidding every successful instance is much stronger.
        • Use the verified formula rather than the damaged extracted glyphs.
      • Compare Dijkstra and uniform-cost search under stated implementations rather than treating queue initialization as an intrinsic difference.
        • The episodic-chess item needs its unit of decision: moves within a match are sequential; independently reset matches can be episodes.
        • Recommendation “most suitable” needs requirements; graph relationships support one choice but do not exclude other designs.
      • References: AI_MOD, AI_DEEP, AI_VISUAL

  • Computer Security

    • Security is reasoning about assets, threats, trust boundaries and justified controls.
      • Learn mechanisms as well as names: identify the damaged property, explain the failure, choose a control and state its limits.
      • The four blueprint outcomes include program security, evaluated trusted operating systems and database security.
    • For each scenario identify the asset, actor, violated property, mechanism and most direct control.
    • Practise key direction, classical cipher arithmetic and small RSA calculations; do not infer correctness from a supplied answer key.
    • Compare confidentiality with integrity models, function with assurance, detection with prevention, and backup with replication.
      • Test assumptions before selecting one answer.
    • Sections in this course
      CIA and the property actually harmedThreat, vulnerability, risk and controlAttack classifications and attacker intentMalware: propagation, disguise and payloadSocial engineering, spoofing and sessionsDoS, wireless attacks and layer-specific defensesIdentification, authentication and factorsPasswords and delegated authorizationAccess control and least privilegeConfidentiality and integrity modelsPhysical protection and resilient designCryptographic vocabulary and security assumptionsSubstitution, shift and affine ciphersVigenère, Playfair and HillTransposition and one-time padsSymmetric keys, AES and distributionDES and Feistel mechanicsPublic keys and hybrid protectionRSA arithmetic and invalid source examplesHashes, MACs and signaturesCertificates, TLS and HTTPSSSH, IPsec, email protection and SETFirewalls and protected boundariesDetection, prevention and diagnostic measuresMemory safety and secure input handlingSQL injection, XSS and request forgeryRaces, testing and secure developmentTrusted OS requirements and reference mediationIndependent evaluation, certification and assuranceDatabase secrecy, permissions and key boundariesDatabase integrity and reliability mechanismsInference control and multilevel databasesPolicy, incident response and recovery objectivesInterpret flawed security questions precisely

    • SEC01 CIA and the property actually harmed

      • Confidentiality restricts disclosure: copying a credit-card database violates secrecy even if the original stays intact.
        • Integrity restricts unauthorized or improper changes: altering a balance or inserting a false message damages correctness.
        • Availability supplies timely, usable service to authorized users: crashes, resource starvation and denied access violate it.
        • One event can harm several goals.
      • Authentication establishes an identity or other claim; authorization decides permitted actions.
        • Accountability links actions to responsible entities through reliable identity and protected logs.
        • Non-repudiation supplies evidence supporting origin or receipt; signatures do not make denial physically impossible.
        • Information assurance includes confidence, risk management, protection, detection, response and restoration across the information lifecycle.
        • Data security protects information at rest, in use and in transit, including accidental corruption as well as intentional attacks.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC02 Threat, vulnerability, risk and control

      • An asset is something valuable: data, software, hardware, service or reputation.
        • A threat is a potentially harmful circumstance; a vulnerability is an exploitable weakness; an attack is an actual attempt; a control reduces likelihood or impact.
        • A software flaw is not automatically an active attack.
        • Risk concerns likelihood and consequence, not a universally meaningful numeric product of two unmeasured labels.
      • Preventive controls block events, detective controls reveal them, corrective/recovery controls restore safe operation, and deterrents discourage attempts.
        • Encryption is preventive for disclosure; an audit log is principally detective/accountability evidence.
        • Physical, technical and administrative are control categories, not competing stages.
        • An external firewall cannot replace a written policy or a locked equipment room.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC03 Attack classifications and attacker intent

      • Interception copies or observes data, modification alters it, interruption blocks it, and fabrication inserts false material.
        • The 4D classification uses disclosure, deception, disruption and usurpation, the last meaning unauthorized control.
        • DoS primarily demonstrates disruption/availability loss; it need not give control of the victim.
      • Passive attacks observe without changing the target exchange: sniffing and traffic analysis.
        • Active attacks inject, alter, replay or disrupt.
        • These are not synonyms for offline and online.
        • Traffic analysis can infer relationships from timing/size even when content is encrypted.
        • Neither category is universally easy to prevent or detect.
      • White-hat testing requires authorization and scope; black-hat activity is malicious or unauthorized.
        • A competitor may seek commercial secrets; hacktivists pursue a cause. “Hacker” alone does not establish legality.
        • Insider versus outsider describes origin/trust position, not the specific mechanism.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC04 Malware: propagation, disguise and payload

      • A virus replicates by attaching to a host program or document; execution of the infected host spreads it.
        • A worm replicates independently, commonly across networks.
        • A Trojan disguises malicious behavior as something useful and does not require self-replication.
        • These labels describe different properties, so a malware package may contain several components.
      • Spyware monitors users; a keylogger records keystrokes.
        • Adware displays unwanted advertising and may also track users.
        • Ransomware denies access through encryption/locking and extortion.
        • A logic bomb waits for a trigger.
        • A backdoor bypasses ordinary access paths; a rootkit hides malicious presence or privileged activity.
        • A zombie/bot follows remote commands; a botnet is a collection.
        • Malware is the umbrella term, not a specific replication method.
        • Update, restrict execution, isolate compromise and maintain tested offline backups; no antivirus guarantees complete protection.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC05 Social engineering, spoofing and sessions

      • Phishing impersonates a trusted source to obtain secrets or induce an unsafe action; spear phishing targets a specific person.
        • Verify a request through an independently known channel.
        • Shoulder surfing observes entry; pretexting invents a reason for disclosure.
        • Monitoring software used with authorization is not necessarily an attack merely because it records activity.
      • Masquerade claims another identity.
        • ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address.
        • An intermediary attack intercepts and can alter exchanges.
        • A replay reuses a valid old message; nonces, timestamps and sequence checks can reject it.
        • Session hijacking steals or predicts a valid session token.
        • Protect transport, regenerate session IDs after login, restrict cookies and check authorization server-side on every sensitive request.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC06 DoS, wireless attacks and layer-specific defenses

      • DoS exhausts or disables a resource; distributed DoS uses multiple sources, often bots or reflected/amplified responses.
        • A SYN flood leaves many incomplete TCP handshakes occupying state.
        • DNS flooding targets query capacity; NXDOMAIN attacks generate queries for nonexistent names to stress resolvers.
        • Fragment floods abuse reassembly or packet-processing resources.
        • Rate limits, SYN cookies, filtering and upstream capacity controls address different bottlenecks.
      • Rogue access points imitate or bypass approved wireless service.
        • Bluesnarfing steals Bluetooth information; bluejacking sends unsolicited Bluetooth messages.
        • Phishing is not specific to wireless.
        • Match a defense to its layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data, TLS authenticates/protects application transport, and bounds-safe code prevents overflows.
        • HTTPS cannot fix an unsafe memory copy in a server.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC07 Identification, authentication and factors

      • A common access sequence is identify the subject, authenticate the claim, authorize the operation, then record relevant events.
        • Identification is the username/claim, not its proof.
        • If identification is omitted from choices, authentication is the first available access-control stage.
        • User-to-host means a user proves identity to a host; host-to-user means the host proves its identity to a user; the arrow names the prover and verifier.
      • Knowledge is a password/PIN, possession is a token/card, and inherence is a biometric such as a fingerprint.
        • Behavioral biometrics include typing rhythm or handwriting; some textbooks call these “something one does.” A body characteristic is not “three-factor authentication”: one biometric is one factor.
        • Password plus PIN remains one factor class; card plus PIN is two.
        • An OTP’s factor depends on its delivery/generation mechanism.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC08 Passwords and delegated authorization

      • Brute force enumerates guesses; dictionary attacks prioritize likely words; credential stuffing tries previously leaked credentials on another service.
        • Online attempts face server rate limits; offline attacks against stolen verifiers do not.
        • Short passwords can fail in either setting.
        • Use unique long secrets and password managers, rate limiting and suitable MFA; store salted slow password hashes, not reversible plaintext passwords.
        • A salt prevents shared precomputed lookup, but is not secret.
      • OAuth is an authorization framework: a client obtains limited access tokens, the authorization server authenticates/obtains approval from the resource owner, and the resource server validates tokens for protected data.
        • The authorization server can delegate identity checks.
        • OAuth alone does not define a complete end-user login identity protocol; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N, SEC-OAUTH

    • SEC09 Access control and least privilege

      • Subjects request operations on objects.
        • An ACL associates an object/resource with allowed subjects or actions; a network ACL matches traffic such as address, protocol and port.
        • Classification and filtering are direct effects; high availability or malware detection is not guaranteed by an ACL.
      • DAC lets owners grant permissions; mandatory control enforces labels and policy that ordinary owners cannot override.
        • RBAC gives permissions to roles and assigns users to roles.
        • ABAC evaluates subject, object, action and environment attributes.
        • Rule-based controls apply explicit conditions, such as time or source network.
      • Least privilege gives only needed rights, for needed time.
        • Separation of duties splits sensitive steps across parties.
        • Deny by default, mediate every access and revoke stale permissions.
        • Allowing SELECT but denying UPDATE is an access-control decision that helps integrity; it does not by itself enforce all valid business-state transitions.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC10 Confidentiality and integrity models

      • Bell–LaPadula protects confidentiality.
        • The simple-security rule prohibits reading above a subject’s level; the star rule prohibits writing down.
        • The strong-star variant permits writing only at the same level.
        • With TS>S>C>U, an S subject can read C under the simple rule but cannot write C under star; compartments and discretionary restrictions may still deny access.
      • Strict Biba protects integrity by preventing read down and write up: untrusted lower-integrity input should not contaminate higher-integrity results.
        • Clark–Wilson protects integrity through certified well-formed transformations, integrity checks and separation of duties.
        • It is not a confidentiality model. “MAC” is an enforcement category and does not force every system to use Bell–LaPadula rather than another label policy.
      • References: SEC-N, SEC-MODELS

    • SEC11 Physical protection and resilient design

      • Protect equipment against theft, unauthorized connections, heat, humidity, water, electrical surges and fire.
        • A UPS supplies temporary conditioned power; it is normally protective, but faulty installation/battery failure can itself be hazardous.
        • A disconnected machine loses many network attack paths yet remains exposed to insiders, removable media, supply-chain attacks and physical access.
        • There is no universal “most secure computer” without a threat model.
      • Defense in depth layers independent controls.
        • Minimization removes unnecessary software and services; compartmentalization limits blast radius.
        • Fail securely means errors do not silently grant permission.
        • Uniform configurations simplify patching and prediction but create correlated failures; diversity may reduce common-mode compromise while raising administration cost.
        • Choose protection proportional to asset value and credible threats.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC12 Cryptographic vocabulary and security assumptions

      • Plaintext is the original message, ciphertext its encrypted representation, a key is input to an algorithm, encryption computes C=E_k(P), and decryption recovers P=D_k(C).
        • The five conventional symmetric ingredients are plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext and decryption algorithm.
        • Cryptanalysis seeks recovery or other breaks without the authorized secret; cryptology includes cryptography and cryptanalysis.
        • Steganography hides that a message exists; encryption hides its meaning.
      • Assume the algorithm is known and protect keys: secrecy of implementation is not the main security argument.
        • A b-bit key has 2^b possibilities; exhaustive search averages roughly half the space if keys are uniformly random.
        • Security depends on algorithm, key size, randomness, mode and implementation.
        • Symmetric cryptography is not inherently less secure than public-key cryptography, and speed ratios are not fixed constants.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC13 Substitution, shift and affine ciphers

      • Substitution replaces symbols; transposition changes their positions.
        • A monoalphabetic substitution preserves one mapping throughout the message and leaks frequency patterns despite a large nominal key space.
        • Classical ciphers are teaching devices, not modern data protection.
      • With A=0 through Z=25, Caesar encryption is C=(P+k) mod26 and decryption P=(C-k) mod26.
        • A shift of 3 maps A→D and HELLO→KHOOR.
        • Key25 moves back one: ATTACK→ZSSZBJ.
        • Ensure negative results wrap into 0–25.
        • A multiplicative cipher uses C=kP mod26 with gcd(k,26)=1; decryption uses k’s modular inverse.
        • Affine uses C=aP+b mod26 and requires gcd(a,26)=1.
        • The inverse-key relation, not simply the same numeric multiplication, recovers plaintext.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC14 Vigenère, Playfair and Hill

      • Vigenère repeats or otherwise supplies shifts K_i and computes C_i=(P_i+K_i) mod26.
        • The same plaintext letter may encrypt differently by position; repeated short keys still leak periodic structure.
        • An autokey scheme extends its initial key using message material.
      • Playfair uses a keyed 5×5 grid, commonly combining I/J, and encrypts letter pairs.
        • Specify duplicate-letter fillers and padding.
        • Same row moves right, same column moves down, and rectangle pairs take the other column in their original row; decryption reverses shifts.
      • Hill uses C=KP mod26 for letter vectors.
        • K needs an inverse modulo26, equivalently determinant coprime to26.
        • It is linear: enough independent known plaintext/ciphertext blocks reveal K=CP^-1 mod26.
        • The supplied claim of resistance to known-plaintext attacks is false; polygraphic substitution alone is not modern strength.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N, SEC-NKU

    • SEC15 Transposition and one-time pads

      • Rail-fence writes along a specified zigzag and reads rails; columnar transposition writes rows and reads columns in a specified order.
        • They preserve the symbols and their counts.
        • Since source examples use inconsistent conventions, always state rows, column order, padding and direction before computing.
        • Two-rail zigzag for ABCDEF writes ACE on the first rail and BDF on the second, producing ACEBDF.
      • A one-time pad XORs bits with an independent uniformly random secret key at least as long as the message and never reused.
        • Its perfect secrecy depends on every condition.
        • Reusing a pad leaks C1 XOR C2=P1 XOR P2.
        • A Vernam XOR construction is not automatically a one-time pad: a predictable/reused keystream loses that guarantee.
        • Key delivery and storage remain substantial costs.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC16 Symmetric keys, AES and distribution

      • Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret and efficiently protects bulk data.
        • Pairwise independent keys for n users require n(n-1)/2 shared keys; a trusted key distribution center changes that architecture.
        • A session key is temporary for a communication context; a master/key-encryption key protects subordinate keys.
        • Distribute keys physically, via an authenticated protected channel, or through a trusted third party.
        • An uncompromised old key can protect a new key, although this does not restore secrecy after the old key is stolen.
      • AES is a 128-bit block cipher with 128/192/256-bit keys and 10/12/14 rounds.
        • Its substitution/permutation design uses SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey; the final round omits MixColumns.
        • Block ciphers need a mode and correct nonce/IV handling; authenticated encryption also detects tampering.
        • A stream cipher combines data with a keystream.
        • Never reuse a nonce when the chosen construction requires uniqueness.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC17 DES and Feistel mechanics

      • DES has a 64-bit block, 56 effective key bits (eight other bits serve parity), and 16 Feistel rounds.
        • After initial permutation, each round computes L_i=R_(i-1), R_i=L_(i-1) XOR f(R_(i-1),K_i).
        • Its right-half expansion makes 48 bits, XOR mixes a 48-bit subkey, eight S-boxes each map six bits to four, and permutation rearranges the 32 output bits.
        • The outer S-box input bits select a row and the inner four select a column.
      • The nonlinear S-boxes resist simple linear descriptions.
        • Feistel inversion uses the same overall structure with reversed round keys; f need not itself be invertible.
        • Final swapping/permutation completes DES.
        • DES and triple DES are legacy algorithms, not choices for new protection.
        • Triple DES repeats DES operations but does not provide 168-bit effective security merely because three 56-bit keys are supplied.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC18 Public keys and hybrid protection

      • For confidentiality to B, encrypt with B’s authenticated public encryption key; B decrypts with B’s private key.
        • Do not encrypt to A’s public key if only B should read it, and never assume A possesses B’s private key.
        • For a signature, A signs with A’s private signing key and others verify with A’s public key.
        • These are distinct operations; not every public-key algorithm supports encryption.
      • Public keys ease distribution but require authentic bindings to identities.
        • Hybrid systems establish or encapsulate a symmetric secret with public-key mechanisms, then protect bulk data symmetrically.
        • Diffie–Hellman agrees on a secret but unauthenticated DH permits intermediary substitution.
        • With public p,g, A=g^a modp and B=g^b modp, both derive B^a=A^b=g^(ab) modp.
        • Authenticate the exchange and derive separate traffic keys.
      • For one-way public-key confidentiality the sender need not own a key pair; it needs the recipient’s authenticated public encryption key.
        • A sender key pair is needed when the protocol requires its signature or separate recipient role.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC19 RSA arithmetic and invalid source examples

      • For textbook RSA choose distinct primes p,q; n=pq and φ=(p-1)(q-1).
        • Choose 1<e<φ with gcd(e,φ)=1, then compute d=e^-1 modφ.
        • Public key is (n,e), private includes d. Encrypt 0≤m<n by c=m^e modn; decrypt by m=c^d modn.
        • Use modular repeated squaring for large exponents.
        • Real RSA requires appropriate standardized padding; raw arithmetic is not a secure deployment recipe.
      • With p=7,q=19, n=133 and φ=108, e=5 is the smallest admissible e>1, but 7 and other coprime choices also work.
        • For e=5, d=65 since 325≡1 mod108.
        • With p=3,q=13,e=3,m=5, 5^3 mod39=8 arithmetically, but gcd(3,24)=3, so e has no inverse and this is not a valid RSA key.
        • State the defect rather than endorsing a working encryption/decryption pair.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC20 Hashes, MACs and signatures

      • A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest.
        • It is deterministic and designed to resist preimages and collisions; collisions must exist, so hashes are not mathematically unique fingerprints.
        • An attacker can recompute an unkeyed hash of modified data, so a hash alone needs a trusted reference.
        • A keyed MAC provides integrity and shared-secret authentication; both holders can create it, limiting third-party non-repudiation.
      • A signature algorithm signs a message or its encoded digest with a private key and verifies with the public key.
        • It is not generically “encrypting with a private key,” especially for DSA/ECDSA.
        • Verification checks origin/integrity under key-identity and key-custody assumptions; it does not conceal content.
        • Password verification uses a salt and deliberately expensive password hash.
        • Historical MD5/SHA-1 examples do not justify their use for new collision-resistant signatures.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC21 Certificates, TLS and HTTPS

      • A certificate binds a public key to a named subject through an issuer signature.
        • Validate the chain to a trusted root, intended hostname, time validity and applicable key usage/revocation policy.
        • A genuine certificate is not proof that a business is honest.
      • TLS succeeds obsolete SSL and supplies an authenticated protected channel.
        • A handshake negotiates parameters, authenticates the server and sometimes the client, and establishes keys; record protection uses symmetric authenticated encryption.
        • Exact messages depend on TLS version: the old ChangeCipherSpec narrative is not a universal TLS1.3 sequence.
        • HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
        • It protects HTTP paths, headers and content on the channel, but does not hide all metadata such as IP endpoints and traffic timing, nor protect data after a compromised endpoint decrypts it.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC22 SSH, IPsec, email protection and SET

      • SSH protects remote login, commands and file transfer such as SFTP; it supports host keys and several client-authentication methods.
        • IPsec protects IP traffic at network layer.
        • AH provides integrity/origin authentication, not encryption; ESP can provide confidentiality and integrity; IKE negotiates security associations and keys.
        • Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates an inner IP packet inside an outer header.
        • A VPN is a logical private connection; its actual security depends on the chosen authenticated tunnel.
      • PGP/OpenPGP combines symmetric content protection with public-key key handling and signatures.
        • S/MIME uses certificates for signed and/or enveloped MIME content.
        • Signatures can be sent separately/clear-signed without confidentiality; enveloped data encrypts content and wraps content keys for recipients.
        • SET, Secure Electronic Transaction, was a Visa/Mastercard-led specification for protecting card transactions using certificates and signatures; it is distinct from a payment-processing system or ordinary HTTPS.
      • One signed-and-encrypted S/MIME construction first signs the MIME entity, packages its content and signature, then encrypts that signed entity with a fresh symmetric content key.
        • Protect a copy of that key for each recipient.
        • A recipient recovers the key, decrypts the signed entity and verifies its signature using the validated signer certificate/public key.
        • Signing is not generic private-key encryption.
        • S/MIME permits other nesting orders; specify the order and resulting coverage.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N, SEC-IBMSET, RFC8551

    • SEC23 Firewalls and protected boundaries

      • A firewall enforces traffic policy.
        • Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports.
        • Stateful inspection tracks permitted connection context; application proxies terminate and relay application exchanges and can inspect their content.
        • A circuit gateway relays connections, commonly SOCKS, without full application-content interpretation; textbooks associate it with session/transport functions.
        • Such a gateway need not encrypt and is not automatically a VPN.
      • Host firewalls protect individual machines; network firewalls segment networks and can create a DMZ for public-facing services.
        • Rules should be explicit, ordered as implemented, least-privilege and logged appropriately.
        • Stateful and next-generation devices also filter ports, so a stem asking merely which device “can filter ports” is nonexclusive.
        • Bypass paths, insiders, encrypted uninspected content and infected removable media limit firewall protection.
        • Hardware firewall does not imply any fixed number of ports.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC24 Detection, prevention and diagnostic measures

      • An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline.
        • Host-based sensors examine host events, network-based sensors inspect traffic.
        • Signature detection recognizes known patterns; anomaly detection compares with a baseline and may detect novel behavior.
        • Neither guarantees every attack is detected; anomaly detection can raise many false positives, and signatures can sometimes match variants.
      • A true positive is a real attack detected, false negative is a missed attack, false positive is innocent activity flagged, and true negative is innocent activity accepted.
        • Recall=TP/(TP+FN); precision=TP/(TP+FP).
        • Detecting 90 of 100 spam messages with five innocent messages flagged gives recall90%, precision90/95≈94.7%.
        • Obfuscation makes code harder to understand and can hamper analysis, but does not reliably protect embedded secrets or remove vulnerabilities.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC25 Memory safety and secure input handling

      • A buffer overflow writes beyond allocated bounds and can corrupt data or control information; code execution is a possible consequence, not its definition or an inevitable outcome.
        • An array of eight bytes cannot store eight text characters plus a terminating zero.
        • Bounds-check lengths and indexes, consider integer overflow, use safe abstractions and validate library return values.
        • Canaries, non-executable memory and address randomization reduce exploitability but do not repair the underlying write.
      • Validate expected type, length, range and structure at trust boundaries.
        • Server validation is essential because clients are controllable.
        • Encode output for its destination; validation is not a universal substitute for query parameterization or HTML-context encoding.
        • Security patches repair known weaknesses; a zero-day may lack a vendor fix, but segmentation and other mitigations can still help.
      • References: SEC-N, SEC-CWE787

    • SEC26 SQL injection, XSS and request forgery

      • SQL injection occurs when untrusted values alter SQL syntax through unsafe string construction.
        • A tautology can change which rows match.
        • Bind data values in prepared statements, allow-list identifiers that cannot be parameters, and restrict the application’s database account.
        • Stored procedures/ORMs are safe only when they avoid unsafe dynamic SQL.
      • XSS causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a victim’s browser under the site’s origin.
        • Stored content persists; reflected content returns in a response; DOM-based XSS can arise from unsafe browser sinks.
        • Use safe text insertion and context-specific encoding; carefully sanitize allowed HTML.
        • CSP is added protection, not the sole fix.
      • CSRF exploits ambient credentials to submit an unwanted authenticated action.
        • Use unpredictable request tokens and suitable cookie/origin controls.
        • HttpOnly restricts script access to cookies but does not stop every XSS effect.
        • Fuzzing sends unexpected inputs to discover faults; it is a testing technique, not itself a category of injection.
      • References: SEC-N, SEC-SQL, SEC-XSS

    • SEC27 Races, testing and secure development

      • A race occurs when correctness depends on timing/interleaving over shared state.
        • In a check-then-open file operation, another actor may replace the file between the check and use.
        • In a balance update, two workers can both read100 and each write90, losing one debit.
        • Protect the whole invariant with suitable atomic operations, locks or database transactions; locking an unrelated variable does not help.
      • Vulnerability assessment finds and prioritizes weaknesses; authorized penetration testing attempts to demonstrate consequences.
        • Static analysis inspects code, dynamic testing executes it, and fuzzing varies inputs.
        • Host/network/database scanners see different exposures and have false results.
        • Correct findings, patch, test and recheck; testing is not proof of absence.
        • Build threat modeling, review, least privilege, dependency management and safe error handling into development.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N, SEC-CWE362

    • SEC28 Trusted OS requirements and reference mediation

      • A trusted OS is relied on to enforce a stated security policy.
        • Relevant mechanisms include identification/authentication, process and memory isolation, controlled privileges, object access enforcement, protected auditing, safe resource reuse, trusted boot/update paths and recovery behavior.
        • The trusted computing base comprises components whose failure can violate policy; smaller, analyzable boundaries simplify assurance.
      • A reference monitor is an abstract access-checking mechanism: it must mediate every relevant access, resist tampering and be sufficiently small/simple to analyze.
        • A security kernel implements core enforcement.
        • A firewall can mediate its traversing traffic but cannot enforce every host-memory access.
        • Assurance is justified confidence that controls implement the claims; functionality is what controls claim to do.
        • A GUI or multitasking support alone does not establish trust.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N, SEC-NISTAC25

    • SEC29 Independent evaluation, certification and assurance

      • Under Common Criteria, define the Target of Evaluation (TOE), its configuration and environment.
        • A Security Target (ST) states threats, assumptions, objectives, functional requirements and assurance requirements; a Protection Profile describes reusable requirements for a product category.
        • Evaluators examine developer evidence, test and analyze vulnerabilities against those claims.
        • A certification body oversees/reviews the evaluation and issues the certification decision; sponsors commission work and developers supply product/evidence.
      • An Evaluation Assurance Level packages assurance requirements; EAL1–7 express increasing evaluation rigor, not a universal ranking of security functions.
        • A higher number does not make a product with different scope automatically safer.
        • CCRA is a mutual-recognition arrangement, not a single worldwide testing laboratory.
        • A certificate applies to a specified product/configuration and claims, not immunity to all future attacks.
      • References: SEC-CC1, SEC-CCFAQ

    • SEC30 Database secrecy, permissions and key boundaries

      • Database security needs confidentiality, integrity, availability and accountability together.
        • Authenticate connections, give roles only necessary table/column/row privileges, restrict views and audit sensitive changes.
        • A user allowed to read a report need not read the underlying full table.
        • Check application-level authorization as well as database rights.
      • Encryption at rest protects stolen storage/backups when keys remain separate; transport encryption protects the connection.
        • Neither prevents a fully authorized query or guarantees correctness.
        • Strong access controls, encryption and protected transmission can all contribute to secrecy, so a question asking which single technique achieves it may have several true answers.
        • Replication is useful for availability but also copies malicious updates unless separate recovery controls exist.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC31 Database integrity and reliability mechanisms

      • Integrity requires valid data and valid transitions.
        • NOT NULL rejects missing mandatory values; UNIQUE/primary keys prevent duplicate identifiers; foreign keys preserve references; CHECK enforces declared predicates.
        • Transactions group a transfer’s debit and credit atomically; concurrency control prevents unsafe interleavings.
        • Roles/ACLs limit who may update, but constraints and transaction logic determine whether an authorized update is valid.
      • Write-ahead logging persists recovery records before dependent data-file changes, supporting recovery after a crash.
        • Backups, restore tests and separately protected logs recover from deletion/corruption; replication provides alternate service capacity but does not replace backups.
        • Redundancy improves availability only with appropriate failover and independent failure handling.
        • Distinguish confidentiality controls from reliability controls and from integrity constraints.
      • References: SEC-N, SEC-PGC, SEC-PGW

    • SEC32 Inference control and multilevel databases

      • Inference reveals protected facts by combining individually permitted outputs with other knowledge.
        • If a report gives a two-person salary total and one salary is known, subtraction reveals the other.
        • Blocking direct SELECT of a salary column does not stop that inference.
        • Restrict small groups and overlapping queries, track query history, coarsen/suppress results, or introduce carefully designed noise; each trades utility against leakage.
      • A multilevel database stores items at different labels and enforces mandatory policy using subject clearances, classifications and compartments.
        • Bell–LaPadula-style read/write restrictions prevent direct downward confidentiality flow; trusted declassification is a separate controlled action.
        • Views alone are not proof of multilevel isolation.
        • Covert channels, query results and error messages may still reveal information, so evaluate both direct access and indirect inference.
      • References: SEC-N, SEC-INF

    • SEC33 Policy, incident response and recovery objectives

      • A security policy states responsibilities and rules; a procedure supplies the steps.
        • Policies coordinate protection, reduce risk and define acceptable use, access review, incident handling and recovery.
        • They do not prescribe merely “passive system use.” Awareness training teaches reporting and independent verification; enforcement and usable procedures make it operational.
      • Prepare response roles/tools, detect and analyze, contain the incident, eradicate the cause, restore verified service and learn from the evidence.
        • Preserve useful protected logs.
        • Disaster recovery restores IT after disruption; business continuity sustains business functions through workarounds and alternate facilities.
        • RTO is a recovery-time target; RPO measures the tolerable age of lost data.
        • A backup schedule must satisfy the required recovery point, and a restore test must demonstrate that data can actually be recovered.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

    • SEC34 Interpret flawed security questions precisely

      • Do not select an invented unique answer when choices overlap or lack the mechanism.
        • The asymmetric-message question has several wrong key directions; signatures do not generically encrypt whole messages with private keys.
        • Body biometrics do not imply three factors.
        • SSL and SSH can both describe protected channels unless the stem specifies remote shell.
        • A malformed option label cannot be recovered from theory.
      • Undefined “arbitrary code execution” does not uniquely identify buffer overflow: several mechanisms can produce that consequence.
        • A database-security requirement can include both availability and confidentiality.
        • Generic ACLs and RBAC both restrict unauthorized writes but neither independently enforces all integrity constraints.
        • Evaluation organizations must be identified by the actual national scheme; CCRA is recognition, not an evaluator.
        • An answer is supported only after the missing distinction is supplied.
      • References: SEC-M, SEC-N

  • Network and System Administration

    • Administration keeps services useful, available and controlled through configuration, monitoring, troubleshooting and repeatable automation.
      • Diagnose from evidence: a failed connection, expired lease or large organization alone does not identify one cause or one best storage design.
    • Practice service provisioning as a chain: link, address, route, DNS, transport connection, authentication and application.
      • Match each tool to the evidence it can actually provide.
    • Compare account/permission models, RAID layouts, backup types and security controls using stated requirements rather than unconditional best choices.
    • Read and trace small Python 3 or shell scripts.
      • Identify inputs, branching, repeated work, failures and outputs; then construct a reusable check or backup task.
    • Sections in this course
      Roles, principles and change disciplineNetwork foundations for administratorsAddress, prefix, gateway and loopbackDHCP exchange and lease lifecycleDHCP deployment, fallback and diagnosisDNS forward/reverse resolution and evidenceChoose the command that exposes the required stateA repeatable troubleshooting procedureConnectivity diagnosis by layersService catalog and remote accessRouting, NAT and port translationProxies, gateways and quality of serviceWorkgroups, domains and directory servicesLDAP operations and secure directory accessAD logical structure and delegationAD sites, replication and trustsAccounts, rights and password diagnosisWindows permissions and effective accessUnix rwx and octal permissionsLinux paths, filesystems and checksProfiles, registry and persistent configurationPerformance monitoring and bottleneck decisionsMonitoring, capture and assessment toolsBackups, restore and continuityRAID layouts, capacity and selectionSecurity policy development and purposeHardening, controls and vulnerabilitiesEncryption, hashes and script secretsIncidents, evidence and reportsSegmentation, NAC and remote administrationScripting: inputs, control flow and reusable workLaunching commands with Python subprocessFile input, configuration parsing and updatesArguments and targeted error handlingRegex log analysis and rotationCollecting CPU and memory measurementsScheduling a backup and checking restorationConstruct a bounded backup script

    • NSA01 Roles, principles and change discipline

      • System administrators maintain hosts, accounts, storage, software and availability; network administrators maintain connectivity, addressing, routes, network devices and performance.
        • Security administrators coordinate controls and policy.
        • These duties overlap, so account management, testing patches and training users are not exclusive to one job title.
        • Patience, communication, ethics, technical understanding and organization matter alongside command knowledge.
      • Use documentation, standardization, least privilege, automation and measured change.
        • Record the current state, intended change, rollback and validation.
        • Schedule maintenance according to service impact and urgency, not merely because a calendar date arrived.
        • Fault management restores failures; performance management measures service behavior; configuration management tracks settings; security management controls access; accounting tracks usage.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA02 Network foundations for administrators

      • Clients request services; servers provide them.
        • Peer-to-peer systems can do both.
        • A server can also be a client of DNS or backups, so dedicated role does not mean it never makes requests.
        • A network OS is not universally installed only on a dedicated server: clients also require networking support.
        • Specify centralized service software versus the OS on all participants.
      • Switching normally forwards frames using MAC addresses within a LAN; routing forwards IP packets between networks.
        • TCP supplies an ordered reliable byte stream, while UDP preserves datagrams without that guarantee.
        • Ports distinguish application endpoints, not physical connectors.
        • Draw switches, links, subnets, gateways, service hosts and dependencies in a network diagram.
        • A topology’s shape alone does not guarantee security.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-N

    • NSA03 Address, prefix, gateway and loopback

      • An IPv4 address is 32 bits; a CIDR prefix determines its network.
        • Compute network=address AND mask; devices use a route/gateway for remote subnets.
        • Private ranges are 10/8,172.16/12 and 192.168/16; private addresses are not directly Internet-routable.
        • Neither IP alone nor a class label determines today’s subnet.
      • 127.0.0.1 conventionally names the local IPv4 loopback interface; 127/8 is reserved for loopback.
        • Loopback tests local protocol processing, not cable, switch or remote reachability.
        • Programs can use it for local services.
        • Thus several loopback descriptions or several 127/8 addresses may be valid, even when the bank expects one.
      • Worked microexample
        • 192.168.2.70/26 has 64-address blocks: network .64, broadcast .127, ordinary host range .65–.126. A gateway must be reachable through an appropriate route; NAT does not repair a missing route.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-N, NSA-LOOP

    • NSA04 DHCP exchange and lease lifecycle

      • DHCP supplies addresses and configuration options.
        • Typical initial IPv4 allocation is Discover→Offer→Request→ACK.
        • The server manages its scope/pool, allocated leases, exclusions and reservations; options may include mask, gateway and DNS servers.
        • A dynamic lease lasts for a specified interval, not forever.
      • A client renews before expiry; it later tries rebinding if renewal fails.
        • A disconnected host does not automatically renew forever.
        • On lease expiry the address becomes eligible for reuse, subject to server policy.
        • Reconnection normally triggers validation/renewal/new allocation, so an expired lease alone does not prove persistent failure.
        • A reservation gives a predictable address to a known client while retaining DHCP configuration.
      • Worked microexample
        • If a disconnected client’s lease expires while other clients obtain addresses, its old address may be reassigned. It must not simply resume using it without validating its configuration.
      • References: NSA-DHCP

    • NSA05 DHCP deployment, fallback and diagnosis

      • Use a scope matching the subnet, exclude manually assigned server/router addresses, set correct options and provide a relay when client broadcasts must cross a router.
        • Static assignments and DHCP can coexist; avoid address conflicts.
        • DHCP lowers repetitive administration but availability/security depend on deployment and protection from rogue replies.
        • It does not guarantee connectivity whenever a device changes location.
      • For a returning client, inspect current lease/address, reachable server/relay, free pool capacity and logs.
        • New devices can exhaust a pool, but absent observations this is only a hypothesis.
        • Some clients self-configure IPv4 link-local addresses such as 169.254.2.33 after DHCP failure; these support same-link communication, not ordinary routed Internet access. 0.0.0.0 is unspecified and 255.255.255.255 is limited broadcast.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-LL, NSA-DHCP

    • NSA06 DNS forward/reverse resolution and evidence

      • Forward resolution obtains an address from a name, using A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6.
        • Reverse lookup uses a PTR record in the reverse namespace to obtain a name from an address.
        • CNAME aliases a name, MX identifies mail exchangers and NS identifies authoritative name servers.
        • Forward and reverse records need not both exist or be perfect inverses.
      • Resolvers cache answers for their TTL.
        • Query nslookup name or specify the DNS server explicitly; compare the configured resolver with the authoritative answer when appropriate.
        • A successful ping by address but failed name lookup suggests naming/configuration trouble.
        • Ping by name may display a resolved address, but nslookup is the direct DNS diagnostic. “Resolving” is a general term that includes forward resolution.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-N, NSA-DNS, NSA-NSLOOKUP

    • NSA07 Choose the command that exposes the required state

      • Windows ipconfig shows addresses, mask and gateway; ipconfig /all adds complete adapter configuration including physical/MAC address, DHCP and DNS information. /renew requests renewal, /release releases a dynamic address and /flushdns clears the client DNS cache.
        • Linux ip addr and ip route show interface addresses and routes; exact persistent configuration varies by distribution.
      • netstat displays connections/endpoints/protocols and TCP states; netstat -ano displays numeric addresses/ports and PIDs.
        • The bank’s literal netstart is not netstat and cannot be silently accepted. ping probes IP reachability; traceroute/tracert reveals responding hops using TTL/hop-limit expiry.
        • ICMP filtering can prevent replies without proving the service is down. nslookup inspects DNS.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-IPCONFIG, NSA-NETSTAT, NSA-NSLOOKUP

    • NSA08 A repeatable troubleshooting procedure

      • Define the symptom, scope, time and recent changes; gather the configuration, baseline and logs.
        • Form a testable hypothesis, test the least disruptive explanation, isolate the failing component, apply a targeted fix, verify the user service and document the result.
        • Change one relevant factor at a time when possible.
        • A reboot can hide evidence and is not a diagnosis by itself.
      • Use bottom-up checks from physical link, top-down checks from application errors, or divide-and-conquer by testing a middle layer.
        • Divide-and-conquer narrows the working/failing boundary; it is not random trial-and-error.
        • Rebooting, updates, resetting settings and scanning can all be troubleshooting actions in suitable circumstances; a question without fault evidence cannot rank them uniquely.
      • Worked microexample
        • One client fails while others work: inspect that client’s link, address and policy first. All clients fail name lookup but reach server IPs: inspect shared DNS/its configuration before replacing every cable.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA09 Connectivity diagnosis by layers

      • Check power, cable/connector and link state, then NIC/driver state, VLAN membership, address/prefix, local gateway, route, DNS and finally application port/authentication.
        • A recognized NIC makes a missing driver less likely, not proof of a working physical link.
        • Ethernet commonly uses RJ45 connectors; an RJ11 telephone jack is not the expected Ethernet connection.
      • If same-subnet traffic works but remote traffic fails, compare gateway/routes and filtering.
        • If ping fails but the application connection works, ICMP filtering is plausible.
        • If an application port is refused, the destination is reachable enough to reject it; inspect service/listener policy.
        • A timeout can result from loss, filtering or a down host and needs more evidence.
      • Worked microexample
        • After NIC replacement, recognized/enabled adapter but no link light: try a known-good Ethernet cable and switch port. Merely knowing that the OS recognizes the NIC cannot prove one particular cable is defective.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA10 Service catalog and remote access

      • DNS resolves names; DHCP supplies host configuration.
        • SMTP sends/relays mail, while IMAP/POP retrieve it.
        • FTP is a named file-transfer protocol; HTTP also transfers files, so “transfers files” is not an exclusive FTP description.
        • HTTP/HTTPS serve web resources.
        • SSH provides encrypted remote login; SFTP transfers files over SSH and differs from FTP or FTPS.
      • A VPN extends private connectivity over another network; secure tunneling commonly encrypts/authenticates traffic but depends on protocol/configuration.
        • RTP carries real-time media timing/sequence information, often over UDP; it does not guarantee timely delivery.
        • Network printers expose services shared by clients.
        • Provide accounts, permissions, configuration, monitoring and recovery for each service, not just its protocol name.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-N

    • NSA11 Routing, NAT and port translation

      • Routing selects a next hop using a destination prefix; NAT rewrites addresses.
        • Many-to-one address-and-port translation (PAT/NAPT) maps internal flows to one public address using distinct port bindings.
        • For example, two private client sockets can appear as public-address ports 40001 and 40002, with replies translated back to the correct clients.
      • NAT is often used when private IPv4 clients access public networks; it does not itself replace a gateway, route, firewall or authentication.
        • One-to-one NAT and destination translation are other forms, so NAT does not always mean many hosts share one address.
        • Public addressing inside a LAN does not automatically require NAT.
        • Unsolicited inbound service access may require explicit mapping and filtering.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA12 Proxies, gateways and quality of service

      • A proxy acts on behalf of a client or backend service and can cache, filter or mediate application requests.
        • A default IP gateway is a next-hop router; an application gateway may translate protocols.
        • It need not be a modem/router combination.
        • These terms describe functions that can coexist on one machine.
      • QoS classifies, queues and prioritizes traffic to meet performance objectives such as low delay or limited loss.
        • It can operate across layers and support applications, so it is not exclusively an application-layer service.
        • Installing a new service is an administrative action; email configuration is another action and proxies/agents are components.
        • A question mixing these labels needs a specified service-management taxonomy before a unique exclusion can be chosen.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-N

    • NSA13 Workgroups, domains and directory services

      • A workgroup has locally managed accounts on individual machines; sharing may require local credentials and per-host configuration.
        • A domain centralizes identities and policies through directory infrastructure.
        • These are administrative arrangements, not physical topologies.
        • Avoid treating an old recommended workgroup size as a hard protocol limit.
        • HomeGroup is a historical Windows sharing feature, not another name for an AD domain.
      • A domain controller runs AD DS, authenticates domain accounts and participates in directory replication.
        • Redundant controllers improve service continuity only if dependencies and failure domains are considered; two virtual controllers on one failed physical host are not independent availability.
        • Provisioning requires correct addressing, DNS, time and supported OS/hardware; version-specific minimum sizes are not universal architecture rules.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA14 LDAP operations and secure directory access

      • LDAP accesses directory entries/attributes identified by distinguished names.
        • Bind authenticates a session; search retrieves matching entries; compare tests an attribute value; add/delete/modify change entries; modify-DN renames or moves; unbind ends the session.
        • StartTLS upgrades a connection to TLS where supported; LDAPS uses TLS from connection setup.
        • Protect credentials and verify server identity.
      • LDAP commonly uses TCP 389 and LDAPS TCP 636; an acronym/port alone does not make authentication secure.
        • AD also uses DNS and Kerberos; LDAP is not identical to the entire directory product.
        • The module’s broad assertion that LDAPS is simply retired with LDAPv2 should not be used as a rule for modern TLS-protected LDAP.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-LDAPS

    • NSA15 AD logical structure and delegation

      • A directory object represents a user, computer, group or resource and has schema-defined attributes.
        • Security principals have SIDs; display names are not the sole security identity.
        • A domain groups directory objects and a replicated domain database.
        • A tree groups domains in a contiguous DNS namespace; a forest groups trees with a shared schema/configuration and global-catalog framework.
      • OUs organize objects and provide convenient scopes for delegated administration and Group Policy; they are not separate forests/security boundaries.
        • Use groups to assign access and OUs to structure policy/delegation.
        • Schema changes require care because they propagate broadly; ordinary directory objects can be deleted, unlike the special restrictions on schema definitions.
        • Do not copy the module’s schema restrictions onto every kind of object.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA16 AD sites, replication and trusts

      • Sites group IP subnets to model network locality, influence controller selection and manage replication traffic.
        • They are distinct from domains/OUs.
        • AD replicates directory changes among controllers; notification can trigger pulls within a site while schedules/link costs influence traffic between sites.
        • Replication is not an independent backup of previous good states.
      • If domain A trusts B, B’s identities can be authenticated for resources in A, subject to permissions.
        • Trust alone grants no automatic file access.
        • Direction (one/two way) and transitivity (extends/does not extend) are independent.
        • An explicit trust is not necessarily one-way or nontransitive; the trust type/configuration determines that.
        • State the direction in words before drawing arrows.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-TRUST

    • NSA17 Accounts, rights and password diagnosis

      • Create named accounts, assign only needed groups/rights, disable departed users and audit privileged activity.
        • Authentication verifies the account; authorization permits operations.
        • A user right such as remote logon differs from a permission on one file.
        • Group-based administration is easier to review than many hidden individual grants.
      • If only one domain user cannot change a password, inspect that account’s cannot-change-password setting and relevant policy/permission before blaming all directory infrastructure.
        • Other possibilities include minimum password age, password rules or account state; the setting is a plausible exam cause, not a conclusion from failure alone.
        • Membership in Administrators does not inherently prohibit changing one’s password.
        • Privileged reset and user-initiated password change are different operations.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA18 Windows permissions and effective access

      • Windows file/folder permissions include read, write, read/execute, modify and full control, plus more granular rights such as delete.
        • Inherited and explicit entries, group membership, deny entries and object scope affect effective access; use the effective-access view for a real account rather than adding labels informally.
        • Network access can be constrained by both share and filesystem permissions.
      • Deleting can be an explicit permission; therefore an OS-unspecified question claiming Delete is not a permission is false in Windows.
        • Modify and full control are not identical: full control includes changing permission/ownership capabilities.
        • Separate data access from logon rights.
        • A user allowed to read a file is not necessarily allowed to write it or administer its parent folder.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA19 Unix rwx and octal permissions

      • The nine ordinary permission bits are owner, group and other triplets.
        • In each triplet read=4,write=2,execute=1; sum enabled bits to get an octal digit.
        • A leading ls -l character denotes file type, not another permission bit.
        • For directories, read lists names, execute permits traversal/search, and write changes entries subject to other checks.
        • File deletion usually depends on parent directory permissions, with sticky-bit/ACL rules also possible.
      • Worked microexample
        • -rwxr--r-- means ordinary file, owner7/group4/other4, hence 744. 755 means rwxr-xr-x. The bank string -rwxr-r— is damaged; missing hyphens cannot be guessed. Confirm the full nine-bit string before selecting 744 or another value.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-MODE

    • NSA20 Linux paths, filesystems and checks

      • / is the filesystem root; /root is the administrative user’s home. /etc stores configuration, /home ordinary user homes, /var variable data/logs, /dev device nodes, /proc kernel/process information, /boot boot material and /tmp temporary files.
        • Cleanup/mount layouts vary; do not assume every partition has lost+found or every reboot erases every temporary directory.
      • ext2 is a Linux filesystem; ext4 is a later filesystem; HPFS is historically associated with OS/2, while swap is backing space rather than an ordinary user-file filesystem. fsck checks and optionally repairs filesystems through filesystem-specific tools; it is not init, halt or an inittab file.
        • Repairs require the filesystem’s supported offline/safe procedure.
        • Mount attaches a filesystem to a directory; partitioning, mounting, quotas and capacity belong to storage administration.
      • Linux can access some foreign-origin filesystems, including HPFS when its driver is available.
        • Filesystem origin and Linux driver support are different questions.
        • Swap is a paging area rather than an ordinary user-file filesystem.
        • In Q00635, ext2 is the intended native Linux-filesystem example only if that scope is stated; the broad used-for-Linux wording does not establish a unique ext2-versus-HPFS answer.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-FSCK, LINUX-HPFS

    • NSA21 Profiles, registry and persistent configuration

      • A local profile keeps settings on one client; a roaming profile synchronizes supported user settings/data through a server at logon/logoff.
        • Large profiles can slow these operations; redirected folders avoid repeatedly copying selected folders.
        • A central profile is backed up only if the server’s backup policy actually includes it.
        • A cached profile is not a newly created independent local security account.
      • The Windows registry is a hierarchical configuration database with keys, subkeys and typed values.
        • HKLM describes machine settings and HKCU the current user view.
        • ACLs protect registry access.
        • Not all historical root handles apply to current versions.
        • Record/export the relevant configuration before an authorized change, and verify the intended service behavior afterward.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA22 Performance monitoring and bottleneck decisions

      • Measure a baseline, sample over an interval, compare with workload and correlate symptoms before changing hardware.
        • CPU utilization/run queues identify processing pressure; low free memory alone is weak evidence because cache may be reclaimable.
        • Persistent paging with high latency indicates memory pressure.
        • Storage capacity and I/O latency are separate: a disk can be nearly empty but saturated, or nearly full while lightly loaded.
      • Measure interface bytes/second, errors, drops, packet delay/loss and utilization against link rate.
        • Distinguish capacity (maximum available rate) from observed throughput.
        • Logs can reveal both security incidents and performance faults.
        • Performance counters expose measured events; system calls/APIs or log parsers are ways scripts collect them, so those options are not mutually exclusive methods.
      • Worked microexample
        • Transferring 80 MB in 10 s gives 8 MB/s≈64 Mb/s before overhead. A 95%-busy CPU with a growing runnable queue suggests CPU pressure; a 95%-full disk requires capacity action even if its latency is low.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA23 Monitoring, capture and assessment tools

      • Task Manager shows running processes/resource use; Resource Monitor/Performance Monitor give more detailed counters.
        • Wireshark captures and dissects packets.
        • Nmap discovers hosts/ports/services.
        • Nessus assesses vulnerabilities/configuration.
        • Snort can detect suspicious traffic and alert, and can prevent traffic in suitable inline deployments; it also has sniffing/logging roles.
        • Thus packet-capture capability is not exclusive to one product, although Wireshark is the conventional analyzer choice.
      • An IDS detects/alerts; an IPS can block inline.
        • Scanning identifies potential weaknesses rather than proving successful exploitation.
        • A captured packet, open port or alert needs context.
        • Monitoring network usage is not the same as configuring access control or encrypting communications.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-WIRE, NSA-NMAP, NSA-SNORT, NSA-NESSUS

    • NSA24 Backups, restore and continuity

      • Backups recover previous data after deletion, compromise, corruption, failed upgrades/migrations or hardware loss.
        • Authorization controls current access, a different function.
        • A mirror/replica also copies deletions or corruption and does not replace versioned independent backups.
        • Keep protected copies in separate failure domains, define retention and test restores.
      • A full backup copies the chosen dataset; incremental copies changes since the last backup; differential copies changes since the last full backup.
        • Restoring incrementals generally needs the full plus each subsequent incremental, whereas differential needs the full plus latest differential.
        • RPO is tolerable lost-data time and RTO tolerable restoration time.
        • Compression reduces storage, scheduling runs the operation and restore testing establishes whether recovery actually works.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA25 RAID layouts, capacity and selection

      • RAID0 stripes for capacity/throughput with no disk-failure tolerance.
        • RAID1 mirrors; a two-disk mirror has one disk’s usable capacity and survives one disk failure.
        • RAID2 uses bit striping/Hamming-code redundancy, RAID3 byte striping with dedicated parity, RAID4 block striping with dedicated parity and RAID5 block striping with distributed parity.
        • RAID6 distributes dual parity and tolerates two disk failures.
        • RAID10 stripes mirrored pairs; survival depends on which disks fail.
      • With N equal disks of capacity D, RAID0 usable=ND, paired RAID1/10≈ND/2, RAID5=(N−1)D and RAID6=(N−2)D. Hardware RAID may offload work to controller resources/cache but does not universally outperform software RAID.
        • Rebuilds consume bandwidth; parity writes have overhead.
        • A large university/bank alone does not select a level.
        • Striping plus parity is not uniquely RAID5 unless distributed block parity is specified.
      • Worked microexample
        • Four 2 TB disks give 8 TB RAID0, 4 TB RAID10, 6 TB RAID5 or4 TB RAID6, ignoring metadata. Choose using failure tolerance, workload, capacity and recovery requirements; none of these layouts replaces backups.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-RAID

    • NSA26 Security policy development and purpose

      • A security policy states required behavior, scope, accountable roles and enforcement.
        • Begin with assets/service objectives, assess threats and weaknesses, choose controls, define exceptions/incident procedures, approve/communicate, monitor and periodically review.
        • CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability; neither sensitive-data protection nor availability alone is the universal primary goal.
      • A policy can require password controls, approved encryption, restricted administrative access, backups and patch deadlines; firewall rules implement part of it.
        • Open unrestricted wireless access conflicts with controlled internal access unless intentionally isolated as a guest service. “Use the system passively” is not a purpose of security policy.
        • Policies coordinate action and reduce risk; they do not guarantee every attack will fail.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-G

    • NSA27 Hardening, controls and vulnerabilities

      • Hardening reduces exposure through unnecessary-service removal, supported patches, restricted accounts/permissions and appropriate port filtering.
