        • Blocking an unused known port can be hardening; blocking every useful port merely destroys availability.
        • Weak passwords and unpatched exploitable software are vulnerabilities; attacks exploit weaknesses, and risk combines likelihood with impact.
      • Preventive controls restrict harmful actions, detective controls expose them and recovery controls restore service.
        • Account lifecycle, backup procedures, device configuration and traffic analysis can all be security controls under a stated objective.
        • A vulnerability scan checks known weakness patterns, not bandwidth.
        • Test/stage patches, prepare rollback, deploy and verify; testing and installation are both legitimate administrator duties.
      • References: NSA-M

    • NSA28 Encryption, hashes and script secrets

      • Encryption provides confidentiality with correct key/nonce use; authenticated encryption adds integrity/authenticity.
        • Unspecified encryption alone does not guarantee both properties.
        • A password hash supports verification without recovering the original password; it is not a reversible credential store.
        • Encryption can protect a recoverable credential only if its key is separately protected.
      • Keep reusable secrets out of source code and routine logs; obtain them from an appropriately protected credential service or restricted runtime source.
        • Environment variables and configuration files are transport/storage choices, not automatic encryption.
        • A script that must authenticate to another service often needs the actual credential/token, so replacing it with a one-way hash will not work.
        • State whether the question is about password verification or recoverable service credentials.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-AEAD

    • NSA29 Incidents, evidence and reports

      • Incident response prepares, detects/analyzes, contains, removes the cause, restores service and learns from the event.
        • Investigation is reactive response; routine patching and backup are normally preventive/preparatory operations.
        • Document timestamps, affected systems, evidence, impact, actions, responsible people and recovery results.
        • An incident report may record policy violations, but its scope is broader than that alone.
      • DoS harms service availability; DDoS uses distributed sources.
        • Phishing deceives users, brute force tries credentials and an interception attack reads/alters communications.
        • Correlate logs using time and identity/context.
        • Preserve relevant evidence before resetting systems.
        • A suspicious event is not automatically confirmed compromise; record facts and uncertainty.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-G

    • NSA30 Segmentation, NAC and remote administration

      • Segmentation separates groups of systems and enforces allowed flows with routing/filtering policies; VLAN membership alone does not establish complete security.
        • NAC assesses device/user admission and can reject or quarantine unauthorized/noncompliant devices.
        • Authentication proves an identity, while access rules decide which resources it may use.
      • Use authenticated protected remote administration such as SSH or properly secured management services, with restricted source access and auditing.
        • VPNs provide protected connectivity under their defined security model; they are not packet analyzers.
        • Firewall filtering permits/blocks traffic according to policy; it is not inherently encryption.
        • Losing remote connectivity while changing a management route/firewall is an operational risk to plan for.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-NAC

    • NSA31 Scripting: inputs, control flow and reusable work

      • Scripts automate repeatable administration; they are not inherently faster than compiled programs or automatically secure.
        • Python, shells and PowerShell are common choices; HTML is markup.
        • Define inputs and outputs, use variables for state, if/elif/else for decisions, loops for repeated work and functions for reusable operations.
        • Python indentation defines blocks; == compares while = assigns.
      • Make reruns predictable: compute the desired state, compare with current state and change only what differs.
        • Validate a small dry run before mutation.
        • Avoid requiring privilege for read-only reporting.
        • A good script reports failures and has a meaningful exit status rather than printing success unconditionally.
      • Worked microexample
        • def warn_percent(values, limit): for name, percent in values: if percent >= limit: print(name, "high", percent) warn_percent([("root", 92), ("data", 40)], 90) # Output: root high 92 (with spaces from print). Only the first pair meets the threshold.
      • References: NSA-FLOW

    • NSA32 Launching commands with Python subprocess

      • Python subprocess is a module, not a universal shell command. run launches a child program and returns its result; capture_output collects stdout/stderr, text=True decodes text, timeout bounds waiting and check=True raises for nonzero exit.
        • Pass an argument list to avoid accidental shell interpretation; quote handling differs from composing a shell string.
      • Echo prints, grep searches text and ipconfig/ifconfig reports/configures networking; none is the general Python child-process abstraction.
        • Explain the language before choosing subprocess in a generic “which command” question.
      • Worked microexample
        • import subprocess result = subprocess.run(["ip", "addr", "show"], text=True, capture_output=True, check=True, timeout=5) print(result.stdout) # Linux with iproute2 installed. Missing program raises OSError; # nonzero status raises CalledProcessError; timeout raises TimeoutExpired.
      • References: NSA-PROC

    • NSA33 File input, configuration parsing and updates

      • File I/O obtains/persists configuration; string operations parse values; regex can recognize patterns.
        • All can help manipulate configuration, so a broad “useful concept” question may have several answers.
        • Use the format’s parser for structured JSON/INI rather than blindly replacing every matching substring.
        • Open text with an explicit encoding and use with so files close even when processing fails.
      • For changes, validate the desired output, preserve a known-good copy, write to a temporary file in the same filesystem, then atomically replace the target where supported.
        • Check permissions and configuration syntax, reload the affected service, verify and retain a rollback.
        • Merely appending the same setting on every run is not idempotent.
      • Worked microexample
        • import json with open("settings.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle: config = json.load(handle) port = config["port"] if not isinstance(port, int) or not 1 <= port <= 65535: raise ValueError("port must be 1..65535") print("validated port", port) # This example validates/reports and does not alter a system file.
      • References: NSA-IO

    • NSA34 Arguments and targeted error handling

      • Command-line parsing converts user inputs into named, typed values and displays usage.
        • In Python argparse, positional arguments supply required inputs and flags enable options.
        • Validate ranges and paths before work; do not let unchecked input become executable shell text.
      • Worked microexample
        • import argparse from pathlib import Path p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("logfile", type=Path) p.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10) a = p.parse_args() if a.limit <1: p.error("limit must be positive") try: print(a.logfile.read_text(encoding="utf-8")[:a.limit]) except (OSError, UnicodeError) as exc: p.exit(1, f"read failed: {exc}\n") # Input limit controls characters here. Exceptions skip the rest of try; # catching specific failures makes unexpected programming errors visible.
      • References: NSA-ARGS, NSA-ERR

    • NSA35 Regex log analysis and rotation

      • Regex recognizes textual patterns; it does not encrypt, compress or rotate logs. search finds a match anywhere, while fullmatch requires the entire string to fit.
        • Use raw Python strings for backslash-heavy patterns, capture only the needed fields and treat unmatched/malformed lines explicitly.
        • Log rotation bounds file size and preserves historical segments; it is complementary to parsing.
      • Count the event actually requested, use timestamps/hosts to correlate, and separate absence of matches from failure to read the log.
        • Logs support security and performance analysis, so neither purpose is universally exclusive.
      • Worked microexample
        • import re pattern = re.compile(r"status=(\d{3})\b") counts = {} for line in ["status=200 ok", "status=503 unavailable", "noise"]: match = pattern.search(line) if match: code = match.group(1) counts[code] = counts.get(code,0)+1 print(counts) # {"200":1,"503":1}; noise is deliberately ignored.
      • References: NSA-RE

    • NSA36 Collecting CPU and memory measurements

      • A cumulative CPU counter must be sampled twice to calculate interval use; a single lifetime total is not current utilization.
        • On Linux /proc/stat exposes cumulative CPU categories; define which categories count as idle and avoid double-counting guest fields.
        • A simple convention is busy fraction=1−Δidle/Δtotal using idle+iowait as the chosen nonbusy categories.
        • Iowait interpretation has limitations.
      • /proc/meminfo exposes MemAvailable, an estimate of memory available without swapping; MemFree alone excludes reclaimable memory.
        • Windows Performance Counters and OS APIs expose analogous measurements through different interfaces.
        • System calls, counters and log parsing can all contribute; selecting one as the only monitoring technique is unjustified without a platform/API.
      • Worked microexample
        • If total CPU counters grow by 1000 ticks and chosen idle counters by 250, measured busy≈75%. If MemTotal=8192 MiB and MemAvailable=2048 MiB, approximate unavailable/used fraction is75%, not a prediction that an allocation of exactly 2048 MiB must succeed.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-CPU, NSA-MEM

    • NSA37 Scheduling a backup and checking restoration

      • Schedule recurring work using cron/systemd timers on suitable Unix systems or Task Scheduler on Windows.
        • A user crontab uses minute,hour,day-of-month,month,day-of-week then command.
        • Use absolute paths, known environment, protected inputs, logs, bounded runtime and a lock when overlap is unsafe.
        • Do not assume an interactive PATH, current directory or stored credentials exist in a scheduled job.
      • Compression packages data; scheduling chooses when the operation runs.
        • Test exit status and the archive contents, then restore a sample into an isolated destination.
        • A successful command alone does not prove a usable backup.
        • Version control of scripts helps review but does not replace data backup.
      • Worked microexample
        • One user-crontab entry (keep the command on one line): 0 2 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /opt/backup.py /srv /bak >>/var/log/bak.log 2>&1 This runs daily at 02:00 in the scheduler’s timezone as the crontab owner. The script takes its configured source and destination arguments. Paths, permissions, logging and the backup program must already be configured. Standard user crontabs omit a username field; system crontabs may include one.
      • References: NSA-M, NSA-CRON

    • NSA38 Construct a bounded backup script

      • Separate argument parsing, preconditions, copying/archive creation and result reporting.
        • Require a source directory, avoid putting the backup inside that source, create unique output names and ensure a failed partial file is not mistaken for a completed backup.
        • Real backup policies also need application consistency, capacity checks, retention and independent protected copies.
        • The following teaching script packages a directory; it does not silently install a scheduled job.
      • Worked microexample
        • import argparse, shutil from pathlib import Path from datetime import datetime, timezone p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("source", type=Path) p.add_argument("destination", type=Path) a = p.parse_args() src, dst = a.source.resolve(), a.destination.resolve() if not src.is_dir() or not dst.is_dir(): p.error("source and destination must be existing directories") if dst == src or src in dst.parents: p.error("destination must be outside source") name = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("copy-%Y%m%dT%H%M%S%fZ") base = dst /name try: archive = shutil.make_archive(str(base), "gztar", root_dir=src) except OSError as exc: base.with_suffix(".tar.gz").unlink(missing_ok=True) p.exit(1, f"backup failed: {exc}\n") print(archive) # Run against a teaching directory, verify archive members, then restore # into a different empty directory and compare selected files.
      • References: NSA-FLOW, NSA-IO, NSA-ERR, NSA-SHUTIL

  • Automata and Complexity Theory

    • Connect a language to a grammar and recognizer, prove limits of weaker models, and distinguish computability from resource complexity.
      • Explicit alphabets, epsilon conventions, decision formulations and reduction directions resolve the banks’ most common traps.
    • Design a DFA/grammar/PDA and justify its invariant, soundness and completeness, not merely examples.
    • For pumping, choose a witness after the pumping length and defeat every allowed split.
    • For reductions, write the map, the time/computability bound and both yes/no implications; known-hard source reduces to new target.
    • Treat language hierarchy, decidability and complexity as separate questions.
      • Recalculate symbols and source options instead of memorizing highlighted keys.
    • Sections in this course
