    • AUT01 Symbols, alphabets, words and length

      • An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols.
        • A word/string is a finite ordered sequence of symbols from Σ; a language is a set of words, L⊆Σ*.
        • An empty word ε, also written λ, has length zero.
        • The empty language ∅ contains no words; {ε} contains one.
        • Neither ε nor ∅ is the numeric symbol 0.
      • Length counts occurrences, not distinct symbols: |caddba|=6, so |caddba|²=36.
        • By contrast |(caddba)²|=12 because the word is concatenated twice.
        • If choices offer 12 for |Z|², they require changing the expression; do not silently move the exponent.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT02 Concatenation, powers and reversal

      • Concatenation xy writes x followed by y: cddc·ababb=cddcababb; order generally matters. εx=xε=x. Define x⁰=ε and xⁿ as n copies for n≥1.
        • Reverse xᴿ reads symbols backward: caddba reverses to abddac; (xy)ᴿ=yᴿxᴿ and (xᴿ)ᴿ=x.
      • For languages, LM={xy:x∈L,y∈M}, L⁰={ε}, and Lⁿ⁺¹=LⁿL.
        • Thus {e,fgh}{c,d}={ec,ed,fghc,fghd}; fghe is absent.
        • A language power is a set, so L⁰=ε is a type error unless braces are understood.
        • Symbols are case-sensitive; uppercase choices cannot literally equal lowercase words without a declared transcription repair.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT03 Language operations and empty-word edge cases

      • Σⁿ contains words of exactly n symbols; for |Σ|=k, |Σⁿ|=kⁿ, including Σ⁰={ε}. Σ*=⋃n≥0Σⁿ and Σ⁺=⋃n≥1Σⁿ.
        • Over a nonempty alphabet, Σ⁺ excludes ε and Σ*=Σ⁺∪{ε}. Σ² over {a,b} is {aa,ab,ba,bb}.
      • For an arbitrary language L, L*=⋃n≥0Lⁿ and L⁺=LL*.
        • Unlike alphabet positive closure, L⁺ can contain ε when ε∈L. ∅*={ε}, ∅⁺=∅, and {ε}*={ε}.
        • Union means membership in either set; intersection requires the same word in both, not concatenation.
        • Complement is Σ*−L and needs a fixed alphabet.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT04 Grammars generate; automata recognize

      • Write G=(V,Σ,P,S): finite variables V, terminals Σ disjoint from V, productions P and start variable S∈V. A production replaces its left side by its right side.
        • The language is L(G)={w∈Σ*:S⇒*w}.
        • A recognizer processes a word and accepts exactly the language members.
        • Grammars generate languages; automata recognize languages, not grammars.
      • Two grammars are equivalent when their generated languages are equal, regardless of rule counts or variable names.
        • One common word, equal alphabets or one-way inclusion is insufficient.
        • A regular expression denotes a language but is not itself the set of matched words.
        • Natural languages such as English are not the intended formal-language examples; give a precisely specified set instead.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT05 Chomsky hierarchy and the epsilon convention

      • Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs; type 1 context-sensitive/noncontracting grammars to nondeterministic LBAs; type 0 unrestricted grammars to Turing recognizers.
        • In an unrestricted production α→β, α contains at least one variable; unrestricted does not mean any meaningless rewrite is allowed.
      • Use REG ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ DECIDABLE ⊊ RE, under the usual convention allowing S→ε with S absent from right sides when needed.
        • Strict noncontracting grammars otherwise cannot generate ε.
        • Stronger families can describe lower-family languages: asking which grammar is capable is often nonunique.
        • Ask for the least sufficient family or the exact family equivalent to a machine model.
        • This is an expressiveness hierarchy, not a runtime ranking.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT06 DFA definition and acceptance

      • A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is M=(Q,Σ,δ,q₀,F), with finite nonempty Q, start q₀∈Q, accepting set F⊆Q and total δ:Q×Σ→Q. Exactly one next state is specified per state/symbol pair; this does not mean the whole machine has one transition.
        • F may be empty, recognizing ∅.
        • State names q₀,q₁,… do not determine accepting status.
      • Start at q₀ and consume the entire input.
        • Accept iff the ending state is in F; visiting an accepting state earlier is insufficient. ε is accepted exactly when q₀∈F. A nonaccepting sink loops on every symbol and cannot reach acceptance; it still finishes after finite input.
        • Finite automata have finite memory encoded by states, not no state or no ability to remember any history.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT07 Design and trace a finite-state recognizer

      • Choose states with invariant meanings: the information about the consumed prefix needed to decide future acceptance.
        • For binary words ending 01 use q₀=no useful suffix, q₁=last suffix 0, q₂=last suffix 01; only q₂ accepts.
        • Transitions on (0,1) are q₀→(q₁,q₀), q₁→(q₁,q₂), q₂→(q₁,q₀).
        • Input 10101 follows q₀,q₀,q₁,q₂,q₁,q₂ and accepts.
      • For length at least two use meanings 0 symbols, 1 symbol, at least 2 symbols.
        • Every input advances toward the third state, which loops and accepts.
        • Calling it q₂ is a naming choice: without a diagram or state definitions no numbered-state answer follows.
        • To verify a design, test ε, shortest accepted/rejected words and overlaps; sample agreement alone is not a proof.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT08 Minimum states: prefix, suffix and valid alphabets

      • For a fixed valid word w of length n, a DFA for strings ending in w needs n+1 states representing the longest consumed suffix that is a prefix of w. Overlapping prefixes determine fallback transitions.
        • Distinct prefixes are distinguishable by suitable continuations, proving the lower bound; do not add an unnecessary rejecting sink.
      • For strings starting with w, a complete DFA ordinarily has n matched-prefix stages, an accepting continuation state and a rejecting sink: n+2 when n≥1 and the alphabet allows mismatches.
        • Over a unary alphabet the sink may be unreachable.
        • If w contains a symbol outside Σ, the language is empty, whose minimal complete DFA has one rejecting state.
        • Thus starting abc over {a,b} needs one state, not five; five requires an alphabet containing a,b,c.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT09 NFA and epsilon transitions

      • A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) permits zero, one or many successors: δ:Q×Σ→𝒫(Q).
        • An ε-NFA additionally permits moves without consuming input, using domain Q×(Σ∪{ε}).
        • Some books include ε moves in the term NFA; state the convention.
        • An NFA accepts iff at least one finite path consumes the complete word and finishes in F, including permitted ε moves before/after symbols.
        • Other paths may get stuck.
      • An NFA is not more expressive than a DFA: both recognize exactly REG.
        • Nondeterminism can make a description smaller.
        • A DFA is a special NFA after interpreting its unique successor as a singleton set. ε is a zero-input move, not an ordinary input character or permission to accept with unread input.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT10 Subset construction with epsilon closure

      • ε-closure(T) contains T and every state reachable through ε moves.
        • Start the DFA at ε-closure({q₀}); for each current subset T and symbol a compute ε-closure(⋃q∈Tδ(q,a)).
        • A subset accepts iff it intersects F. Explore only reachable subsets; the empty subset is the rejecting sink when reached.
        • An n-state NFA yields at most 2ⁿ DFA states, not necessarily exactly 2ⁿ.
      • Example over Σ={a}: states p,r, start p, final r; δ(p,a)={p,r}, δ(r,a)=∅.
        • The subset machine starts {p}, reaches {p,r} on a, and stays there on further a's. It accepts a⁺.
        • With an ε edge p→r, the starting subset would already contain r and ε would also be accepted.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-GUIDE, AUT-SUBSET

    • AUT11 Equivalence, minimization and diagram checks

      • First discard unreachable DFA states.
        • Partition remaining states into accepting/nonaccepting blocks; repeatedly split a block when two states transition on some symbol into different blocks.
        • Stable blocks are equivalence classes and can be merged.
        • Equivalent states have identical acceptance for every continuation; current acceptance alone is insufficient.
      • For DFA equivalence build pairs of states and search from the start pair.
        • Any reachable pair with exactly one accepting component supplies a distinguishing word; if none exists, the languages agree.
        • A partial diagram must first be completed consistently with a sink.
        • To reject a proposed RE quickly, compare ε and the shortest cycles: an accepting start plus an ab return cycle forces ε and ab into the language.
        • Every equivalent expression must contain both.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-GUIDE, AUT-EQUIV

    • AUT12 Regular-expression notation and precedence

      • Classical expressions use ∅, ε, symbols, union, concatenation and star.
        • A union B is written A|B or A+B; postfix r⁺ means one-or-more r repetitions and is a different use of +.
        • Parenthesize when conventions might clash.
        • Star binds tightest, concatenation next, union last. r? means r|ε; r⁺=rr*.
      • (a|b)*a denotes words ending a; 0*10* denotes exactly one 1; a*(b|c) gives zero-or-more a's then exactly one b or c, so aab belongs but aaa and aaabc do not. (0|ε)(0|1)* is simply all binary words because ε permits any suffix.
        • Programming regex features such as backreferences may exceed classical regular-language power; wildcard dot is an extra notation, not a basic alphabet-independent theorem.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT13 Build expressions and convert representations

      • To require at least one a anywhere over {a,b}, use (a|b)*a(a|b)*. b*ab* requires exactly one a. At least two zeros uses (0|1)*0(0|1)*0(0|1)*; the zeros need not be adjacent.
        • Testing 010 distinguishes it from a requirement for substring 00.
        • For S→aS|ε, any number of a's is generated, giving a*.
      • RE→automaton uses ε-NFA fragments: parallel alternatives for union, connect accepting ends to the next fragment for concatenation, and add bypass/repetition ε moves for star.
        • Then apply subset construction.
        • For automaton→RE, eliminate a state k while updating edge i→j as rᵢⱼ | rᵢₖ(rₖₖ)*rₖⱼ; include new start/final nodes where required.
        • These operations preserve the whole language, not just tested examples.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-GUIDE, AUT-RECONVERT

    • AUT14 Regular grammars and closure constructions

      • Right-linear rules have form A→aB, A→a or permitted ε rules; left-linear rules put the single variable at the opposite end, A→Ba.
        • Both consistent orientations generate REG; arbitrarily mixing them can generate nonregular languages, for example S→aA|ε, A→Sb generates aⁿbⁿ.
        • A CFG rule A→aBA is legal but not regular-grammar form.
      • For right-linear grammar→NFA, variables become states, A→aB becomes an a edge, A→a leads to a fresh final state, and A→ε makes A accepting.
        • Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, intersection, difference and complement.
        • Reverse edges and exchange start/final roles using an ε-NFA to obtain reversal.
        • Complement requires a complete DFA; then swap accepting/nonaccepting states.
        • Product-state constructions implement intersection/difference.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-CLOSURE

    • AUT15 Regular pumping lemma: use the quantifiers

      • If L is regular, some p≥1 satisfies: every s∈L with |s|≥p has a split s=xyz, |xy|≤p, |y|≥1, and xyⁱz∈L for every i≥0.
        • To disprove regularity, assume an arbitrary pumping length p, choose s, then show every allowed split can be broken by some i. Finding one bad split proves nothing; satisfying this necessary condition alone does not prove regularity.
      • For L={aⁿbⁿ:n≥0}, choose aᵖbᵖ.
        • Every allowed y=aᵏ with k≥1; pumping i=0 leaves fewer a's than b's. The contradiction excludes every DFA.
        • For an n-state DFA, an accepted word of length at least n repeats a state along its path, giving an accepted cycle that can be repeated indefinitely.
        • Thus a fixed DFA's language is infinite iff it has an accepted word of length at least its state count.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT16 CFG derivations, sentences and parse trees

      • In a context-free grammar (CFG) each production has one variable on the left, A→α with α∈(V∪Σ)*.
        • The left side therefore also belongs to V∪Σ and its string closure; alternatives stating these weaker memberships can all be true.
        • A sentential form is any string derived from S, including terminal-only sentences and S itself.
      • A leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable; a rightmost one replaces the rightmost variable.
        • This is not scanning the completed input in opposite directions.
        • A complete parse tree has root S, internal variable nodes expanded by productions and terminal leaves, with ε leaves when that convention is used.
        • Read the leaves left-to-right for the yielded word.
        • The whole tree represents derivation structure; a path in a derivation graph is a different object.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT17 Design and validate context-free grammars

      • Use a recursive rule to enforce matched structure and a base rule to stop.
        • S→aSb|ε generates exactly aⁿbⁿ for n≥0: n recursive steps add n a's on the left and n b's on the right.
        • Derive aabb by S⇒aSb⇒aaSbb⇒aabb.
        • For n≥1 replace ε by base ab.
      • For aⁿbᵐ with n>m≥0, use S→aSb|A and A→aA|a: each S recursion adds a matched pair, then A adds at least one extra a. For balanced parentheses use S→(S)S|ε.
        • Validate soundness—each rule preserves the intended property—and completeness—decompose any desired nonempty word into pieces matching a production.
        • Merely producing several examples does not establish exact language equality.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT18 Ambiguity and precedence

      • A CFG is ambiguous when some word has two distinct parse trees, equivalently two different leftmost derivations.
        • Different expansion orders that give the same tree do not prove ambiguity.
        • E→E+E|E*E|id allows id+id*id to group as (id+id)*id or id+(id*id).
      • Separate precedence levels: E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→id|(E).
        • Multiplication binds inside T before addition at E, and left recursion encodes left association.
        • Uniqueness follows by the top-level last operator split and induction.
        • S→SS|ε is already ambiguous for ε.
        • S→A|B is ambiguous if A→ab and B→abB|ε both produce ab.
        • Ambiguous grammar and inherently ambiguous language differ: another grammar may remove ambiguity.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT19 Simplification, CNF and membership

      • A null production is A→ε; a unit production is A→B with one variable.
        • Mark nullable variables and add alternatives omitting nullable occurrences, preserving ε through a fresh start when needed.
        • Remove unit rules by copying nonunit productions reachable through unit chains.
        • Remove nongenerating variables, then unreachable symbols.
        • Do not delete a nullable variable's every use and lose valid nonempty words.
      • Chomsky normal form uses A→BC or A→a, with an optional isolated S₀→ε.
        • Replace terminals in long right sides by variables and split long variable sequences into binary steps: A→aBC becomes A→XC₁, X→a, C₁→BC.
        • For CNF membership, CYK fills variables generating each substring, combining splits with A→BC.
        • For a fixed grammar its time is O(n³); n>0 derivations contain n terminal rules and n−1 binary rules.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-CNF

    • AUT20 Greibach form and left recursion

      • Greibach normal form requires A→aA₁…Aₖ, k≥0: one leading terminal followed only by variables.
        • Handle ε separately through a fresh start that never appears on a right side.
        • A nonempty word of length n takes exactly n leftmost rule applications because each contributes one terminal to the prefix.
      • A constructive route removes ε/unit/useless rules, orders variables, substitutes rules beginning with earlier variables, removes left recursion, and substitutes until every rule begins with a terminal.
        • Some algorithms first convert to CNF; this is a method choice, not a universally mandatory first step.
        • Direct A→Aα|β can become A→βR, R→αR|ε, then further normalization handles ε.
        • GNF cannot retain direct or indirect left recursion.
        • A question demanding the first step must name its chosen algorithm.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-GUIDE, AUT-GNF

    • AUT21 PDA configuration and acceptance

      • A nondeterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) adds a stack to finite control: (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,Z₀,F).
        • Its transition relation maps (state,input symbol or ε,stack top) to possible (new state,replacement stack string) pairs.
        • Fix which end denotes the top before tracing.
        • Replacing X by X leaves the stack unchanged; ε input means consume no symbol, while replacing X by ε pops it.
        • These are different uses of ε.
      • A configuration records state, unread input and stack.
        • Final-state acceptance requires all input consumed and a final state; empty-stack acceptance requires all input consumed and an empty stack.
        • For NPDAs the modes characterize the same language family, through a construction, not necessarily the same unmodified machine.
        • Deterministic-PDA acceptance conventions need extra care and are not automatically interchangeable.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT22 Construct PDA recognizers and compare determinism

      • For aⁿbⁿ, push one X per a, switch to a b-reading phase, pop one X per b, and accept when input ends at the bottom marker.
        • Reject a after entering the b phase and b when no X remains.
        • Handle ε explicitly if n=0 is permitted.
        • A stack counts without storing the full input as random-access memory.
      • For even palindromes wwᴿ over {a,b}, push the first half, nondeterministically guess its midpoint, then pop matching symbols.
        • No center marker makes that language context-free but not deterministic context-free.
        • With a marker wcwᴿ the switch point is visible and a DPDA suffices.
        • Unary even palindromes are merely even-length words and regular.
        • A PDA cannot compare two arbitrary halves in the same forward order: {ww:w∈{a,b}*} is the copy language, not the palindrome language.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-PAL

    • AUT23 CFL closure and counterexamples

      • CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal and intersection with a regular language.
        • For CFL∩REG combine PDA control with DFA control, using the original stack; each consumed symbol updates both states, while an ε move leaves the DFA state unchanged.
        • The result is guaranteed context-free, not necessarily regular: intersect aⁿbⁿ with a*b* to get aⁿbⁿ.
      • CFLs are not closed under arbitrary intersection.
        • Both {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} are context-free; their intersection aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not.
        • Nor are CFLs closed under complement or arbitrary difference.
        • CFL minus a regular language remains CFL by intersecting with the regular complement.
        • A failed construction of one proposed PDA proves only that construction fails, not that every PDA fails.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-CFL

    • AUT24 CFL pumping proof and copy versus mirror

      • If L is context-free, some p ensures each sufficiently long s∈L has s=uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, |vy|≥1 and uvⁱxyⁱz∈L for every i≥0.
        • The two pieces v and y are pumped together; either may be empty, not both.
        • A non-CFL proof must defeat every allowed decomposition.
      • For s=aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vxy cannot contain both an a and a c. Pumping affects at most two blocks and at least one count.
        • Use i=0 or 2: the unaffected third block retains p while another count changes, or symbol order breaks.
        • Hence aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not CFL.
        • The copy language ww is also non-CFL over two symbols, whereas wwᴿ has the explicit grammar S→aSa|bSb|ε.
        • An expression that writes ww and calls it a palindrome is contradictory.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT25 Context-sensitive rules and linear bounded automata

      • A context-sensitive rule αAβ→αγβ replaces A in context, with γ nonempty.
        • Equivalently, noncontracting grammar presentations preserve/increase total length, with the isolated ε exception.
        • The condition is on the complete sides, not an unrelated comparison |β|≥|α|.
      • A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a TM with O(n) tape cells on length-n input; the standard CSL characterization uses nondeterministic LBAs.
        • For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.
        • All marks stay within the input region.
        • A fixed input has finitely many configurations, at most |Q|m|Γ|ᵐ for m cells.
        • Reachability search in that finite graph decides acceptance, even if some machine branches loop.
        • Thus every CSL is decidable.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-LBA

    • AUT26 Classify bank languages with justified boundaries

      • a*b* and {aⁿb:n≥0} are regular. aⁿbⁿ is CFL but not regular.
        • Over a two-symbol alphabet, wwᴿ is CFL, ww is not CFL; both are decidable. aⁿbⁿcⁿ is CSL but not CFL, and therefore decidable.
        • Every finite language is regular.
        • A stronger grammar or TM can still recognize any of these lower-family languages.
      • Unary prime length {aᵖ:p prime} is nonregular: choose prime q above pumping length p; if pump piece has length k≥1, using exponent q+1 gives length q(k+1), composite.
        • Every unary CFL is regular, so this language is not CFL either.
        • It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors.
        • Therefore none of the bank's balanced-three-count, prime-length, palindrome or aⁿb examples is nonrecursive.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-UNARY

    • AUT27 TM components, transitions and configurations

      • For a Turing machine (TM), use M=(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,qaccept,qreject), with finite state/tape alphabets, Σ⊆Γ and blank □∈Γ−Σ.
        • The module's statement blank∉Γ is wrong.
        • The standard machine has finite control, a read/write head and an unbounded tape.
        • Input is initial tape content, not a separate hardware organ; no separate stack is required.
      • δ(q,a)=(p,b,L) means read a in q, write b, move one cell left and enter p. Accept/reject halting states have no further moves under this convention.
        • In ID u q av the head scans a; the left-move successor, when u=u'c, is u' p cbv.
        • For a right move it is ub p v, showing a blank if the head enters unused tape.
        • State and transition names must follow the diagram's declared convention.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT28 TM design, variants and computation limits

      • To decide aⁿbⁿcⁿ, repeatedly mark matching triples, resetting the head between scans, then verify no unmatched symbol remains.
        • Each round marks additional input cells, so finitely many rounds suffice.
        • To decide ww, reject odd length, locate the midpoint using marks/counters, and compare corresponding symbols of the two halves; writable tape permits access a single stack lacks.
        • State both the acceptance test and why every input halts.
      • An off-line TM has a read-only input tape and separate read/write work tape.
        • Multitape, multihead, two-way-infinite-tape and nondeterministic TMs have the same language-recognition power as standard TMs, though simulation costs differ.
        • Two unbounded stacks can simulate a tape.
        • Turing completeness means ability to simulate general TM computation, not polynomial speed or literally using infinitely many cells in a finite run.
        • The Church–Turing thesis connects effective procedures to this formal model; it is not a proved runtime theorem.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT29 Deciders, recognizers and complements

      • A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language; these languages are recursive/decidable.
        • A recognizer must halt and accept every member, but on a nonmember may halt-reject or loop.
        • Its languages are recursively enumerable (RE), Turing-recognizable or semidecidable.
        • Looping is nonacceptance, not a rejecting halt.
        • An undecidable language may still have a recognizer.
      • Every decidable language is RE, and the containment is strict.
        • If L and its complement are both RE, simulate their recognizers in dovetailed steps until one accepts, obtaining a decider.
        • Conversely complementing a decider works because it always halts.
        • Flipping final states in an arbitrary recognizer fails to handle nonmembers that loop.
        • Recursive function theory's total computable functions are not merely programs written with recursive self-calls; partial computable functions may be undefined where computation does not halt.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT30 Halting, diagonalization and Rice’s theorem

      • HALT={⟨M,w⟩:M halts on w} is recognizable: simulate and accept upon any halt.
        • Suppose a decider H determines halting.
        • Construct D(x) that loops if H(x,x) says halt, otherwise halts.
        • Running D on its own description contradicts H in both cases.
        • Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE.
        • Its complement is not RE, or both recognizers would yield a decider.
      • Rice's theorem makes every nontrivial semantic property of a TM's recognized language undecidable.
        • Nontrivial means some recognized languages have it and some do not.
        • Empty language, contains ε and at least three accepted words qualify.
        • Number of states and whether a particular symbol is written are machine-behavior/syntactic properties, not automatically language properties; prove such claims separately.
        • Undecidable means no general decider exists, not merely no algorithm is currently known.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT31 Which decision questions are solvable?

      • DFA/NFA word membership is decidable by simulation or reachable state sets.
        • FA emptiness is reachable-accepting-state search; DFA equivalence searches the product for an acceptance disagreement.
        • CFG membership is decidable by parsing/CYK and emptiness by marking variables that can generate terminal strings.
        • These procedures halt and are not the same as deciding arbitrary TM membership.
      • TM acceptance on input is RE-complete and undecidable; HALT is undecidable.
        • General CFG ambiguity and CFG equivalence are undecidable even though membership for a given CFG and word is decidable.
        • A concrete grammar's two parse trees can establish that particular grammar is ambiguous; this does not give an algorithm deciding ambiguity for every grammar.
        • FORTRAN/programming-language questions must distinguish CFG-style syntax, semantic restrictions and Turing-complete computation; a language's name alone does not choose one formal classification.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-DECIDE

    • AUT32 Computable reductions for undecidability

      • A many-one reduction A≤mB is a total computable transformation f satisfying x∈A iff f(x)∈B. If B had a decider, compute f and invoke it to decide A. Therefore known-undecidable A reduced to B proves B undecidable.
        • Showing B≤mA alone does not establish B's hardness.
      • Example HALT≤mA_TM: given ⟨M,w⟩, construct N that ignores its input, simulates M(w), and accepts if M ever halts, including rejecting halts.
        • Then ⟨N,ε⟩ is accepted iff M(w) halts.
        • Construction of N's finite description terminates; the simulation inside N may not.
        • Reductions require both yes and no directions and a computable mapping, not just a resemblance between two problems.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-REDUCE

    • AUT33 Measure resources with the right input size

      • Time counts computation steps; space counts cells/memory used, specifying whether read-only input is excluded.
        • For a deterministic decider use the maximum over all length-n inputs; for a time-bounded nondeterministic decider every branch meets the bound.
        • Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound, not inherently a worst-case label: it can describe a worst-, average- or best-case function. Θ adds a matching lower bound.
      • Growth typically orders 1,log n,n,n log n,n²,2ⁿ,n!.
        • A fixed polynomial nᵏ differs from exponent 2ⁿ.
        • Encoding matters: the number N in binary has Θ(log N) bits, so O(N) work is not polynomial in its binary input length.
        • Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on numeric magnitude rather than encoding length.
        • A polynomial of enormous degree need not be practical.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT34 P, NP and polynomial verification

      • Complexity classes here contain decision languages.
        • P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decidable languages; NP consists of nondeterministic polynomial-time decidable languages, equivalently polynomially verifiable yes-instances with polynomial-size certificates.
        • A verifier must accept some certificate exactly for yes-inputs; no certificate may falsely establish a no-instance.
        • NP means nondeterministic polynomial, not non-polynomial.
      • For CLIQUE, the certificate lists k vertices; verify they are distinct and every pair is an edge.
        • This is polynomial in the graph encoding.
        • P⊆NP because a verifier can ignore its certificate and run the P algorithm.
        • P=NP remains open; NP does not mean definitely hard or definitely outside P. Finding versus verifying is an intuition for witnesses, not a rule that all NP instances need exponential search.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-PNP, AUT-OPEN, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT35 Polynomial reductions: direction and consequences

      • A≤pB means f is computable in polynomial time and x∈A iff f(x)∈B. Solving B then solves A, so B is at least as hard under this reduction.
        • If B∈P then A∈P; if A is NP-hard then B is NP-hard.
        • A∈P does not force B∈P, and the reduction alone does not place both problems in the same class.
        • Polynomial reductions compose.
      • To prove a new target X hard, reduce a known hard problem Y to X, not X to Y. The mapping and target instance must have polynomial size.
        • For undecidability, general computable reductions suffice; for NP-completeness, an arbitrarily slow computable transformation is insufficient.
        • Always state which reduction and resource bound are being used.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT36 NP-hard versus NP-complete; decision versus optimization

      • X is NP-hard if every A∈NP satisfies A≤pX.
        • It need not belong to NP and can even be undecidable.
        • X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard.
        • Thus NP-complete languages lie inside NP and can be decided by finite exhaustive certificate search in exponential time; both statements can be true options.
        • They are not known to require exponential time.
      • SAT asks whether a Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment; Cook–Levin establishes SAT NP-complete.
        • CNF-SAT and 3-SAT are NP-complete versions.
        • TSP decision asks whether a tour of cost at most B exists; it is NP-complete for standard finite encoded inputs.
        • Finding the shortest tour is optimization and NP-hard; call it NP-complete only after specifying a decision formulation.
        • Fixed 2-colorability is in P, while fixed k-colorability for k≥3 is NP-complete.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT37 Work a hardness proof: 3-SAT to CLIQUE

      • First CLIQUE belongs to NP by the pairwise-edge certificate check.
        • For a 3-CNF formula with m clauses, make one vertex for each literal occurrence.
        • Connect two vertices iff they come from different clauses and are not complementary literals.
        • Ask whether the graph has a clique of size m. Construction takes polynomial time and space.
      • A satisfying assignment supplies one true literal per clause; they are mutually consistent and form a clique.
        • Conversely an m-clique selects one occurrence per clause, with no variable chosen both positively and negatively, so assign those literals true and extend remaining variables arbitrarily.
        • Both implications prove equivalence.
        • For the short note's formula (x₁∨¬x₂)∧(¬x₁∨x₂∨x₃)∧¬x₃, assignment (true,true,false) actually satisfies all clauses: ¬false is true, contrary to the note.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-NPC

    • AUT38 PSPACE, quantifiers and space reuse

      • PSPACE is ⋃kSPACE(nᵏ), using deterministic polynomial workspace.
        • NP⊆PSPACE because candidate polynomial witnesses can be enumerated and checked one at a time, reusing memory; exponentially many candidates do not require retaining them all.
        • Savitch's theorem gives NSPACE(s)⊆DSPACE(s²) for appropriate s≥log n, hence NPSPACE=PSPACE.
        • It does not prove P=NP.
      • TQBF asks whether a fully quantified Boolean formula is true and is PSPACE-complete.
        • Evaluate ∃x by trying one branch or the other; evaluate ∀x by requiring both.
        • Depth-first evaluation stores assignments and recursion state using polynomial space despite potentially exponential time.
        • For example ∀x∃y(x↔y) is true, but ∃y∀x(x↔y) is false.
        • PSPACE-complete means membership plus hardness for every PSPACE language under the stated reduction.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-SPACE, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT39 Known hierarchy and open separations

      • Use L⊆NL⊆P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME⊆EXPSPACE.
        • Here L/NL use logarithmic workspace; EXPTIME is ⋃kTIME(2^(nᵏ)), an upper-bound class that also contains P, not a statement that every member requires exponential time.
        • Suitable hierarchy theorems prove P⊊EXPTIME and PSPACE⊊EXPSPACE.
        • They do not establish every adjacent containment strictly.
      • P versus NP, NP versus PSPACE and PSPACE versus EXPTIME remain unresolved. coNP contains complements of NP languages; P⊆NP∩coNP, and NP=coNP is open.
        • If any NP-complete language is in P, all NP collapses to P. This does not make every decidable language polynomial or make undecidable problems decidable.
        • Avoid blanket claims about all cryptography or all problems becoming easy; the class and encoding matter.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE, AUT-HIERARCHY, AUT-BLUEPRINT

    • AUT40 Derive the unusual bank grammar examples

      • For S→11S|0A|1A and A→0|1|0S, every reachable form has at most one variable, at the right end.
        • A complete terminal word is still a sentential form.
        • For example S⇒11S⇒1111S⇒111111S⇒1111110A⇒11111101.
        • Returning to S appends a pair 11,00 or 10; use that invariant to rule out impossible prefixes rather than guessing from string length.
      • For A→aB|bA|bBa and B→bB|cA|b, specify a start variable first.
        • With A assumed, a terminating membership test recursively removes the required a/b prefix or b…a wrapper; B either matches b or removes b before B/c before A. Every recursive residual is shorter.
        • Checking all four offered words yields no member, contradicting the marked source choice.
        • Correct reasoning can reveal that no option works.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

    • AUT41 Precise source defects and missing information

      • Use the exact readable language formula and alphabet when testing membership.
        • State labels are arbitrary: use the transition diagram, initial state and accepting markings, or a definition assigning meanings to states.
        • Language theory alone cannot identify an arbitrary state label.
      • Q00334's previously image-verified accepting start and ab return cycle require both ε and ab, while none of its offered expressions contains both.
        • Q00194 lacks a declared start and has no successful choice even with A assumed.
        • Q00981 writes the non-CFL copy language ww but calls it an even palindrome; explicitly choose between ww and wwᴿ.
        • Generic capable, contains and most difficult questions need a least-family, exact-class or reduction qualifier.
        • For GNF first-step questions identify the conversion algorithm.
        • No unique key should be invented where choices overlap.
      • References: AUT-MOD, AUT-NOTE

  • Compiler Design

    • Follow one program from characters to tokens, grammatical structure, checked meaning, intermediate code and target instructions.
      • Practise the constructions and transformations: recognizing a phase name alone is insufficient to diagnose an error or justify an optimization.
    • Allocate this course its official six-item priority.
      • Compare scanner/parser/semantic checker and LL/LR, then trace concrete examples.
    • Practise token counting, FIRST/FOLLOW, predictive and LR actions, attribute flow, three-address code and safe optimization.
      • State language and target assumptions.
    • Treat source keys as claims to check.
      • Some choices overlap, omit the correct result, or make universal claims that compiler theory does not support.
    • Sections in this course
      Translation, interpretation and compilation timeTools, host, target and incremental workCompiler phases and shared servicesToken, lexeme and patternRegular expressions for lexical structureConstruct and run a scanner automatonLongest match and counting tokensLocate the error by evidenceCFGs, derivations and treesAmbiguity, precedence and associativityTop-down parsingRemove left recursion and factor prefixesCompute FIRST and FOLLOWBuild and use an LL(1) tableBottom-up actions and handlesConstruct LR(0) item statesLR families and conflictsParser limits and operator grammarsSymbol tables and scopeNames, types and advanced language featuresSemantic checking: static and dynamicType rules, inference and compatibilityConversions need a named languageAttributes and syntax-directed definitionsTranslation actions, ASTs and postfixIntermediate representations and three-address codeControl flow, arrays and SSABasic blocks, flow graphs and dominatorsData-flow questions and equationsFolding, propagation and dead codeReuse, strength reduction and peepholesLoops: invariants, induction and fusionOptimization legality and aliasingTarget code generationDescriptors and getRegInterference graphs and spillingRuntime storage and calling conventionsInlining and dynamic dispatchRecovery and compiler-construction toolsTrace one expression through the compilerRepair missing or conflated lexical answersRepair parser questions with overlapping choicesRepair semantic and translation claims

    • COMP01 Translation, interpretation and compilation time

      • A compiler translates a source program into an equivalent target representation while preserving defined observable behavior.
        • The target may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language.
        • A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler, not a fundamentally separate noncompiler technology.
        • A compiler preserves language semantics, not the programmer’s unstated intention.
      • An interpreter executes a program representation; it need not work one source line at a time.
        • Systems can compile to bytecode and then interpret or JIT-compile it.
        • AOT compilation happens before execution; JIT compilation happens during execution and may use runtime profiles.
        • Neither is universally faster; startup cost, optimization and workload matter.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP02 Tools, host, target and incremental work

      • A preprocessor handles directives such as file inclusion and macros.
        • An assembler translates assembly to object code.
        • A linker combines object files and libraries, resolves external symbols and performs relocation.
        • A loader maps an executable into memory and starts it.
        • Compilation alone does not necessarily produce a ready executable.
      • A cross-compiler runs on a host platform and generates code for a different target.
        • Multiple targets require appropriate backends, not a special definition of cross-compilation.
        • A retargetable compiler supports changing target descriptions.
        • Incremental compilation recompiles affected fragments or dependent units after edits; it is more than literally replacing changed lines.
        • One-pass versus multipass counts traversals, not supported targets.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP03 Compiler phases and shared services

      • The conventional sequence is lexical analysis → syntax analysis → semantic analysis → intermediate-code generation → optimization → target-code generation.
        • Scanning turns characters into tokens; parsing builds structure; semantics checks declarations and types; synthesis produces implementation code.
        • A phase is a logical activity; a pass is a traversal that can combine activities.
      • The front end handles source-language rules; a middle end analyzes and transforms IR; the backend handles target details.
        • Symbol-table management and error reporting support multiple phases rather than forming one mandatory seventh final phase.
        • Optimization can occur at several levels, including after instruction selection. “Final phase” means code generation in the standard six-phase teaching pipeline.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP04 Token, lexeme and pattern

      • A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42).
        • A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42.
        • A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class.
        • The scanner emits an ordered token stream, not an unordered mathematical set.
      • Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes.
        • Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained.
        • In indentation-sensitive or newline-sensitive languages, layout can carry tokens.
        • Parse-tree construction is a parser task; scanning can intern identifier spellings, but declaration scope and types need later analysis.
      • Scan a statement
        • int x = 42; gives keyword(int), ID(x), assignment(=), integer(42), semicolon(;): five tokens.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP05 Regular expressions for lexical structure

      • Regular expressions use concatenation, alternation r|s, Kleene star r* for zero or more, and r+ for one or more.
        • In a simplified alphabet, identifier = Letter(Letter|Digit)*; it permits a single letter and forbids a leading digit.
        • A C-like ASCII rule commonly also allows underscore: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* State the convention instead of claiming this covers every language’s identifiers.
      • Letter(Letter+|Digit*)* denotes the same language as Letter(Letter|Digit)* under ordinary regular-expression semantics: repeated blocks can contain any trailing letter/digit sequence.
        • Thus two such options are equivalent.
        • Regular patterns handle ordinary tokens; arbitrary balanced nesting generally needs grammar/stack structure.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP06 Construct and run a scanner automaton

      • A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional.
        • For concatenation rs, connect r’s final state to s’s start by ε.
        • Alternation introduces branching ε paths; star adds a way to skip and repeat the fragment.
      • The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges.
        • A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)).
        • Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting.
        • Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP07 Longest match and counting tokens

      • At each input position, choose the longest matching lexeme; if equal lengths match multiple flex rules, choose the earliest rule.
        • Thus ifx is an identifier rather than if followed by x; <= and ++ are each one operator token.
        • An implementation may recognize an identifier first and then consult a keyword table.
      • For the ordinary C++ header: for (int i = 0; i <= 10; i++) The tokens, split into two display lines, are: for, (, int, i, =, 0, ; i, <=, 10, ;, i, ++, ) There are 14 tokens, irrespective of spacing.
        • The increment operator is one token.
        • A comment contributes no ordinary parser token after preprocessing.
        • Bank choices 4,5,9,10 omit the correct count.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_DEEP, COMP_FLEX

    • COMP08 Locate the error by evidence

      • A lexical error prevents forming a legal token, such as an invalid character or unterminated literal.
        • A syntax error is an illegal token arrangement, such as a missing delimiter.
        • A semantic error violates name, scope or type rules after grammatical recognition.
        • A wrong algorithm can compile successfully; compilers do not detect all logical mistakes.
      • In the malformed C line fro ((I = o, I;, fro and lowercase o are legal identifier lexemes.
        • Misspelling for does not turn fro into a lexical error; mismatched syntax is definite, and undeclared o can also produce a semantic diagnostic.
        • Recovery order and exact diagnostics depend on the compiler.
        • Do not silently replace o by 0 or fro by for.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP09 CFGs, derivations and trees

      • A context-free grammar G=(N,T,P,S) has nonterminals N, terminals T, productions P and start S. A production A→α rewrites one nonterminal.
        • A sentential form is any string of terminals/nonterminals derivable from S; a sentence contains only terminals.
        • A leftmost derivation rewrites the leftmost remaining nonterminal; a rightmost one rewrites the rightmost.
      • A parse tree shows grammar productions: root S, internal nonterminals, and terminal leaves, with ε sometimes shown for empty productions.
        • Its left-to-right yield is the input.
        • An AST omits grammar scaffolding and punctuation; expression operands are leaves and operators internal nodes.
        • The parser can build either representation, depending on implementation.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP10 Ambiguity, precedence and associativity

      • A grammar is ambiguous if at least one terminal string has two different parse trees, equivalently two leftmost derivations.
        • Merely changing derivation order on the same tree does not establish ambiguity.
        • E→E+E|E*E|id allows different trees for id+id*id.
      • Use E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→(E)|id to give * higher precedence and both operators left associativity.
        • For subtraction, a−b−c then groups (a−b)−c. The dangling-else grammar permits else to attach to either nested if; a nearest-unmatched-if rule or grammar rewrite resolves it.
        • Taking a leftmost derivation by itself does not resolve ambiguous interpretation.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP11 Top-down parsing

      • Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation.
        • Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal.
        • A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking.
        • LL(1) scans Left to right, produces a Leftmost derivation and uses one lookahead token.
      • A nonrecursive predictive parser stores grammar symbols on an explicit stack and consults a table.
        • It is another implementation of predictive parsing, not a wholly different language class.
        • Table-driven and recursive predictive implementations can both be linear for a fixed suitable grammar.
        • Efficiency cannot be ranked from their names alone.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP12 Remove left recursion and factor prefixes

      • Immediate left recursion has A→Aα.
        • For A→Aα|β, where β does not start with A, introduce a new nonterminal A′ and use: A→βA′ A′→αA′|ε This preserves the generated language; tree shape changes, so semantic actions must preserve intended associativity.
        • Indirect left recursion follows a cycle through other nonterminals and also needs removal for ordinary predictive descent.
      • Left factoring rewrites A→αβ|αγ using: A→αA′ A′→β|γ It postpones a choice until after the common prefix.
        • It does not by itself remove ambiguity or guarantee LL(1).
        • LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP13 Compute FIRST and FOLLOW

      • FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin strings derived from α, plus ε when α can vanish.
        • For a sequence, add FIRST of each symbol except ε, continue while symbols are nullable, and add ε only if every symbol is nullable.
      • FOLLOW(A) contains possible next terminals after A, plus end marker $ where appropriate; never ε.
        • Put $ in FOLLOW(S).
        • For B→αAβ, add FIRST(β)−{ε} to FOLLOW(A); if β is nullable, add FOLLOW(B).
        • Repeat all rules until no sets grow.
      • Small grammar
        • S→AB, A→a|ε, B→b gives FIRST(A)={a,ε}, FIRST(S)={a,b}, FOLLOW(A)={b}, FOLLOW(B)={$}.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP14 Build and use an LL(1) table

      • For every A→α, put it in M[A,a] for each terminal a in FIRST(α).
        • If α is nullable, also enter it under every symbol in FOLLOW(A).
        • More than one production in a cell is a conflict.
        • Pairwise SELECT sets must be disjoint; SELECT(α)=FIRST(α)−{ε}, plus FOLLOW(A) when α is nullable.
        • This also detects two nullable alternatives.
      • Initialize stack with $S. Match and pop terminals; for a nonterminal consult its row and lookahead, then push the chosen RHS in reverse.
        • An ε production consumes no input.
        • Accept when stack and input reach $.
        • For A→a|ε with b∈FOLLOW(A), choose a on lookahead a and ε on b.
      • Exam trap
        • Ambiguous useful grammars are not LL(1). Overlapping FIRST, FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts and left recursion cannot be dismissed by an “A and B only” key.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_DEEP, COMP_LL

    • COMP15 Bottom-up actions and handles

      • Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse.
        • A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation.
        • Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.
      • Shift pushes the next input token and a state; reduce replaces a recognized RHS by its LHS and consults GOTO; accept recognizes completion; error reports an invalid situation.
        • For A→XYZ, pop three grammar symbols and their states, expose state q, then push A and GOTO[q,A]. “Go” is not a separate standard shift-reduce ACTION, although GOTO is essential table machinery.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP16 Construct LR(0) item states

      • Augment the grammar with S′→S. An LR(0) item A→α·β records progress through a production.
        • CLOSURE(I) repeatedly adds B→·γ whenever an item has its dot before nonterminal B and B→γ is a production.
      • GOTO(I,X) moves the dot past X in every eligible item and takes closure.
        • Start with CLOSURE({S′→·S}); repeatedly compute nonempty GOTO sets for all grammar symbols until no new state appears.
        • The resulting set of item sets is the canonical collection, not GOTO itself.
      • One transition
        • For S→a, call the initial closure I0: I0 = {S′→·S, S→·a} GOTO(I0,a) = {S→a·} GOTO(I0,S) = {S′→S·} Each complete set above is one state, not one state per item.
      • References: COMP_LR0

    • COMP17 LR families and conflicts

      • SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production.
        • Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items.
        • LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts.
        • The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.
      • A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions.
        • An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous.
        • Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG.
        • Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_DEEP, COMP_BISON

    • COMP18 Parser limits and operator grammars

      • LL, LR and recursive-descent parsers can all handle nested parentheses for suitable grammars.
        • An explicit or implicit stack, not the LR label alone, supports unbounded nesting.
        • Both LL and LR can use parsing tables.
        • Deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous; a general ambiguous grammar requires rewriting, disambiguation policy or a generalized method such as GLR.
      • An operator grammar conventionally forbids adjacent nonterminals on a RHS and usually ε productions.
        • Operator-precedence parsing additionally requires conflict-free precedence relations.
        • Ordinary right-linear regular grammars also lack adjacent nonterminals, so that property alone does not uniquely identify the operator-grammar category.
        • Regular patterns are chiefly lexical specifications; CFGs chiefly describe nested syntax.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP19 Symbol tables and scope

      • A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage.
        • A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting.
        • Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.
      • Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type.
        • Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal.
        • Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table.
        • A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP20 Names, types and advanced language features

      • Distinguish lexical recognition, grammatical structure and semantic constraints.
        • In obj.method(x), the scanner recognizes identifiers and punctuation; the parser recognizes a member call; semantic analysis resolves the receiver, accessible member and argument types.
        • Overload resolution chooses among signatures using static types; overriding can select an implementation at runtime.
      • Nested scopes require declaration identity rather than spelling alone: an inner int x can shadow an outer float x. Closures capture free variables from lexical environments; lifetime can outlive the creating stack frame.
        • Generic functions need parameter constraints or instantiation checks.
        • These features require symbol/type information beyond a CFG, even when their surface syntax is context-free.
      • Specify and check a member call
        • For object.resize(3), the token kinds are id, dot, id, left parenthesis, integer, right parenthesis. One small grammar is Call → Expr . id ( Args ); Expr → id; Args → Expr | integer | ε. Derive Call ⇒ Expr . id ( Args ) ⇒ id . id ( integer ), then bind the tokens object, resize and 3. The parser checks this shape. Name and type analysis then require object to be in scope, resize to be an accessible member and an overload accepting one integer-compatible argument. If only resize() exists, the text still parses but fails the argument/type check.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP21 Semantic checking: static and dynamic

      • Static checks occur before execution: type compatibility, duplicate declarations within a restricted scope, valid names, argument counts, return compatibility and control-flow placement.
        • A break is valid only in constructs allowed by the language; in C/C++ it can exit a loop or switch.
        • A compiler may annotate an AST or create typed IR; there is no mandatory uniquely named output tree.
      • Dynamic checks depend on runtime values, such as some bounds and null checks.
        • Static analysis can prove some accesses safe or faulty; “all memory errors cannot be statically checked” is too strong.
        • Unreachable code is not universally a semantic error: some languages reject it in specified cases, others merely warn or optimize it away.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP22 Type rules, inference and compatibility

      • A type checker verifies that operations are defined for their operands.
        • In a simple strict language, integer mod requires two integers; array indexing requires an array and integer index; an if condition requires Boolean; assignment requires equal or convertible types.
        • Function calls check parameter count and compatibility, and returns match result types.
      • Type inference derives types from constraints: if x is integer and + expects numeric operands, infer the expression type from numeric promotion rules.
        • It is a static technique even without explicit annotations.
        • Operator overloading supplies multiple operation meanings, not a substitute for type checking. int x="hello" is a type mismatch in ordinary C++/Java; division by zero and bounds violations are not automatically operand-type mismatches.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP23 Conversions need a named language

      • Coercion is an implicit conversion permitted by the language; a cast requests an explicit conversion.
        • Widening often increases representable range, but can still lose precision: Java int→float is widening although large integers round.
        • Java int→long is exact.
        • Narrowing can lose range or fractional information.
      • In C++ ordinary int x=3.14 converts to 3 when representable; it is not inherently a type error. int x{3.14} is rejected as narrowing.
        • C++ floating-to-integer conversion discards the fraction and has undefined behavior if the truncated value is unrepresentable.
        • Java ordinary double→int assignment needs a permitted explicit cast.
        • Mixing char and int is ordinarily valid after promotion in C++/Java; do not import a fictitious universal ban.
      • References: COMP_CPP, COMP_JAVA, COMP_SHORT

    • COMP24 Attributes and syntax-directed definitions

      • A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions.
        • An annotated parse tree displays computed attribute values; it is not itself an inherited or synthesized attribute.
        • Synthesized attributes flow from children to a parent; inherited attributes carry context from parent or siblings.
      • For E→E1+T, E.val=E1.val+T.val synthesizes an expression value.
        • A declaration’s type environment passed into its body is inherited.
        • S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit LR reduction-time evaluation naturally; suitable LL parsers can also compute them.
        • L-attributed definitions restrict dependencies so a left-to-right traversal can evaluate inherited context.
        • Attribute dependency cycles can prevent evaluation.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP25 Translation actions, ASTs and postfix

      • A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler.
        • Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code.
        • The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.
      • Create an identifier leaf with mkleaf(id,entry), a number with mkleaf(num,value), and an operator node with mknode(op,left,right).
        • For a−4+c, construct +(−(a,4),c).
        • Postorder traversal prints postfix: a 4 − c +.
        • A stack evaluator pushes operands and pops right then left operands for an operator.
        • Infix-to-postfix is useful for stack machines but not mandatory for all compilers.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP26 Intermediate representations and three-address code

      • IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused.
        • It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.
        • Portability is an architectural benefit, not proof that every IR omits all target-dependent details.
        • ASTs, graphs, bytecode and TAC can all be IRs.
      • Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2.
        • Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions.
        • Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement.
        • Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP27 Control flow, arrays and SSA

      • A conditional expression can generate if a<b goto Ltrue; goto Lfalse; labels join control paths.
        • Short-circuit AND evaluates the right operand only after a true left operand; OR only after a false one.
        • Translating both eagerly can change side effects.
        • For a zero-based array with element width w and lower bound L, element i uses base+(i−L)*w, assuming fixed-width contiguous storage.
      • SSA gives each definition a distinct name.
        • At a join, x3=φ(x1 from B1,x2 from B2) chooses the incoming value according to the predecessor actually taken; it is not an arithmetic average.
        • SSA is a naming discipline over IR and commonly coexists with a control-flow graph.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_DEEP, COMP_SSA

    • COMP28 Basic blocks, flow graphs and dominators

      • A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end.
        • Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch.
        • Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.
      • A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through.
        • A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop.
        • This structure supports loop analysis.
        • An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP29 Data-flow questions and equations

      • Reaching definitions is forward may-analysis: which assignments can reach this point without a replacement definition?
        • OUT=GEN∪(IN−KILL), with IN the union of predecessor OUT sets.
        • Available expressions is usually forward must-analysis: an expression has been computed on every relevant path and its operands have not changed.
        • Join with intersection.
      • Liveness is backward may-analysis: a value might be read before redefinition on some future path.
        • OUT[B]=union of IN over successors; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]).
        • Iterate to a fixed point.
        • Liveness supports register allocation and dead-value removal.
        • Definite-assignment analysis asks whether initialization occurs on every path before use; reaching definitions alone does not prove this.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP30 Folding, propagation and dead code

      • Constant folding evaluates constant expressions during compilation: 3*4→12.
        • Constant propagation substitutes known values: x=3; y=x+2 becomes y=3+2 before folding.
        • Copy propagation substitutes a copied name while its source remains unchanged.
        • Dead-code elimination removes unreachable code or computations whose values are unused and whose evaluation has no necessary side effects.
      • For const int x=8,y=16; if(x>y){int z=x+y;}, propagate the constants, fold 8>16 to false, then remove the unreachable branch.
        • Both compile-time evaluation and dead-code elimination apply.
        • A question asking only which optimization is appropriate cannot isolate these as mutually exclusive choices.
        • Computing an unused volatile read or effectful call may still be required.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP31 Reuse, strength reduction and peepholes

      • Common-subexpression elimination reuses an earlier value only if operand values and relevant memory remain unchanged.
        • A DAG can represent sharing.
        • Algebraic simplification removes identities when valid: integer x+0→x. Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper form, such as unsigned x*8→x<<3 for a valid width and shift count.
        • Target costs determine whether it is actually cheaper.
      • Peephole optimization examines short instruction windows.
        • It can remove redundant loads/stores, replace machine idioms and shorten jump chains: jump L1 where L1 immediately jumps L2 can become jump L2. “Local optimization” is a wider category; peephole is a concrete method, so a question offering both must specify the level requested.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP32 Loops: invariants, induction and fusion

      • A loop-invariant expression has unchanged inputs during a loop.
        • Hoist it to a preheader only when evaluation is safe on the paths where it will newly run.
        • Induction variables change by a loop-invariant increment, such as i=i+1.
        • For repeated t=4*i, maintain a running t increased by 4 when equivalent, reducing repeated multiplication.
      • Loop fusion or jamming combines loops with compatible bounds and safe dependence order.
        • Unrolling replicates a body to reduce branch overhead and expose parallelism; handle remaining iterations and increased code size.
        • Loop-invariant code motion, fusion, unrolling and strength reduction are different transformations.
        • A finite taxonomy needs a criterion: machine dependent/independent versus local/global/loop are different classifications.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP33 Optimization legality and aliasing

      • Optimization preserves defined observable behavior, including required side effects and exceptions.
        • Alias analysis asks whether references can denote the same memory.
        • After *p=5, a previous load through q cannot be reused unless p and q are known not to alias or an equivalent proof applies.
        • Function calls can also invalidate memory facts.
      • Do not move a potentially trapping division outside a loop that might execute zero times.
        • Floating-point reassociation can change rounding and NaN behavior.
        • Signed C/C++ overflow and shift rules differ from unsigned modular arithmetic; a mathematical identity is not automatically a legal transformation.
        • Dependence analysis must show that fusion or scheduling preserves the required order of memory accesses.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP34 Target code generation

      • Code generation lowers checked IR to a target form.
        • Instruction selection chooses target operations; register allocation chooses where values reside; scheduling orders instructions while respecting dependencies; storage layout assigns offsets and follows ABI requirements.
        • Register assignment names actual physical registers after allocation decisions.
      • For t=a+b, a simple target could emit LOAD R1,a; LOAD R2,b; ADD R3,R1,R2; STORE t,R3.
        • Other targets may combine loads with arithmetic or keep t in a register.
        • Machine idioms, register availability and instruction order affect execution time.
        • Absolute machine code, relocatable object code, assembly and VM bytecode can be legitimate compiler targets; TAC is normally intermediate, but “cannot ever be target code” is an unjustified universal.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_DEEP, COMP_CODEGEN

    • COMP35 Descriptors and getReg

      • A register descriptor records which current values are held in a register.
        • An address descriptor for a name records all current locations containing its value, possibly memory and multiple registers.
        • A memory copy can become stale after a register-only assignment.
        • These are code-generator bookkeeping structures, not source-language types.
      • A simple code-generation algorithm calls getReg for a TAC instruction to select operand/result registers, emits necessary loads, emits the operation, then updates descriptors.
        • Prefer an already suitable register or a reusable dead operand; otherwise choose a spill victim and store any live value lacking another current copy.
        • At a block exit, preserve values needed by successors.
      • References: COMP_DESC

    • COMP36 Interference graphs and spilling

      • A value is live where it can be used before redefinition.
        • In the interference model, values that must coexist in distinct registers are connected by an edge; each register is a color.
        • Nonoverlapping live ranges may share a register.
        • If a valid assignment cannot fit the available registers, spilling places selected values in memory and inserts loads/stores.
      • The general graph k-colorability decision problem is NP-complete for fixed k≥3; optimal register assignment/spill minimization is a hard optimization problem in general, so practical allocators use heuristics.
        • Restricted interference graphs or SSA formulations can have different properties.
        • Do not describe every possible register-allocation algorithm as NP-complete merely because a general model is difficult.
      • References: COMP_DEEP, COMP_COLOR

    • COMP37 Runtime storage and calling conventions

      • Static storage lasts throughout execution; stack frames support nested calls and recursion; heap storage supports lifetimes beyond a call.
        • A frame may contain parameters, return address, saved registers, locals and temporaries.
        • Sizes, alignment and offsets are target-dependent; a module’s two-byte int is an example, not a C++ guarantee.
      • A calling convention specifies argument and result locations, caller/callee-saved registers, stack alignment and frame responsibilities.
        • Escape analysis asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside a region such as its allocating call.
        • Proven nonescaping allocations may use stack storage or be eliminated by scalar replacement, provided identity and lifetime semantics remain correct.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP38 Inlining and dynamic dispatch

      • Inlining replaces a call with a suitably renamed copy of its body, preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects.
        • It can remove call overhead and expose optimization opportunities, but may increase code size and instruction-cache pressure.
        • A recursive function cannot simply be expanded without limit.
      • Virtual dispatch chooses an overridden method based on a receiver’s runtime class.
        • A common implementation uses a per-class virtual-method table and an object pointer to the table; the call loads the selected entry.
        • This is an implementation strategy, not a universal language requirement.
        • Name mangling distinguishes linker symbols, often for overloads; it is not itself runtime method selection.
        • Proven receiver types may permit devirtualization.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP39 Recovery and compiler-construction tools

      • Panic-mode recovery skips input until a synchronizing token such as ; or } permits parsing to resume.
        • Phrase-level recovery makes a local insertion/deletion.
        • Report the location and cause while avoiding cascades of misleading diagnostics.
        • Lexical, syntax and semantic phases each detect their own errors; error handling is a shared service.
      • Lex/flex generates scanners from patterns and actions.
        • Yacc means Yet Another Compiler Compiler; Yacc/Bison generates parsers from grammar rules and semantic actions.
        • Typical specification files have definitions, %% rules, and %% user code.
        • Classic Yacc uses LALR; Bison supports additional LR and generalized modes.
        • Scanner generation does not replace the CFG parser.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP40 Trace one expression through the compiler

      • For a=b+c*d;, the scanner recognizes names and operators, the parser forms an assignment with +(b,*(c,d)), and semantic analysis resolves declarations and operand/result types.
        • A declaration such as float a; int b,c,d; can require a conversion before storing the numeric result, according to language arithmetic rules.
      • Generate t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=convert_if_needed(t2).
        • Constant operands can fold; repeated unchanged expressions can share values.
        • Finally choose target instructions and registers.
        • The same spelling a can denote different declarations in nested scopes.
        • At each step ask what representation enters, what new information is added, and which errors can now be justified.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP41 Repair missing or conflated lexical answers

      • If a lexical-output question omits token stream, do not choose symbol table, AST or assembly as a substitute; some are side structures, not the primary output. “Smallest meaningful sequence” mixes the token-category and lexeme-text definitions unless the desired abstraction is specified.
        • Counting the loop header still gives 14, even if no option matches.
      • Grouping characters into token classes is lexical analysis; grouping tokens into expressions and statements is syntax analysis.
        • A vague stem saying “parsing into syntactic classes” needs to say which units it groups.
        • Symbol tables store identifiers and their attributes, not obligatorily every kind of token.
        • Trees store hierarchical constructs, while a symbol table stores declaration metadata.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP42 Repair parser questions with overlapping choices

      • Shift-reduce and LR are both bottom-up, so both answer a negative top-down question when offered separately.
        • Recursive and nonrecursive predictive parsers can both be efficient.
        • Nested parentheses and parsing tables do not uniquely identify LR.
        • Ambiguity does not disappear merely by choosing LR, and leftmost derivation is not an ambiguity-resolution policy.
      • The LL(1) conflict item offering A overlapping FIRST, B left recursion, C ambiguity, D A and B only is not a valid unique-choice question: C also rules out LL(1) for a useful grammar.
        • Ask for all applicable conditions or for a conflicting table cell.
        • Precedence versus operator-precedence parsing needs a concrete conflict and policy, not a blanket claim that every shift-reduce conflict has one solution.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP

    • COMP43 Repair semantic and translation claims

      • Type checking and symbol tables are both important to semantic analysis: one is an activity and one a data structure.
        • Semantic rules generally compute attributes, including but not limited to types, values and code; no listed specialized purpose is automatically exhaustive.
        • Both names and types belong in symbol records.
      • Division by zero, bounds violations, indentation mistakes and syntax errors are not a clean list of type errors; supply an incompatible operand example and a language.
        • Code generation is conventionally last in a simplified pipeline even if later target optimization exists.
        • A compiler may emit an annotated AST or typed IR, so distinguish representation, annotation and phase before forcing one tree name.
      • References: COMP_MOD, COMP_SHORT, COMP_DEEP
